As they debated whether this information about Lu Xun made him a cultural connoisseur to emulate or a leisured and thus hypocritical social critic, I realized that this literary gossip was about trying to figure out, via a reevaluation of a symbol like Lu Xun, their place in the national order of things.

在他所贬斥的那类艺术家的饭局上，矛盾依然浮现。他们聚集在一位画家翻新的公寓里，这套公寓刚被一本室内设计杂志报道。讨论过家居装饰原则、宜家在北京影响的好坏，以及出国参展签证的种种麻烦之后，话题转向知识分子在中国社会中的位置。一场关于鲁迅的争论爆发了。这位20世纪作家、社会批评家和左翼木刻运动倡导者备受尊崇，1936年去世后被中国共产党奉为经典。一位艺术家评论说，尽管他们近来积累了物质财富、追求文化修养，却远远比不上鲁迅的生活方式。他一直在读鲁迅日记，对其拥有的资源感到震惊。把鲁迅记载的收入换算成现代货币，他声称每月可达数万元。按他的判断，鲁迅大部分空闲时间都在买东西——书、画、古董，甚至旧四合院。其他人开玩笑说，鲁迅之所以成为如此尖刻的社会批评家，是因为他每天早上都在琉璃厂街与书画商和古董商讨价还价。因被坑了价钱而愤怒，他回家后用笔骂人。当他们争论这些关于鲁迅的信息究竟使他成为值得效仿的文化鉴赏家，还是一个有闲因而虚伪的社会批评家时，我意识到，这些文学八卦其实是在通过重新评价鲁迅这样的象征，弄清自己在国家秩序中的位置。


〔原书 52, 53〕

The images that many of these artists produced are cultural signs that point in different directions, a characteristic that emerges from and interrupts a Communist past. Tani Barlow observes, “All signs in a Maoist culture regime would, by definition, always have two potential referents. In theory, all national forms pointed backward to the national (and thus feudal) past and simultaneously forward to the bright potential of socialism. The Maoist framing of culture institutionalized this instability.”[^en-ch01-19] As Chinese contemporary artists wrangled with what it meant to be avant-garde, they continued to embrace the instability of the Maoist cultural sign, even as they worked in a space of encounter like that of Shi Xinning’s painting, where “avant-garde” sparks different chains of genealogical signification.

这些艺术家中的许多人创作的图像，是指向不同方向的文化符号；这一特征从共产主义过去中浮现，并打断那个过去。白露观察到：“在毛泽东主义文化体制中，按定义，所有符号总会有两个潜在的指涉对象。理论上，所有民族形式既向后指向民族的（因而也是封建的）过去，同时向前指向社会主义的光明潜能。毛泽东主义的文化框定使这种不稳定性制度化。”[^zh-ch01-19] 当中国当代艺术家争论前卫意味着什么时，他们继续拥抱毛泽东主义文化符号的不稳定性，即使他们是在像石心宁绘画那样的相遇空间中工作——在那里，“前卫”激发不同的谱系意指链条。


〔原书 53〕

The term’s French origins date to the nineteenth century, when it connoted a close association between culture and socialist politics. Baudelaire used it in the 1860s as a term of contempt for leftist writers. Renato Poggioli traces how, after the 1871 suppression of the Paris Commune, the term came to refer to a separate artistic movement. The avant-garde, in his description, maintained an autonomous but parallel existence with the political left. Its practitioners were bohemian iconoclasts devoted to innovation and futurity. Poggioli further argues that the avant-garde could only flourish in a liberal society: “Avant-garde art is by nature incapable of surviving not only the persecution but even the protection or the official patronage of a totalitarian state and a collective society, whereas the hostility of public opinion can be useful to it.”[^en-ch01-20] It thus depends on, even if through opposition to, free-market liberalism. Peter Bürger further argues that the embrace of the avant-garde by the very establishment institutions it opposed led to its death. When museums absorbed avant-garde art into a system complicit with capitalism, they neutralized its critical function.[^en-ch01-21]

这个词的法国起源可追溯至19世纪，当时它意味着文化与社会主义政治的紧密关联。波德莱尔在19世纪60年代用它来蔑视左翼作家。雷纳托·波焦利追溯了1871年巴黎公社被镇压后，这个词如何转变为指涉一个独立的艺术运动。在他笔下，前卫与政治左派保持自主但平行的存在。其实践者是献身创新与未来的波西米亚式偶像破坏者。波焦利进一步论证，前卫只能在自由社会中繁荣：“前卫艺术在本质上不仅无法在极权国家和集体社会的迫害下生存，甚至无法在其保护或官方赞助下生存，而舆论的敌意却可能对它有益。”[^zh-ch01-20] 因此，它依赖自由市场自由主义，哪怕是通过与之对立的方式。彼得·比尔格进一步论证，正是前卫所反对的建制机构对它的接纳导致了它的死亡。当博物馆把前卫艺术吸收进与资本主义同谋的体系，它们便中和了它的批判功能。[^zh-ch01-21]


〔原书 53〕

“Avant-garde” entered Chinese through neologisms produced by early-twentieth-century translations of French, Japanese, and Russian sources. Chinese intellectuals working under the conditions of semicolonialism produced an era of furious translingual practice, as they brought concepts from foreign sources to bear on their struggle for national sovereignty. Art and politics in this context could not be understood as separate, as Gao Minglu argues in his theorization of China’s “total modernity,” marking its cultural and historical difference from the autonomous conception of the avant-garde in the West.[^en-ch01-22]

“Avant-garde”经由20世纪初从法文、日文和俄文来源翻译中产生的新词进入中文。在半殖民主义条件下工作的中国知识分子，经历了狂热的跨语言实践时代，他们引入外来概念，以服务于争取民族主权的斗争。在这种语境中，艺术与政治不能理解为彼此分离，正如高名潞在关于中国“总体现代性”的理论化中所论证的，中国与西方前卫的自主观念之间存在着文化和历史差异。[^zh-ch01-22]


〔原书 53, 54〕

An early use of the term appears in Lin Wenzheng’s review of the first *Capital Fine Arts Exhibition*, held in Nanjing in 1928. He praises the work by several artists as “the avant-garde [*qianfeng*] of modern China’s art world,” and advocates an art of the people, supported by public institutions, that will raise their spiritual consciousness and national sensibility to a level equivalent with European society.[^en-ch01-23] In Japan, the term appeared in formations such as Sasaki Takamaru’s Avant-Garde Theater and Kurahara Korehito’s Alliance of Avant-Garde Artists. Chinese dramatist Tian Han met both during his 1927 visit to Tokyo, during which Sasaki warned him against the empty rhetoric of artistic autonomy.[^en-ch01-24] Kurahara had recently returned from the Soviet Union and became the leading Marxist theoretician during the Japanese proletarian art movement of the late 1920s and early 1930s. The kanji they used for avant-garde traveled back to China as qianwei.[^en-ch01-25]

这个词的早期使用出现在林文铮对1928年在南京举办的首届首都美术展览会的评论中。他称赞几位艺术家的作品是“中国现代艺术界的前卫（qianfeng）”，并倡导一种由公共机构支持的人民艺术，以把他们的精神意识和民族感受力提升到与欧洲社会相当的水平。[^zh-ch01-23] 在日本，这个词出现于佐佐木孝丸的《前卫剧场》和藏原惟人的“前卫艺术家同盟”等组合中。中国剧作家田汉1927年访问东京时见过两人，佐佐木警告他不要空谈艺术自主。[^zh-ch01-24] 藏原惟人最近从苏联归来，成为20世纪20年代末和30年代初日本无产阶级艺术运动的主要马克思主义理论家。他们用于“avant-garde”的汉字传回中国，成为“前卫”。[^zh-ch01-25]


〔原书 54〕

Other versions emerged in usages by the Guomindang, as well as by critics like Lu Xun. In 1930, the Guomindang government promoted a nationalist literary movement to counter the rise of revolutionary literature. New journals such as *Qianfeng zhoubao* (Avant-garde weekly) and *Qianfeng yuebao* (Avant-garde monthly) published patriotic stories featuring heroic battle scenes. Lu Xun attacked one of these writers for his comparison of Chinese nationalists fighting warlords with French colonists fighting native Arabs in the African desert, as a telling identification with imperial masters.[^en-ch01-26] One year later, he published a commemorative issue of the underground magazine *Qianshao* (Vanguard or Frontline) mourning the Guomindang execution of five left-wing writers. Through his support of the 1930s woodcut movement, Lu Xun advocated an avant-garde aesthetic that publicly called for a collective political struggle. After the Communist defeat of the Guomindang in 1949, the party codified this association in its claim to be the vanguard (xianfeng) of the proletariat, a term that in 1989 would be resignified once again by Chinese art world participants, through and in relation to previous histories.

国民党以及鲁迅等批评家的用法中，也出现了其他版本。1930年，国民党政府推动一场民族主义文学运动，以对抗革命文学的兴起。《先锋周报》（Qianfeng zhoubao）和《先锋月刊》（Qianfeng yuebao）等新刊物发表描写英雄战斗场面的爱国故事。鲁迅抨击其中一位作家把与军阀作战的中国民族主义者比作在非洲沙漠中与土著阿拉伯人作战的法国殖民者，认为这暴露了其对帝国主子的认同。[^zh-ch01-26] 一年后，他在地下刊物《前哨》（Qianshao，意为 Vanguard 或 Frontline）出版纪念专号，哀悼被国民党处决的五位左翼作家。通过支持20世纪30年代木刻运动，鲁迅倡导一种公开呼吁集体政治斗争的前卫美学。1949年共产党击败国民党后，党把这种联系编入其作为无产阶级先锋队（xianfeng）的主张；这个术语在1989年又被中国艺术界参与者通过并与先前历史相关联地再次重新意指。


〔原书 54〕

In her critique of modernist art discourse, Rosalind Krauss argues that the notion of the avant-garde depends on a discourse of originality, even though “the actual practice of vanguard art tends to reveal that ‘originality’ is a working assumption that itself emerges from a ground of repetition and recurrence.”[^en-ch01-27] Promoters of Western modernism as an advancing force produce the avant-garde doctrine of newness, in part, by casting artists from other parts of the world as belated and derivative, closing off a history of the Western canon as itself a series of borrowings.[^en-ch01-28] The rise of artistic modernism coincided with a period of rapid decolonization when European powers established legal agreements such as the Berne Convention to protect their ownership of works developed in colonial contexts and through non-Western influences.[^en-ch01-29] Modern intellectual property regimes define and protect innovation, granting individual creators rights vis-à-vis the nation-state. The repressions of avant-gardism are deeply linked to the development of the modern militant nation-state and ideologies of surpassing. Introducing gender into the picture makes the act of deconstruction even more imperative.

罗莎琳德·克劳斯在批判现代主义艺术话语时论证，前卫观念依赖原创性话语，尽管“前卫艺术的实际实践往往揭示出，‘原创性’本身是一个从重复与再现的土壤中浮现的工作假设”。[^zh-ch01-27] 把西方现代主义作为进步力量加以推广的人，部分通过把世界其他地区的艺术家塑造成迟到的、派生的，来生产前卫的新颖教义，同时封闭西方正典自身作为一系列借鉴的历史。[^zh-ch01-28] 艺术现代主义的兴起恰逢快速去殖民化时期，欧洲列强建立伯尔尼公约等法律协议，以保护它们对在殖民语境中、通过非西方影响发展出的作品的所有权。[^zh-ch01-29] 现代知识产权制度界定并保护创新，赋予个体创作者相对于民族国家的权利。前卫主义的压制与现代战斗性民族国家和超越意识形态的发展深刻相连。把性别引入图景，使解构行动更加迫切。


〔原书 55〕

In *Take Hold of the Brush, Struggle to the End* (1997; plate 3), Wang Qingsong reworks a widely circulated propaganda poster from the end of the Cultural Revolution (plate 4). Xiao Zhenya and Liu Enbin’s work reproduces in the background a well-known 1972 portrait of Lu Xun by Tang Xiaoming, *Never Give Up the Struggle*. The two lines of calligraphy on the right are a couplet from a poem by Lu Xun: “Fierce-browed, I coolly defy a thousand pointing fingers, / Head bowed, like a willing ox I serve the children.” In 1942, Mao Zedong ended his talks on art and literature at the Communist guerrilla base in Yan’an with this couplet. The talks, which came to serve as party doctrine, compelled cultural workers to “enter life” (*shenru shenghuo*), meaning that of workers and peasants, to learn from the people in order to create revolutionary, consciousness-raising works. Mao’s thinking reversed the Marxist understanding of culture as superstructure reflecting the economic base and instead envisaged culture as leading the base. He interpreted Lu Xun’s couplet in the following way: “The ‘thousand pointing fingers’ are our enemies, and we will never yield to them, no matter how ferocious. The ‘children’ here symbolize the proletariat and the masses. All Communists, all revolutionaries, all revolutionary literary and art workers should learn from the example of Lu Xun and be ‘oxen’ for the proletariat and the masses, bending their backs to the task until their dying day.”[^en-ch01-30] With this history as backdrop, a female young pioneer (a member of the shaonian xianfeng dui) stands with a calligraphy brush poised over a blank sheet of paper. In 1958, Mao had exhorted the nation’s citizens to use calligraphy to express their demands through big-character posters: “Apart from their other characteristics, the outstanding thing about China’s 600 million people is that they are ‘poor and blank.’ This may seem a bad thing, but in reality it is a good thing. Poverty gives rise to the desire for change, the desire for action and the desire for revolution. On a blank sheet of paper free from any mark, the freshest and most beautiful characters can be written, the freshest and most beautiful pictures can be painted.”[^en-ch01-31] In 1974, Xiao and Liu’s poster advocated a leftist line that upheld calligraphy over the practice of romanizing Chinese, seen as subservient to the West. Their inclusion of Lu Xun as a historical force overseeing a yet unwritten future also presents an incongruence, since he had proposed abandoning characters for an alphabet.[^en-ch01-32]

在《拿起笔，战斗到底》（1997；图版3）中，王庆松改写了文革末期广泛流传的一张宣传画（图版4）。Xiao Zhenya与Liu Enbin的作品在背景中复现了汤小铭1972年为鲁迅所作的名画《永不休战》。右侧两行书法是鲁迅一首诗中的对联：“横眉冷对千夫指，俯首甘为孺子牛。”1942年，毛泽东在延安共产党游击根据地的文艺座谈会讲话末尾引用了这副对联。那次讲话后来成为党的方针，要求文化工作者“深入生活”（shenru shenghuo），即深入工农生活，向人民学习，以创作革命的、提高觉悟的作品。毛泽东的思想颠倒了马克思主义关于文化是反映经济基础的上层建筑的理解，转而把文化设想为引领基础。他对鲁迅这副对联的解释是：“‘千夫指’，就是敌人，无论多么凶恶，我们绝不屈服。这里的‘孺子’，是指无产阶级和人民大众。一切共产党员，一切革命家，一切革命的文艺工作者，都应该学鲁迅的榜样，做无产阶级和人民大众的‘牛’，鞠躬尽瘁，死而后已。”[^zh-ch01-30] 以这段历史为背景，一位女少先队员（少年先锋队成员）站在一张空白纸前，手持毛笔。1958年，毛泽东曾号召全国人民用书法写大字报表达诉求：“除了其他特点之外，中国六亿人口的一个显著特点是一‘穷’二‘白’。这看起来是坏事，其实是好事。穷则思变，要干，要革命。一张白纸，没有负担，好写最新最美的文字，好画最新最美的画图。”[^zh-ch01-31] 1974年，Xiao与Liu的宣传画倡导一条坚持书法、反对汉字拉丁化的左倾路线，因为拉丁化被视为屈从西方。他们把鲁迅作为俯瞰一个尚未书写的未来的历史力量，也造成某种不协调，因为鲁迅曾提议废除汉字改用字母。[^zh-ch01-32]


〔原书 55, 56〕

In Wang Qingsong’s 1997 restaging of the poster, one of his earliest experiments in conceptual photography, the artist himself replaces the “red, bright, and shining” girl. A male entrepreneurial subject represents the new vanguard poised to compete on the international cultural market. His raised hand holds an oil painting brush, the tool that facilitated his entry into that market. While he remains caught in the middle ground of the picture plane, the future before him is no longer “poor and blank” but filled with cultural trappings of wealth: traditional gold ingots symbolizing prosperity, preparatory textbooks for the national university entrance exam, and a fan of foreign currency. In place of Mao’s little red book in the lower left-hand corner lies a thin publication. Wang’s reworked version of the poster appears on the cover, harking back to the ubiquity of Cultural Revolution propaganda while also alluding to the artist’s image as a form of currency that enables the spatiotemporal extension of his personhood, a sign of having entered the world. Incongruous now is the Lu Xun couplet, which begs the question of what the “thousand pointing fingers,” the “children,” and the “oxen” symbolize in the current era.

在王庆松1997年对这张宣传画的重新摆拍中——他最早的概念摄影实验之一——艺术家本人取代了“红、光、亮”的女孩。一个男性创业主体代表准备在国际文化市场角逐的新先锋。他举起的手握着油画笔，那是帮助他进入这一市场的工具。虽然他仍被困在画面的中景，他面前的未来不再是“一穷二白”，而是充满财富的文化装饰：象征兴旺的传统金元宝、高考复习教材，以及呈扇形展开的外币。左下角毛泽东的小红书不见了，取而代之的是一本薄薄的出版物。王庆松改写的宣传画出现在封面上，既回顾文革宣传画的无处不在，也暗示艺术家的形象作为一种货币，使他的人格性得以跨时空延展，成为进入世界的标志。如今不协调的是鲁迅的对联，它引出这样的问题：在当今时代，“千夫指”“孺子”和“牛”究竟象征什么。


〔原书 56, 57〕

In visual exchanges over space and time, Chinese contemporary artists negotiated different systems of artistic evaluation. They complained about intermittent Chinese state cultural control, but also their management by Western gallerists. Wang Qingsong, for example, worked as an oil painter until 1997 and was represented by a London gallery specializing in Chinese contemporary art. A series of his paintings titled *Speechless*, depicting distorted faces and bodies trapped in plastic sheets, sold well to their clientele. When he informed the gallery managers of his plan to move into conceptual photography, they advised him to stick with his established style of painting, which guaranteed a predictable return value. Surprised by this lack of support for creative innovation, he began to question the purported freedom of the market system.[^en-ch01-33] On the other side of the equation, Western gallerists complained that Chinese artists undermined themselves by not following established market rules. They alluded to instances of artists placing their work with more than one gallery, selling work directly out of their studios, or printing additional images on demand of what they once claimed was a limited run.[^en-ch01-34] At a 2002 symposium at the Asia Society in New York, a major collector announced that Chinese contemporary art had lost its international allure because Chinese artists had failed to fully embrace the dealer system.[^en-ch01-35] Curators affiliated with Western museums described the difficulty of convincing their boards to acquire Chinese artwork without a gallery to guarantee its limited edition status. This discourse characterized Chinese artists as market primitives. Yet as these artists experimented with the international market, they sent into the world images haunted by temporalities forged in previous cultural encounters. Their failure to conform could also be understood as a critique of how Western institutions confer value on art; or of the Chinese state’s narrative of global capitalism as the desired future of Maoist socialism.

在跨越时空的视觉交换中，中国当代艺术家协商不同的艺术评价体系。他们抱怨国家间歇性的文化控制，也抱怨西方画廊经营者的管理。例如，王庆松直到1997年都是油画家，由伦敦一家专营中国当代艺术的画廊代理。他题为《无语》的系列油画描绘扭曲的面孔和被困在塑料布中的身体，在客户中销路很好。当他告诉画廊管理者自己计划转向概念摄影时，他们建议他坚持已经确立的绘画风格，因为那能保证可预测的回报。这种对创意创新的不支持令他惊讶，他开始质疑市场体系所谓的自由。[^zh-ch01-33] 在等式的另一端，西方画廊经营者抱怨中国艺术家不遵守既定市场规则，因而损害自身。他们提到一些例子：艺术家同时与多家画廊合作，直接从画室卖作品，或按需求为原称限量的作品加印图像。[^zh-ch01-34] 在2002年纽约亚洲协会的一次研讨会上，一位重要收藏家宣称，中国当代艺术已失去国际吸引力，因为中国艺术家未能完全接受经销商制度。[^zh-ch01-35] 与西方博物馆有关联的策展人描述了说服董事会购藏中国艺术品的困难，因为没有画廊能保证其限量身份。这套话语把中国艺术家说成市场原始人。然而，当这些艺术家在国际市场上实验时，他们送入世界的图像，萦绕着在先前文化相遇中锻造的时间性。他们不遵从的行为，也可以被理解为对西方机构如何赋予艺术价值的批判，或对国家把全球资本主义叙述为毛泽东主义社会主义理想未来的批判。


〔原书 57〕

Placing these *Take Hold of the Brush* images, produced two decades apart, alongside each other creates a stereoscopic vision that cuts into historical shadows. It makes visible a disappearing act, in which the female artist whose command of the brush once symbolized national progress vanishes from the scene. No longer pictured as vanguard producer of images, she has become instead the soft-glow cover girl of a masculinist avant-garde preoccupied with its place in the nation and the world. The girl with the brush was once a stock image of socialist liberation; a return to her early appearance reveals the persistent presence of a patriarchal figure hovering in the background. In Wang Huaiqing’s 1964 woodblock print *Revolution*, a young girl sits at a table, pencil in hand. An older man in military uniform sits behind her, folds his hand over hers, and guides the pencil to write *geming* (revolution) on the sheet of paper before them. If the woodblock movement of the early twentieth century represents, as Tang Xiaobing argues, the origins of the Chinese avant-garde, the gendered evolution of its imagery in the post-1989 encounter with Western ideologies of the avant-garde disappears women. The repressive effects of this collusion include a hidden aspect of the *China/Avant-Garde* exhibit that came to light years after the fact.

把相隔二十年产生的这些《拿起笔，战斗到底》图像并置，创造了一种切入历史阴影的立体视觉。它使一场消失术变得可见：那位曾以笔墨象征国家进步的女性艺术家从场景中消失了。她不再被表现为图像的前卫生产者，而成了男性主义前卫的柔光封面女郎——这个前卫正专注于自己在民族与世界中的位置。拿笔的女孩曾是社会主义解放的标准图像；回到她早期的形象，会揭示一个徘徊在背景中的父权人物的持续在场。在王怀庆1964年版画《革命》中，一个小女孩坐在桌边，手握铅笔。一位穿军装的年长男子坐在她身后，把她的手拢在自己手中，引导铅笔在面前的纸上写下“革命”（geming）。如果唐小兵所论成立——20世纪初的木刻运动代表中国前卫的起源——那么其图像在1989年后与西方前卫意识形态相遇时的性别化演变，则使女性消失。这种合谋的压制效果之一，是中国现代艺术展多年后才为人所知的一面。


〔原书 57, 58, 59〕

All historical accounts of that seminal 1989 moment mention Xiao Lu’s installation piece *Dialogue*, which she fired into, causing the exhibit’s first closure. Some even retrospectively called it “the first shots of Tiananmen.”[^en-ch01-36] All of these accounts name Tang Song, a classmate present at the time and arrested together with Xiao, as cocreator of the work. This version of history dominated, to the exclusion of a nuanced interpretation of a piece dealing so obviously with gender relations. Two public telephone booths stand several feet apart. The black-and-white image of a woman’s back appears in one, with that of a male counterpart in the other. Receivers pressed to their ears, they seem engaged in dialogue. On a white plinth between the booths rests a red telephone, whose receiver dangles from its cord over the side. A mirror the size and shape of the booths is positioned behind the telephone, with the lines of a red cross dividing it like a windowpane. This became the target that Xiao Lu stood before and fired into. Tang Song never denied the attribution of authorship he was granted, and he and Xiao became a couple after the incident, spending years together in Australia. After their break up and Xiao’s return to China in 1997, she attempted to reclaim authorship of the piece, only to meet with general art world disdain and dismissal. She responded by creating *Fifteen Shots: 1989–2003* (figure 1.04), which consists of fifteen panels, one for each of the intervening years. Life-size photographs of her grimly taking aim fade in a progression from dark intensity to washed-out grays. At a Beijing shooting range, she fired through each glass-covered panel. The bullet holes inflicted on her own image mark her injury as well as her reassertion of agency in the scene. Xiao also wrote an autobiographical novel titled *Dialogue*, which provides a different history for the piece. She had grown up the well-connected daughter of respected socialist realist artists. Her father became the president of Hangzhou’s China Academy of Art. As a teenager she attended the attached high school of Beijing’s Central Academy of Fine Arts. During her senior year, she endured sexual abuse by one of her parents’ best friends, a painter her father had studied with in the Soviet Union, into whose care they had entrusted her. Xiao writes that before his final violation, he stood over the bed where she lay and said, “I’d like to paint a nude portrait of you.”[^en-ch01-37] Her controversial shots intended to shatter this personal but also institutional art history. Her arrest-worthy offence represented not just a rebellion against academic style but against patriarchal power perpetuated by the academy system.

所有关于1989年那个开创性时刻的历史叙述，都会提到肖鲁的装置《对话》；她向作品开枪，导致展览首次关闭。一些叙述甚至事后称之为“天安门的第一枪”。[^zh-ch01-36] 所有这些叙述都把当时在场、与肖鲁一同被捕的同学唐宋列为作品共同创作者。这一版本的历史占据主导，排除了对一件如此明显涉及性别关系的作品作细致解读的可能。两个公共电话亭相隔数英尺。一个电话亭里出现一个女人背影的黑白图像，另一个里是男性对应者。他们把听筒贴在耳边，似乎正在对话。两个电话亭之间的白色基座上放着一部红色电话，听筒从电话线垂在边缘外。电话后面立着一面与电话亭同样大小和形状的镜子，红十字把镜面分成窗格状。这成为肖鲁站到面前开枪的目标。唐宋从未否认被赋予的作者身份；事件后他和肖鲁成为情侣，一起在澳大利亚生活多年。他们分手、肖鲁1997年回国后，她试图重新主张这件作品的作者身份，却遭遇艺术界普遍的轻蔑与否定。她以《十五枪：1989—2003》回应（图1.04），作品由十五块画板组成，对应其间的每一年。她神情凝重地瞄准的原尺寸照片，从幽暗浓烈逐渐褪淡为灰白。在北京一家射击场，她向每块玻璃覆盖的画板开枪。射在自己形象上的弹孔，标记她的创伤，也标记她重新主张能动性。肖鲁还写了一部题为《对话》的自传体小说，为这件作品提供了另一种历史。她成长于人脉广泛的家庭，父母都是受尊敬的社会主义现实主义艺术家。父亲后来成为杭州中国美术学院院长。十几岁时，她进入中央美术学院附中。高三那年，她遭到父母一位挚友的性侵。那是一位画家，父亲曾在苏联与他同学，父母把她托付给他照看。肖鲁写道，在他最后一次侵犯之前，他站在她躺着的床边说：“我想给你画一幅裸体肖像。”[^zh-ch01-37] 她那几声引发争议的枪响，意在击碎这段既是个人也是制度性的艺术史。她足以被捕的罪行，不仅是对学院风格的反叛，也是对学院制度延续的父权权力的反叛。


〔原书 58〕

![图1.04　肖鲁，《十五枪：1989—2003》（局部），2003年10月19日。十五张带框照片（每张100厘米×45厘米），十五颗子弹。艺术家惠允。](web/assets/ch01-b032.jpg)

FIG 1.04 Xiao Lu, *Fifteen Shots: 1989–2003* (detail), October 19, 2003. Fifteen framed photographs (each 100 cm × 45 cm), fifteen bullets. Courtesy of the artist.

图1.04　肖鲁，《十五枪：1989—2003》（局部），2003年10月19日。十五张带框照片（每张100厘米×45厘米），十五颗子弹。艺术家惠允。


〔原书 59〕

Academy

学院


〔原书 59〕

Although a number of private art schools existed in early twentieth-century China, including several focused on female education, the Shanghai Art School is often credited as China’s first modern art academy.[^en-ch01-38] Founded in 1912 as a response to a new market for commercial art, it offered tutorials in Western painting, photography, and copperplate art.[^en-ch01-39] The young oil painter Liu Haisu, who signed his work “Art Renegade,” became its most famous teacher. He adopted the Western technique of painting from a nude studio model or from nature *en plein air*. His defense of nude figure painting as essential to modern art education drew ongoing criticism. Accused of corrupting Chinese morality, he resisted personal attacks and bans on the practice.[^en-ch01-40] During the May Fourth Movement (1917–21), when Chinese reformers upheld science, democracy, new culture, and women’s emancipation as the path to modern nationhood, the school’s situation stabilized.[^en-ch01-41] By 1919, it received government funding and became integrated in an emerging system of national art academies that included the China Academy of Art, founded in 1928, and culminated in the 1950 establishment of the Central Academy of Fine Arts (cafa) in Beijing.[^en-ch01-42]

尽管20世纪初中国已存在若干私立美术学校，其中包括几所专注女子教育的学校，上海美术专科学校仍常被称为中国第一所现代美术院校。[^zh-ch01-38] 它创办于1912年，回应商业美术的新市场，开设西画、摄影和铜版画课程。[^zh-ch01-39] 年轻的油画家刘海粟在作品上署名“艺术叛徒”，成为该校最著名的教师。他采用画室裸体模特和户外写生的西方技法。他为裸体人物画作为现代美术教育之必需所作的辩护，招来持续批评。被指败坏中国道德，他顶住人身攻击和对这种做法的禁令。[^zh-ch01-40] 五四运动（1917—1921）期间，中国改革者把科学、民主、新文化和妇女解放奉为现代民族国家之路，学校的处境稳定下来。[^zh-ch01-41] 到1919年，它获得政府资助，并融入一个正在形成的国立美术院校体系，其中包括1928年创办的国立艺术院，最终以1950年在北京成立的中央美术学院告成。[^zh-ch01-42]


〔原书 59〕

In 2000, a graduate from the cafa oil painting department drew a chart for me of what she considered the three main groups involved in contemporary art production: (1) those from the *huangjia* (imperial family), artists who had trained in China’s national academies, especially cafa, and continued to benefit from these connections; (2) qianwei (avant-garde) artists who went through the academy system but then produced experimental works that departed significantly from the styles of their training; and (3) *waidi* (outside) artists who migrated to urban art centers and tried to make a name for themselves. An art history graduate student at the Sichuan Fine Arts Institute produced a more rigid mapping for me: those inside the system (*tizhi nei*) and those outside the system (*tizhi wai*). “The system” included the eight main national art academies and the Chinese Artists Association. She characterized those inside the system as having social position, stability, and the security to pursue their art. In her view, those outside it felt unrecognized by Chinese society and had to appeal to foreigners for acceptance.

2000年，一位中央美术学院油画系毕业生给我画了一张图，列出她认为参与当代艺术生产的三个主要群体：（1）“皇家”（huangjia），指在中国国立美术院校、尤其是中央美院受训，并继续从这些关系中获益的艺术家；（2）“前卫”（qianwei），指经历学院体系、但后来创作显著偏离所受训练风格的实验作品的艺术家；（3）“外地”（waidi），指迁入城市艺术中心、努力闯出名声的艺术家。四川美术学院一位艺术史研究生给我画了一张更僵硬的地图：体制内（tizhi nei）与体制外（tizhi wai）。“体制”包括八所主要国立美术院校和中国美术家协会。她把体制内描述为拥有社会地位、稳定性和追求艺术的保障。在她看来，体制外的人感到不被中国社会承认，必须求诸外国人获得认可。


〔原书 60〕

Most of the artists I met were well trained in the types of drawing and painting—referred to by some as *men piao* (admissions tickets)—required in the rigorous art academy entrance examination. Prospective students gathered each year at testing centers around the country for several days. They jockeyed in crowded classrooms for the best angle and completed exercises in still life, figure drawing, charcoal and watercolor technique, and creative expression. This emphasis on technical facility reveals the influence of European pedagogy, brought back by Chinese overseas students and transmitted by Soviet advisors. Rigorous testing through set, timed exercises was a hallmark of France’s nineteenth-century École des Beaux-Arts, itself modeled after the first Western art academy, established in 1563 in Florence.[^en-ch01-43]

我遇到的大多数艺术家，在严格美术院校入学考试所要求的素描和绘画类型上都受过良好训练——有人称之为“门票”（men piao）。每年，考生聚集在全国各地考点，连续数日应考。他们在拥挤的教室里争抢最佳角度，完成静物、人物写生、炭笔与水彩技法以及创意表现等题目。这种对技术熟练度的强调，显示出欧洲教育学的影响——它由中国留学生带回，又经苏联顾问传播。通过固定、限时的练习进行严格测试，是法国19世纪巴黎国立高等美术学院的标志，而该学院本身以1563年佛罗伦萨创办的西方第一所美术学院为范本。[^zh-ch01-43]


〔原书 60〕

Chinese visual arts curricula combined this Euro-Soviet academic tradition with Maoist practices, such as the adaptation of open-air painting to the socialist dictum of art for and of the people. During summer *shixi* (practicum) trips, art students shenru shenghuo (entered life) in rural locations. Their sketches and paintings focused on landscapes, traditional architecture, or local people. In the reform era, as domestic tourism replaced the political mandate to go “down to the countryside,” many teachers and students talked to me about these trips with excitement, which allowed them to visit historic cultural sites, such as the Dunhuang caves.[^en-ch01-44] Favored locations for these trips, usually arranged by the teacher assigned to accompany the students, included the northwest and southwest, hinterland areas that were also often ethnic minority regions.

中国视觉艺术课程把这一欧苏学院传统与毛泽东主义实践结合起来，例如把户外写生改造为“艺术为人民、属于人民”的社会主义箴言。在夏季实习（shixi）期间，美术学生到农村“深入生活”（shenru shenghuo）。他们的速写和绘画聚焦风景、传统建筑或当地人。改革时代，随着国内旅游取代“下乡”的政治任务，许多师生兴奋地向我谈起这些实习，它们让他们得以参观敦煌石窟等历史文化遗址。[^zh-ch01-44] 这些行程通常由陪同学生的教师安排，青睐的地点包括西北和西南的内陆地区，那里也常是少数民族地区。


〔原书 60〕

I learned about Chinese art education by spending time in classrooms, ranging from elementary to university level. For several weeks in 2001, I drew alongside students in classes taught by Li Tianpian and He Chengyao, two of the artists I write about in part III: Feminist Sight Lines. Li Tianpian was a member of the painting faculty at Beijing’s Central Minorities University, the top-tier institution for students belonging to China’s fifty-five officially recognized ethnic minorities (*xiaoshu minzu*). Like Xiao Lu, she had tested as a teenager into the high school attached to cafa. She studied there for three years before attending the China Academy of Art in Hangzhou, where she received bachelor’s and master’s degrees in oil painting. Two years into her teaching position, she moved around her classroom of wooden easels and painting props with assurance, instructing models on poses, looking over the shoulders of her students, and occasionally picking up a brush to give instruction by adding marks to their canvases.

我通过在不同课堂——从小学到大学——中度过时间来了解中国美术教育。2001年，我有几周在李天翩和何成瑶教的班里与学生一起画画；她们是我在第三部分“女性主义视线”中要写的两位艺术家。李天翩是中央民族大学绘画系教师，该校是中国55个官方认定少数民族（xiaoshu minzu）学生的顶尖学府。像肖鲁一样，她十几岁时考入中央美院附中，在那里学习三年，之后进入杭州中国美术学院，获得油画学士和硕士学位。任教两年后，她在摆满木画架和绘画道具的教室里自信地走动，指导模特摆姿势，从学生肩后查看，偶尔拿起画笔在他们的画布上添几笔示范。


〔原书 61〕

He Chengyao, a graduate of the Sichuan Fine Arts Institute in Chong-qing, had come to Beijing to take a course in contemporary art offered at cafa for the first time in 2001. To help cover expenses, she picked up several temporary jobs, including teaching a figure drawing class to vocational school teachers required to refresh their skills every few years. Gathering on weekend mornings in a chilly, anonymous classroom, the students respected He Chengyao’s academy credentials and eagerly asked her to correct their drawings. Although trained as an oil painter, she had begun experimenting with performance art, and her use of her own nude body had drawn criticism from many quarters. She confided in me that she wanted to share this work with her students but feared what most of them would think. Instead, she gently refused to draw on top of their work and urged them to explore their own styles of expression. To their disbelief, she held up my loose, untutored drawing of the head of David as an example.

何成瑶毕业于重庆四川美术学院，2001年来北京参加中央美院首次开设的当代艺术课程。为补贴开销，她接了几份临时工作，包括给需要定期进修的职业学校教师上人物素描课。周末早晨，学生们聚在一间寒冷、没有特征的教室里，尊重何成瑶的学院资历，热切地请她修改自己的素描。她虽受油画训练，却已开始实验行为艺术，而她使用自己裸体的做法招来各方批评。她私下对我说，她想和学生分享这些作品，却害怕大多数人会怎么想。因此，她没有在他们的作品上动笔，而是温和地拒绝，并鼓励他们探索自己的表达风格。令他们难以置信的是，她举起我那幅松散、未经训练的大卫头像画作为例子。


〔原书 61〕

In He Chengyao’s class, I practiced the academic tradition of drawing from plaster casts. Students began by copying print reproductions of famous classical sculptures, before moving on to drawing from plaster casts of them. Only after mastering this skill could they advance to drawing from a live model. Almost every Chinese art classroom I visited had a plaster head of Michelangelo’s *David*. My first attempt to draw it led me to realize the limitations of my life drawing classes in the United States, which had emphasized the gestural quality of line over precise, three-dimensional rendering of volume, light, and shadow. Many Chinese students complained about the rigidity of academic training but respected those who had mastered its rigors. During an interview, a cafa student who worked mainly in conceptual photography surprised me by talking about an artist who had graduated several years earlier. She admired her, not for the success she had achieved in China and abroad as an oil painter, but for her student-era plaster cast drawings. She exclaimed, “Her sketch of the head of David is still legendary among cafa students!” [^en-ch01-45]

在何成瑶的课上，我练习从石膏像写生的学院传统。学生们先临摹古典名雕的印刷复制品，再转向石膏像写生。掌握这项技能后，他们才能进到真人模特写生。我参观的几乎每间中国美术教室都有一尊米开朗琪罗《大卫》的石膏头像。我第一次尝试画它时，意识到自己在美国的人体写生课的局限：那些课强调线条的姿态性，而非精确的三维体积、光线与阴影表现。许多中国学生抱怨学院训练的僵化，却尊重那些掌握其严苛要求的人。在一次访谈中，一位主要从事概念摄影的中央美院学生让我惊讶地谈起几年前毕业的一位艺术家。她钦佩她，不是因为她在国内外作为油画家取得的成功，而是因为她学生时代的石膏像素描。她感叹道：“她画的大卫头像在中央美院学生中至今仍是传奇！”[^zh-ch01-45]


〔原书 61, 62〕

When I first visited cafa in 2001 at its new Wangjing location, northeast of Beijing’s fourth ring road, the foreign affairs officer gave me a tour. One highlight was an exhibit hall of full-size plaster casts of sculptures by Renaissance masters. Xu Beihong, the first president of cafa, brought back a set of plaster casts when he returned to China from France. I was told that all casts later used in China for teaching were copied from these “originals.” I also received a set of eight commemorative photographs depicting key moments in cafa’s history. One shows a 1960 lecture in the oil painting department (figure 1.05). Students and teachers face a plaster cast of Michelangelo’s *Rebellious Slave*. The figure twists, straining to break from chains binding his hands behind his back, a metaphor in China for revolutionary nationalism. Below a big character slogan imploring students to “work hard,” the instructor stands before an anatomical chart showing the muscular and skeletal structure of the figure’s posture. The only woman in the room sits hunched over, recording the lecture in a notebook.[^en-ch01-46]

2001年，我第一次参观中央美院位于北京四环路东北的新望京校区，外事处官员带我参观。一个亮点是文艺复兴大师雕塑原尺寸石膏像的展厅。中央美院首任院长徐悲鸿从法国回国时带回一套石膏像。我听说，后来中国用于教学的所有石膏像都从这些“原件”复制而来。我还收到一套八张纪念照片，描绘中央美院历史上的关键时刻。其中一张展示1960年油画系的一次授课（图1.05）。师生面对米开朗琪罗《反抗的奴隶》的石膏像。人物扭曲身体，竭力挣脱反绑双手的锁链——在中国，这是革命民族主义的隐喻。在勉励学生“努力”的大字标语下方，教师站在一张解剖图前，图上显示人物姿态的肌肉与骨骼结构。教室里唯一一位女性弓着背，把讲课记在笔记本上。[^zh-ch01-46]


〔原书 62〕

![图1.05　中央美术学院油画系素描课，1960年。1998年为纪念建院八十周年而复制于一套纪念照片中。](web/assets/ch01-b042.jpg)

FIG 1.05 Drawing lecture in the Central Academy of Fine Arts oil painting department, 1960. Reproduced in 1998 for a commemorative set of photographs marking the eightieth anniversary of the academy’s founding.

图1.05　中央美术学院油画系素描课，1960年。1998年为纪念建院八十周年而复制于一套纪念照片中。


〔原书 62, 63〕

cafa’s original location near Tiananmen Square drew its students into another lesson in sculpture’s political uses. Foreign coverage of the “Goddess of Democracy,” which appeared in the Square on May 30, 1989, reported it to be a replica of the Statue of Liberty. It can also be read as a multilayered history of Chinese art academy practice.[^en-ch01-47] When cafa sculpture students agreed to a request from protesting students to replicate the iconic statue, they had to work quickly to complete it. They constructed a model from a preexisting clay sculpture of a man grasping a pole with two raised hands, an academic study done by one of the sculpture department’s studio collectives. They cut off the lower part of the pole and added a torch on top. They changed the figure from a man to a woman, modeling the face after the female figure in Soviet sculptor Vera Mukhina’s *A Worker and Collective Farm Woman*, which stood atop the Soviet Pavilion at the 1937 Paris World’s Fair. With this altered clay figure as their model, they enlarged it, carving and wiring together blocks of styrofoam, then coating them with plaster. The ten-meter-high statue, which stood for five days opposite the portrait of Mao Zedong, combines political symbols from opposite sides of the Cold War. Liberty gazed over the tumultuous square with the face of Collective Farm Woman. In Mukhina’s original, she holds the Communist sickle in her raised arm.

中央美院在天安门广场附近的原址，让学生们上了另一堂关于雕塑政治用途的课。外国媒体对1989年5月30日出现在广场上的“民主女神”的报道称，它是自由女神像的复制品。它也可以被解读为一段多层次的中国美术学院实践史。[^zh-ch01-47] 当中央美院雕塑系学生答应抗议学生的请求复制这座标志性雕像时，他们必须迅速完成。他们以一尊先前已有的男子双手高举抓杆的泥塑为基础制作模型，那是雕塑系一个工作室集体完成的学院习作。他们截去杆的下半部分，在顶端加了一支火炬。他们把人物从男人改成女人，面孔则仿照苏联雕塑家薇拉·穆希娜《工人与集体农庄女庄员》中的女性形象——该雕塑矗立在1937年巴黎世博会苏联馆顶上。以这尊改造过的泥塑为模型，他们把它放大，用泡沫塑料块雕刻，再用金属丝连缀起来，再涂上石膏。这座十米高的雕像在毛泽东画像对面矗立五天，把冷战双方的政治符号结合在一起。自由女神以集体农庄女庄员的面孔，俯瞰喧嚣的广场。在穆希娜的原作中，她举起的手臂握着共产主义的镰刀。


〔原书 63〕

Many mentioned this high-profile contribution to the student protests as a factor behind cafa’s relocation away from the city center. The move also corresponded with the 1990s development of the Malls at Oriental Plaza (*Dongfang xin tiandi*), a massive Hong Kong-financed shopping complex that took over the area of the academy’s historical location. Faculty and students were temporarily displaced in former factory buildings to the northeast. By the time the academy opened in its expanded, thirty-three-acre Wangjing campus, Beijing’s culture industry model of joining tracks with the world was gaining momentum. The Folk Art Department, which once trained artists in traditional arts of the peasantry, was phased out just as a new School of City Design began providing coursework in urban information, image, fashion, and video design. School leadership succeeded in luring back prominent figures who had moved overseas, such as conceptual artist Xu Bing. In 2008, as vice president of international relations, Xu announced, “China is the most avant-garde and experimental site in the world. Everything here is new.” [^en-ch01-48]

许多人提到，这一对学生抗议的高调贡献是中央美院迁离市中心的原因之一。搬迁也恰逢20世纪90年代东方广场（东方新天地）的开发——这是一个香港出资的大型购物综合体，占据了学院历史校址所在区域。师生被临时安置在东北方向的旧工厂建筑中。当学院在扩建后的三十三英亩望京校区开学时，北京“与世界接轨”的文化产业模式正积聚势头。曾培养农民传统艺术人才的民间美术系被逐步取消，同时新的城市设计学院开始提供城市信息、图像、时尚与影像设计课程。学院领导成功请回了移居海外的知名人物，如概念艺术家徐冰。2008年，作为负责国际关系的副院长，徐冰宣布：“中国是世界上最具前卫性和实验性的现场。这里的一切都是新的。”[^zh-ch01-48]


〔原书 63〕

Palace

宫


〔原书 63, 64〕

In my interviews with artists I discovered that many had attended art classes as children in the state-run system of Young Pioneer Palaces (*shao-nian gong*) or Palaces of Culture (*wenhua gong*). Some of them, especially those from provincial cities, rather than the centrally administered municipalities of Beijing, Shanghai, and Tianjin, told me that in their youth the classes had been free and open to anyone interested. One artist explained the classes had served as childcare, especially when her parents were occupied with work or mandatory political meetings. Others described the system as extremely competitive, with students required to test into the classes, which would prepare them to eventually test into an art academy. The Soviet state had developed Palaces of Culture for its workers and children, enabling them to pursue hobbies, sports, arts, and continuing education. They represented a utopian vision of Communist society, whose collectivized labor could support cultural activities for all its citizens. This model spread to other parts of the Communist world, including China.

在访谈中我发现，许多艺术家小时候曾在国营少年宫（shaonian gong）或文化宫（wenhua gong）系统上过美术课。其中一些人——尤其是来自各省城市、而非北京、上海、天津等直辖市的人——告诉我，他们年轻时这些课程免费，任何感兴趣的人都能参加。一位艺术家解释说，这些课起到托儿所的作用，尤其是在父母忙于工作或必须参加政治会议时。另一些人则说这一体系竞争极其激烈，学生必须考试才能进班，为最终考入美术学院做准备。苏联国家曾为工人和儿童发展文化宫，使他们能够从事爱好、运动、艺术和继续教育。它们代表了一种共产主义社会的乌托邦愿景：其集体化劳动可以供养全体公民的文化活动。这一模式传播到共产主义世界的其他地区，包括中国。


〔原书 64〕

To learn more about this history, I sought a palace where I could observe art classes. I networked my way to Teacher Zhao, who taught at the China National Children’s Center (*Zhongguo ertong zhongxin*). Unlike Beijing’s Young Pioneer Palaces, which fall under the authority of the municipal government, the Children’s Center is administered by the All-China Women’s Federation but provides very similar educational programs and activities. Located in Beijing’s Xicheng District behind a gray brick wall surrounding its perimeter, the expansive campus included green lawns, colorful play equipment, a science and technology hall, art complex, gymnasium, and cinema. Glass cases lining the central walkway contained photos of model students and performances by young dancers, musicians, and thespians, as well as announcements about the center’s contributions to the reform-era goal of *suzhi jiaoyu* (quality education/education in quality).” [^en-ch01-49] On my way to Saturday morning classes, I passed a bronze sculpture of a waifish child with a young pioneer scarf tied around his neck, climbing a ladder in pursuit of a bird. The accompanying plaque told the story of Little Turnip Head, a boy whose body hadn’t developed properly because of malnourishment under the Guomingdang. He died at the age of ten, shortly before the 1949 founding of the prc, a model of deprivation and martyrdom incongruous with the aims of the parents who now brought their children to the center. The students in Teacher Zhao’s class didn’t have to test in, but they did pay a class and materials fee. As a result, most of the students were children of educators and professionals from Xicheng District.

为了解这段历史，我寻找一所可以观摩美术课的少年宫或文化宫。我通过人脉找到赵老师，她在中国儿童中心（Zhongguo ertong zhongxin）任教。与隶属市政府的北京少年宫不同，中国儿童中心由全国妇联管理，但提供非常相似的教育项目和活动。它位于北京西城区，四周环绕灰砖墙，宽阔的园区里有绿色草坪、彩色游乐设施、科技馆、艺术楼、体育馆和电影院。中央步道两侧的玻璃柜里陈列着模范学生的照片、少年舞蹈演员、乐手和戏剧演员的演出照，以及关于中心对改革时代“素质教育”（suzhi jiaoyu）目标所作贡献的介绍。[^zh-ch01-49] 走去上星期六上午的课时，我经过一座青铜雕塑：一个瘦弱的孩子脖子上系着红领巾，爬梯子追逐一只鸟。旁边的说明牌讲述小萝卜头的故事：这个男孩因在国民党统治下营养不良，身体发育不良，在1949年中华人民共和国成立前不久去世，年仅十岁。他是匮乏与殉难的典范，与如今送孩子来中心的家长的追求并不协调。赵老师班上的学生不必考试入学，但要交课时费和材料费。因此，大多数学生都是西城区教育工作者和专业人士的子女。


〔原书 64, 65〕

Compared to the other rather austere art classrooms I’d visited, each overseen by a plaster head of David, the classroom I entered in the summer of 2001 at the Children’s Center overflowed with color, visually stimulating decorations, student-teacher banter, and music. Paintings and drawings—students’ work as well as printed pictures from children’s books—hung on three of the walls. Sunlight shone through large windows that extended the length of the fourth wall, illuminating brightly colored pieces of tissue paper taped to the glass. A ledge beneath the window supported a profusion of potted plants. A stuffed hare and birds of prey perched on tree branches nestled amid the green leaves and vines. Small easels were lined up below the windows. A bin of toys for young children to play with when they lost concentration stood in the corner. Along the wall opposite the windows, a massive wooden chest painted light blue held rows of small drawers, each carefully labeled with its contents—watercolor boxes, black ink, acrylic paint, brushes, plates, glasses, crayons, pencils, erasers, clay tools, etc. On top of the chest, goldfish with bulging eyes swam around a big glass bowl.

与我去过的其他相当简朴、每间都由一尊大卫石膏头像看守的美术教室相比，我2001年夏天走进的儿童中心教室充满色彩、视觉刺激的装饰、师生间的玩笑和音乐。三面墙上挂着绘画和素描——既有学生的作品，也有儿童书籍的印刷图片。阳光透过沿第四面墙延伸的大窗照进来，照亮贴在玻璃上的彩色皱纹纸。窗下平台摆满盆栽植物。树枝间栖着兔子和猛禽的标本，掩映在绿叶和藤蔓之中。窗下排列着小画架。角落里放着一箱玩具，供年幼孩子走神时玩耍。窗户对面的墙边，一只刷成浅蓝色的大木柜装着成排小抽屉，每个都仔细标着内容——水彩盒、墨汁、丙烯颜料、画笔、调色盘、玻璃杯、蜡笔、铅笔、橡皮、陶艺工具等。柜顶上，一个玻璃大鱼缸里游着凸眼的金鱼。


〔原书 65〕

Students ranging in age from five to ten sat around tables pushed into a large rectangle at the center of the room. Teenagers who had once studied with Teacher Zhao occasionally came back, especially during school holidays, to work on projects. Parents who wanted to stay and watch sat in chairs along two of the walls. Teacher Zhao bounded around the classroom. She knelt next to young students to view drawings from their vantage point. When older students grew tired with their work, she imitated them by whining like a teenager, making light of their complaints. She jumped up on top of the tables with her camera to take photos of the students, which she announced she would “keep as souvenirs.” She played tapes of classical and jazz music, and sometimes the Beatles, from a boom box on top of a bookshelf. But she also didn’t hesitate to keep order in a way that reinforced a link between “culture” and “quality.” When children started to talk too loudly or make a mess, she reprimanded them by asking, “Don’t you have any culture? How can you act like that? Does your family have culture or not?” Teacher Zhao’s investment in the development of young artists didn’t preclude disciplining their parents. If the adults started to talk among themselves, she shushed them as if they were children. During a field trip to a foreign-managed contemporary art gallery, she insisted that it was already too late to teach parent chaperones how to properly view art. She made them wait outside the gallery while she instructed the children how to behave—they should stand, not squat, and quietly discuss the paintings from a distance without touching them—and then took them in to tour the exhibit.

五到十岁的学生围坐在教室中央拼成大长方形的桌子旁。曾经跟赵老师学画的少年有时会回来，尤其是在学校假期，来做作品。想留下来观看的家长坐在靠两面墙的椅子上。赵老师在教室里蹦来蹦去。她跪在年幼学生旁边，从他们的视角看画。年长学生画累了，她就学着少年的样子撒娇抱怨，把他们的牢骚当玩笑。她跳上桌子，用相机给学生拍照，并宣布要“留作纪念”。她用书架上的手提音响播放古典乐、爵士乐，有时还有披头士。但她也会毫不犹豫地维持秩序，方式强化着“文化”与“素质”之间的联系。孩子开始太大声说话或弄得一团糟时，她责问：“你们有没有文化？怎么能这样？你们家到底有没有文化？”赵老师对培养年轻艺术家的投入，并不妨碍她管教家长。大人们自己聊起来时，她会像对孩子一样嘘他们。在一次去外资当代艺术画廊的参观活动中，她坚持说，现在教陪同家长如何正确看艺术已经太晚了。她让他们在画廊外等着，自己先教孩子该怎么做——站着，不要蹲着，隔着距离安静讨论画作，不要触摸——然后才带他们进去参观。


〔原书 65, 66〕

After I had attended her class for several months, Teacher Zhao finally found time in her busy schedule to talk with me about her teaching philosophy. During the conversation, she emphasized the need to cultivate children’s creativity and imagination, by exposing them to as many different styles and ways of making art as possible, instead of subjecting them to a rigid, test-based model of education. In her classes, she taught traditional Chinese arts, such as mask painting, the folk art of dough sculpture, seal carving, and calligraphy, as well as introducing Western techniques and “great works.” She credited her pedagogical openness to opportunities to travel abroad, many arranged in conjunction with exhibits of work by her husband, a painter represented by the gallery her students had visited on their field trip. During these trips, she tried to learn as much as possible about art, design, architecture, and educational methods outside of China. She stressed, however, that Chinese students were subjected to greater discipline, because of crowded classroom conditions, and therefore knew how to work harder than the American students she had observed. She insisted, for example, that the practice of copying from models (*linmo*) was essential to Chinese art education.

我上她的课几个月后，赵老师终于在繁忙日程中抽出时间，和我谈她的教学理念。谈话中，她强调要培养孩子的创造力和想象力，让他们接触尽可能多的风格和创作方式，而不是让他们服从僵化、以考试为基础的教育模式。在她的课上，她教中国传统艺术，如面具彩绘、面塑、篆刻和书法，也介绍西方技法和“名作”。她把自己在教学上的开放归功于出国旅行的机会，其中许多是配合她丈夫的作品展安排的；丈夫是一位由她学生参观的那家画廊代理的画家。这些旅行中，她尽可能多地学习中国以外的艺术、设计、建筑和教育方法。但她强调，由于教室拥挤，中国学生受到更多纪律约束，因此比她在美国观察到的学生更懂得用功。例如，她坚持认为临摹（linmo）对中国美术教育至关重要。


〔原书 66〕

She then told me, with great enthusiasm, about a new teaching method she’d been developing and would soon implement in her classroom. It would combine the Communist file (*dang’an*) system of tracking citizens’ backgrounds with what she called American mba management style, referring to the growing popularity in China of programs that trained students in international business strategies and norms. Similar to dang’an—the closed records kept by work units on their members’ political standing, work and family history, achievements, and failings—files would be created for all of her students. Over the years, she would add examples of their work as a record of their artistic progress. Her classroom archives, unlike those maintained by work unit officials, would be open, making the system akin to mba-style management, with its techniques of self-discipline and governance.[^en-ch01-50] Students would be able to evaluate their own work over time but also look at the files of other students in order to compare and monitor their progress.

接着，她满怀热情地向我讲述一种她正在开发、即将在教室实施的新教学方法。它将把共产党追踪公民背景的档案（dang’an）制度，与她所谓的美国MBA管理风格结合起来——后者指中国日益流行的、训练学生掌握国际商业策略与规范的项目。与档案类似——单位保存的关于成员政治立场、工作与家庭历史、成绩与缺点的封闭记录——她将为所有学生建立档案。多年间，她会加入他们的作品样本，作为艺术进步的记录。她的教室档案不同于单位官员保存的档案，将是公开的，使这一体系类似MBA式管理及其自我规训与治理技术。[^zh-ch01-50] 学生既能评估自己长期以来的作品，也能查看其他学生的档案，以比较和监测进度。


〔原书 66〕

In February 2002, I attended another field trip arranged by Teacher Zhao, a visit to linmo at an exhibit of prints by Pablo Picasso. I arrived on a cold, sunny Sunday morning at the China Millennium Monument, an imposing concrete structure, built next to the Military Museum to commemorate China’s entry into the twenty-first century. A wide stone walkway gradually ascended almost three hundred meters along a north-south axis from the street to the museum’s main entrance. Inscriptions on a ribbon of bronze, running down the middle of the walkway, record historical events from five thousand years of Chinese history. The monument itself is a circular construction modeled after the shape of an ancient sundial. On the night that Jiang Zemin announced Beijing had won its bid to host the 2008 Olympics, he addressed the nation on television from the steps of the Millennium Monument. I walked under a huge banner featuring a black-and-white photograph of Picasso’s leathery face and entered the museum.

2002年2月，我参加了赵老师安排的另一次参观活动，去中华世纪坛的毕加索版画展临摹。那是一个寒冷晴朗的周日上午，我来到中华世纪坛。这座气势逼人的混凝土建筑建于军事博物馆旁，纪念中国进入21世纪。宽阔的石质步道沿南北轴线从街道缓缓上升近三百米，通向博物馆正门。步道中央一条青铜带上的铭文，记录中国五千年历史上的事件。世纪坛本身是仿古代日晷形状的圆形建筑。江泽民宣布北京赢得2008年奥运会主办权的那一夜，他就站在世纪坛台阶上向全国发表电视讲话。我从一幅印有毕加索皮革般面孔黑白照片的巨大横幅下走过，进入博物馆。


〔原书 66, 67, 68〕

In the lobby, children’s linmo drawings of prints in the exhibit covered the walls. At a sales booth, parents could buy large sheets of drawing paper printed with the motto of the exhibit: “The master paints, I also paint.” Children filled the large gallery space, where they sat on small stools and carefully copied Picasso drawings of animals, bullfights, and opera scenes. After Teacher Zhao’s students had finished several drawings, she gathered them around a diorama of Picasso at a table filled with printmaking tools. A green compact car stood on a raised pedestal behind the display. Only at this point did I realize that the French carmaker Citroën was the main sponsor of the exhibit. Citroën and Dongfeng Motor, a Chinese auto company, had recently launched a new car for the Chinese market, the Picasso, a four-door hatchback with the artist’s signature emblazoned on its side (figure 1.06). Teacher Zhao explained to her students how to use the different printmaking tools laid out on the table. She then instructed the students, as well as their parents, in the business of art. She stressed the point that art is purchasable, a recurring theme in her classroom (figure 1.07). To become a collector, one could start small and learn through practice how to evaluate the worth of a work. She distributed a handout with questions about the exhibit for the students to fill out. One question asked how much they would be willing to spend for one of the Picasso prints. She had asked them a similar question during their field trip to the foreign-managed commercial art gallery several months earlier and was dismayed when they gave unreasonably low prices. When the students handed in their papers this time, she smiled at their progress. Most of them had listed amounts in the one thousand to ten thousand yuan range.

大厅里，展厅版画的儿童临摹作品贴满墙壁。在销售台，家长可以买到印有展览口号的大张画纸：“大师画，我也画。”孩子们挤满巨大的展厅，坐在小凳子上仔细临摹毕加索画的动物、斗牛和歌剧场景。赵老师的学生画完几幅后，她把大家召集到一个场景模型旁：毕加索坐在一张摆满版画工具的桌边。展示装置后的升高基座上停着一辆绿色小型汽车。直到此时我才意识到，法国汽车制造商雪铁龙是展览的主要赞助商。雪铁龙与中国汽车公司东风汽车最近为中国市场推出一款新车“毕加索”，这是一辆四门掀背车，车身侧面印着艺术家的签名（图1.06）。赵老师向学生讲解如何使用桌上摆放的各种版画工具。随后，她向学生和家长讲授艺术生意。她强调艺术是可购买的，这是她课堂上反复出现的主题（图1.07）。要成为收藏家，可以从小的开始，通过实践学习如何评估作品价值。她发了一份关于展览的问卷让学生填写。其中一个问题问他们愿意花多少钱买一幅毕加索版画。几个月前参观那家外资商业画廊时，她问过类似问题，当时他们对价格估得低得不合理，令她沮丧。这次学生交回问卷时，她对他们的进步笑了。大多数人填的金额在一千到一万元之间。


〔原书 67〕

![图1.06　东风雪铁龙“毕加索”汽车广告，《南方周末》，2001年11月8日。广告语写道：“创造新生活：用灵感做材料，用想象去创造。”](web/assets/ch01-b054.jpg)

FIG 1.06 Dongfeng Citroën Picasso car advertisement, *Nanfang zhoumo* (Southern Weekend), November 8, 2001. The slogan reads: “Create a new life: use inspiration as your material, use your imagination to make it.”

图1.06　东风雪铁龙“毕加索”汽车广告，《南方周末》，2001年11月8日。广告语写道：“创造新生活：用灵感做材料，用想象去创造。”


〔原书 68〕

![图1.07　赵老师一位学生的绘画，收入2000年由家长出资出版的学生作品集。这位七岁的画家根据父母在受欢迎的快餐连锁店北京分店给他拍的与麦当劳叔叔雕像合影，创作了这幅自画像。他主动给自己的作品标了价。](web/assets/ch01-b055.jpg)

FIG 1.07 Painting by one of Teacher Zhao’s students in a 2000 catalogue of student work published with financial contributions from parents. The painter, aged seven, created this self-portrait from a photograph his parents had taken of him sitting with a Ronald McDonald statue at the popular chain restaurant in Beijing. He had, on his own initiative, evaluated his work by painting a price on it.

图1.07　赵老师一位学生的绘画，收入2000年由家长出资出版的学生作品集。这位七岁的画家根据父母在受欢迎的快餐连锁店北京分店给他拍的与麦当劳叔叔雕像合影，创作了这幅自画像。他主动给自己的作品标了价。


〔原书 68, 69〕

As the students and their parents dispersed, Teacher Zhao’s husband arrived and said, “Let’s go drive one of the cars!” In a large paved area outside the museum, Dongfeng Citroën employees ran a test-drive center. Zhao’s husband left his driver’s license at the registration table, and we climbed into a Picasso. As we slowly circled the monument, Teacher Zhao commented that the car was too expensive for the general market, but nonetheless would be great for driving students around because it had three seats across in the back. She then launched into a description of a kindergarten she hoped to open using the German Waldorf method that incorporates art and music in all aspects of the curriculum. I laughed, noting how Picasso had become such a profitable commodity. Teacher Zhao looked over her shoulder from the front seat with an incredulous look and said, “Of course, that’s exactly what he was. He painted too many paintings over the course of his life, so none of them are really very precious!”

学生和家长散去时，赵老师的丈夫来了，说：“我们去开一圈车吧！”博物馆外一大片铺砌场地上，东风雪铁龙员工经营着试驾中心。赵老师的丈夫把驾照留在登记台，我们坐进一辆“毕加索”。我们缓缓绕世纪坛行驶，赵老师评论说这车对普通市场来说太贵，但接送学生很棒，因为后排有三座。接着，她谈起希望用德国华德福教育法开办一所幼儿园，把艺术和音乐融入课程的所有方面。我笑了，指出毕加索如何成了如此有利可图的商品。赵老师从前排转过头，露出难以置信的表情说：“当然，他本来就是。他一生画了太多画，所以没有一幅真正珍贵！”


〔原书 69〕

I often heard Teacher Zhao speak disapprovingly of students’ parents who drove expensive foreign cars or invited her out to elaborate meals but never considered purchasing art. Over time, some parents took her criticism to heart. One mother told me, without a hint of irony, that since she’d grown up during the Cultural Revolution she had never learned what culture really was. Even though she had succeeded financially in recent years, she feared this deficit would hold her back. As a result, she was determined to invest in her daughter’s cultural education; she believed it would provide their family an entrée to the world that money alone couldn’t buy. Teacher Zhao’s enthusiasm for the Picasso car differed from the conspicuous consumption she criticized because she framed it in terms of how she would use the car to further her ideal of art education. Linmo exercises at the Millennium Monument Picasso exhibit educated Chinese children in the internationally recognized artwork of a modern Western master, while also teaching them art is a commodity, but one requiring specialized knowledge in order to properly evaluate it. The Little Turnip Head statue at the Children’s Center once modeled a culture of socialist sacrifice; transvalued through suzhi jiaoyu, he now climbed the cultural ladder in order to guarantee the nation’s global future.

我常听赵老师不满地谈起一些学生家长：他们开昂贵的外国车，或请她去豪华饭局，却从不考虑购买艺术。久而久之，一些家长把她的批评听进去了。一位母亲毫不讽刺地告诉我，她成长于文革，从没学过文化究竟是什么。尽管这些年经济上成功了，她仍担心这种缺失会拖累自己。因此，她决心投资女儿的文化教育；她相信这能为家庭提供一张仅靠金钱买不到的进入世界的门票。赵老师对毕加索汽车的热情，与她批评的炫耀性消费不同，因为她把它框定为如何用这辆车推进自己的艺术教育理想。在世纪坛毕加索展上的临摹练习，教中国孩子认识一位现代西方大师获得国际认可的作品，同时也教他们艺术是一种商品，但需要专门知识才能正确评估。儿童中心的小萝卜头雕像曾塑造一种社会主义牺牲文化；经素质教育而价值转换，如今他正在爬文化的梯子，以确保国家的全球未来。


〔原书 69〕

Village

村


〔原书 69, 70〕

Chinese artists who were once xianfeng by traveling to rural and ethnic minority hinterlands to represent village life gradually became avant-garde by participation in international art exhibitions. This transition occurred simultaneously with an increased flow of rural migrants to the city, leading to crossings and comparisons between the two groups. In the 1990s, rural migrants from Anhui, Henan, Xinjiang, and Zhejiang Provinces set up “villages” (*cun*), places of long-term residence and often manufacturing and commercial businesses, in outlying areas of Beijing.[^en-ch01-51] In a smaller-scale movement, hundreds of artists flocked to the capital and developed what became known as the Yuanmingyuan artist village. In an area near the imperial summer palace to the city’s northwest, they found living and working spaces cheap and easy to rent without a Beijing residence permit. Those who likened their circumstances to migrant workers or whose art began to focus on this new social group sometimes referred to themselves as *mangliu* (blind floaters), the often derogatory term used for rural migrants.[^en-ch01-52] Or they invoked the romantic term *jianghu*, the wandering bandits from martial arts genres, who live by a code of loyalty to their sworn brothers and commitment to helping the needy.

曾经作为先锋（xianfeng）、前往农村和少数民族腹地再现乡村生活的中国艺术家，后来通过参加国际艺术展而逐渐成为前卫。这一转型与农村移民涌入城市同时发生，导致两个群体之间的交错与比较。20世纪90年代，来自安徽、河南、新疆和浙江的农村移民在北京边缘地区建立“村”（cun），作为长期居住地，也常常是制造和商业经营之地。[^zh-ch01-51] 在一场规模较小的运动中，数百名艺术家涌向首都，发展出后来所称的圆明园艺术家村。在西北方向皇家园囿附近，他们发现没有北京户口也能廉价、容易地租到生活和工作空间。那些把自己的处境比作农民工、或其艺术开始关注这一新社会群体的人，有时自称“盲流”（mangliu）——常用于农村移民的贬义词。[^zh-ch01-52] 或者他们援引浪漫的“江湖”一词，指武侠类型中的游侠，他们遵循对结义兄弟的忠诚和扶危济困的准则。


〔原书 70〕

While some who took up residence in Yuanmingyuan came from Beijing, many migrated from other provinces, attracted by stories they’d heard about the artist village. The community attracted increasing attention from foreign art collectors and reporters, and Chinese authorities grew wary of this activity and its proximity to key universities as a threat to state cultural control. During a “clean up and reordering” campaign that hit Beijing in 1995, rural migrant and artist villages both experienced police surveillance and eviction. Shi Tou, one of the few female artists at Yuanmingyuan, connected the crackdown to Beijing’s preparation to host the UN Fourth World Conference on Women that September. In a documentary film on China’s emerging lesbian community and its intertwining with transnational feminist and queer activism, she recounts: “At that time, Yuanmingyuan was an art village with a free atmosphere, it had connections with people from all over the world and represented the most pioneering [xianfeng] part of that era. Maybe they were afraid artists from Yuanmingyuan would contact international attendees.... Yuanmingyuan was turbulent and restless in 1995. There were armed police from the security department patrol around all the time, from day to night.”[^en-ch01-53] Bulldozers hit rural migrant compounds, reducing thriving neighborhoods to rubble. While the Yuanmingyuan village was spared physical destruction, artists caught in the sweep there were arrested and fined for illegal residence. Police took those unable to pay the fines to rural locations to do road repairs or other physical labor to work off their debt.

在圆明园定居的人有些来自北京，但许多是从其他省份迁来的，被听到的艺术家村故事吸引。这个社区越来越引起外国艺术收藏家和记者的注意，中国当局开始警惕这类活动，以及它与重点大学的邻近，认为其威胁国家的文化控制。1995年北京“清理整顿”运动中，农村移民村和艺术家村都遭到警方监视和驱逐。圆明园为数不多的女性艺术家之一石头，把这次镇压与北京筹备当年9月联合国第四次世界妇女大会联系起来。在一部关于中国新兴女同性恋群体及其与跨国女性主义和酷儿行动主义交织的纪录片中，她讲述：“那时，圆明园是一个有自由气氛的艺术村，它和世界各地的人有联系，代表了那个时代最先锋（xianfeng）的部分。也许他们怕圆明园艺术家接触国际与会者……1995年的圆明园动荡不安。安全部门的武警从早到晚不停巡逻。”[^zh-ch01-53] 推土机开进民工聚居区，把繁荣社区夷为瓦砾。圆明园村虽免于实体摧毁，但扫荡中被抓的艺术家因非法居留而被逮捕、罚款。警方把付不起罚款的人送到农村修路或做其他体力劳动抵债。


〔原书 70, 71〕

The police had already disbanded another artist village east of Beijing’s third ring road the year before. Residents had dubbed it East Village, suggesting a comparison with New York’s lower east side.[^en-ch01-54] Their activities, especially nude performance pieces by artists Ma Liuming and Zhang Huan, quickly attracted official scrutiny. Artists began moving further east to Tongzhou, a rural county of Hebei Province annexed in 1997 to the Beijing municipal area. Artists lived throughout the county in a variety of housing, ranging from apartment blocks to basic rural courtyard houses to walled compounds with contemporary interiors. The largest group congregated in Songzhuang, where they rented houses and land from famers and transformed the area. Ten years after the police sweep of Yuanmingyuan, the official website for Tongzhou District prominently featured the Songzhuang Artist Village. It boasted that with over five hundred artists, the village constituted the world’s largest art community.[^en-ch01-55] The first annual Songzhuang Art Festival began in 2005, followed a year later by the opening of the Songzhuang Art Museum. State surveillance of artist villages shifted to culture industry incorporation of them. In 2012, the Tongzhou District government commissioned Sasaki Associates, an architectural firm headquartered in Boston, to create a four-thousand-hectare plan for the Songzhuang Arts and Agricultural City.[^en-ch01-56]

前一年，警方已解散北京三环路以东的另一个艺术家村。居民称之为东村，暗示与纽约下东区的比较。[^zh-ch01-54] 他们的活动，尤其是艺术家马六明和张洹的裸体行为作品，很快招来官方审查。艺术家开始进一步向东迁移，前往通州——原属河北的农业县，1997年划归北京市区。艺术家住在全县各处，住房从公寓楼、简陋农家院到内部装修现代的院墙院落不等。最大的群体聚集在宋庄，他们向农民租房租地，改变了这个地区。警方扫荡圆明园十年后通州区官方网站突出展示宋庄艺术家村。网站夸耀说，这里拥有五百多位艺术家，构成世界最大的艺术社区。[^zh-ch01-55] 2005年首届宋庄艺术节开幕，一年后宋庄美术馆开馆。国家对艺术家村的监视，转变为文化产业对它们的收编。2012年，通州区政府委托总部在波士顿的建筑事务所佐佐木事务所，为宋庄艺术农业城制定四千公顷规划。[^zh-ch01-56]


〔原书 71〕

During the early 2000s, the financial circumstances of artists in this and other semirural border areas of Beijing diverged to extremes of wealth and poverty. Many nonetheless felt they had escaped regimented city life for a more carefree and collective existence in the countryside. As they educated themselves about international art trends and worked to cultivate connections and organize exhibits in the city, they expressed nostalgic attachment to a pastoral way of life on the verge of vanishing. Some criticized the environmental impact of rapid urbanization, especially as real estate developments encroached on the fields and outdoor markets of Tongzhou, and sympathized with the treatment of rural migrants working in the city. An artist from Shaanxi Province, who was involved with environmental protection groups, told me the saddest moment in recent history for him occurred in 1999 when the government evicted migrant workers in another mass sweep before the official celebration of the prc’s fiftieth anniversary.

21世纪初，这个地区以及其他北京半乡村边缘地带的艺术家，经济状况分化到贫富两极。尽管如此，许多人仍觉得自己逃离了被管制的城市生活，来到乡村过更无忧无虑的集体生活。他们学习国际艺术潮流，努力在城市里培养关系、组织展览，同时对一种濒临消失的田园生活方式表达怀旧依恋。一些人批评快速城市化的环境影响，尤其是房地产开发侵占通州的田地和露天市场，并同情在城市工作的农村移民的遭遇。一位参与环保团体的陕西艺术家告诉我，他记忆中近来最悲伤的时刻是1999年：政府为庆祝中华人民共和国成立五十周年，在另一场大规模清查中驱逐了农民工。


〔原书 71〕

Cultural critic Wang Min’an describes this identification with country folk in a way that reveals gendered assumptions about this bohemian ideal: “The group of artists in Songzhuang reside mixed together with peasants.... In appearance, they resemble each other: long messy hair, shiny shaved heads, unkempt beards, and long khaki pants.”[^en-ch01-57] Wang hints at the false promise that such mingling will provide escape from urban commercialism, remarking that these artists often spend their evenings in the city: “They turn the wheels of their cars in the opposite direction of the rest of the city, and for a handful of coins, the backdrop of their nights often includes large quantities of wine, one or two fashionable girls, and the dim lights of a bar.”[^en-ch01-58] The artists’ challenge to the city as the new national object of desire also slid into romanticization of the rural. The countryside became a commodified form of urban leisure, an “artistic lifestyle” urbanites strove to emulate as Tongzhou artists’ houses began appearing in home decorating magazines.

文化批评家汪民安在描述这种对乡民的认同时，透露出关于这一波西米亚理想的性别化假设：“宋庄的艺术家群体与农民混住在一起……从外表看，他们彼此相像：长而凌乱的头发、闪亮的光头、不修边幅的胡子、卡其色长裤。”[^zh-ch01-57] 汪民安暗示，这种混杂会提供逃离城市商业主义的虚假承诺，并指出这些艺术家常在城里度过夜晚：“他们把车轮转向与城市其他人相反的方向；用几个硬币，他们夜晚的背景常常包括大量酒、一两个时髦姑娘和酒吧昏暗的灯光。”[^zh-ch01-58] 艺术家把城市当作新的国家欲望对象来挑战，同时也滑向对乡村的浪漫化。乡村成为城市休闲的商品化形式，一种城市人竞相模仿的“艺术化生活方式”，通州艺术家的房子开始出现在家居装饰杂志上。


〔原书 71, 72〕

During this reconfiguration of rural-urban relations, a number of Beijing artists began making pieces focused on male migrant workers (*mingong*) employed in the city’s many construction sites. When I interviewed ten artists involved in such projects, several told me they’d first come in contact with mingong while remodeling their homes and later hired them to appear in or assist with artworks. As they attempted to collaborate with and represent migrant workers in sculptural, photographic, and performance works, they saw them as emblematic of new forms of social inequality. A piece by the Gao Brothers that staged nude workers embracing against a concrete urban landscape incited criticism in *Meishu* (Fine arts), the official publication of the Chinese Artists Association.[^en-ch01-59] An article in an issue commemorating the sixtieth anniversary of Mao’s “Talks at the Yan’an Conference on Art and Literature” lambasted this trend: “These so-called avant-garde artists not only long ago completely dispensed with the lofty aim of serving the people, but they have started to turn it utterly upside down, using workers and peasants as art’s ‘new material’ or ‘new medium’ so that the ‘people’ pay out their flesh to serve their ‘avant-garde’ art.”[^en-ch01-60]

在这种城乡关系重构中，一些北京艺术家开始创作聚焦在城里众多建筑工地受雇的男性民工（mingong）的作品。我访谈了十位参与此类项目的艺术家，其中几位告诉我，他们最初是在装修房屋时接触民工的，后来雇用他们出镜或协助创作。他们尝试在雕塑、摄影和行为作品中与民工合作并再现民工，把民工视为新社会不平等形式的象征。高氏兄弟一件让裸体工人相拥于混凝土城市景观前的作品，在中国美术家协会官方刊物《美术》上引发批评。[^zh-ch01-59] 一篇文章刊于纪念毛泽东《在延安文艺座谈会上的讲话》发表六十周年专号，猛烈抨击这一潮流：“这些所谓前卫艺术家不仅早已彻底抛弃了为人民服务的崇高目标，而且开始把它完全颠倒过来，把工农当作艺术的‘新材料’或‘新媒介’，让‘人民’用自己的血肉之躯来服务于他们的‘前卫’艺术。”[^zh-ch01-60]


〔原书 72, 73〕

I also interviewed a migrant worker who had served as artist assistant for Zhang Dali’s *100 Chinese* (figure 1.08), a sculptural installation of busts cast from the heads of migrant workers.[^en-ch01-61] When Wang arrived in Beijing from Henan Province, he worked for several sculptors, as a handyman, model, and eventually apprentice. He learned the technical skills of the trade and had executed conceptual ideas by several successful contemporary artists. For *100 Chinese*, he recruited friends, relatives, and neighbors in the rural migrant enclave where he lived and helped develop the process of casting their heads in plaster. Sitters kept their eyes shut and breathed through straws inserted into their nostrils for the ten minutes the plaster took to harden. The resin heads then created from these original casts bear the individual features of each sitter, as well as the frozen, closed-eye, pinched-lip facial expressions exacted by the process. Zhang Dali exhibited them in piles, lined up on shelves, or stacked in individual plexiglass boxes, a mute collection of severed heads. A catalogue of Zhang’s work produced by a British gallery contains the following description: “His latest work is a documentation of faces—faces of the migrant workers who flock to the big cities in search of a job. These people are desperately poor and are usually seeking only to survive. They are not part of the official register of inhabitants and thus have no right to state education, health care or other benefits. There are the fringes of society. They live on the outskirts of major cities, making meager homes in abandoned buildings.”[^en-ch01-62] Zhang emphasized in the interview I conducted with him the collective striving of mingong and society’s callous disregard for them as something he identified with as an artist who had lived in Yuanmingyuan and floated around the city in the 1990s as a graffiti artist.[^en-ch01-63]

我还访谈了一位曾为张大力的《一百个中国人》担任艺术家助手的民工（图1.08）。这是一件用民工头部翻制的半身像组成的雕塑装置。[^zh-ch01-61] 当王从河南来到北京时，他为几位雕塑家工作，做过杂工、模特，最终成为学徒。他学会了这一行业的技术，也替几位成功的当代艺术家实现过概念构想。为创作《一百个中国人》，他在自己居住的民工聚居区招募朋友、亲戚和邻居，并帮助开发用石膏翻制他们头部的流程。模特们闭上眼睛，通过插入鼻孔的吸管呼吸，石膏需要十分钟硬化。随后用这些原始模具翻制出的树脂头像，带有每个模特的面部特征，也带有流程强加的凝固、闭眼、抿嘴表情。张大力把它们成堆摆放、在架子上排开，或分别堆叠在有机玻璃盒中——一组沉默的断头收藏。一家英国画廊制作的张大力作品图录有这样的描述：“他最新的作品是一份面孔记录——涌向大城市找工作的民工的面孔。这些人极度贫困，通常只求生存。他们不在官方户籍登记中，因而无权享受国家教育、医疗或其他福利。他们处于社会边缘。他们住在大城市郊区，在废弃建筑中搭建简陋的住所。”[^zh-ch01-62] 在我对张大力进行的访谈中，他强调民工的集体奋斗和社会对他们的冷漠无视，作为一位曾住在圆明园、90年代在城市里游荡的涂鸦艺术家，他对此深有认同。[^zh-ch01-63]


〔原书 73〕

![图1.08　张大力，《一百个中国人》，2001年。树脂雕塑。展览现场，中国当代画廊，伦敦，2002年。作者摄影。](web/assets/ch01-b066.jpg)

FIG 1.08 Zhang Dali, *100 Chinese*, 2001. Resin sculptures. Exhibit view, Chinese Contemporary Gallery, London, 2002. Photograph by author.

图1.08　张大力，《一百个中国人》，2001年。树脂雕塑。展览现场，中国当代画廊，伦敦，2002年。作者摄影。


〔原书 73, 74〕

As Wang and two other friends whose heads had been cast for Zhang’s piece chatted about the process, they shared stories and examples of their own artistic endeavors. Their small, two-room flat in a low one-story brick building with a metal roof was filled with landscape paintings in oil and watercolor, as well as small abstract and figurative sculptures. Wang’s girlfriend who worked at an advertising company used her spare time and money to take art classes in design and painting. She spoke of how art provided her with a space of focus, challenge, and creative energy but also of the pain of being judged by people in the city, even by her painting teacher, as someone simply from the countryside. Describing it as feeling caught between two existences, she ran to the other room and pulled a piece of paper off the wall. The quote copied on it came from a book, translated from English, she had recently read: “It is a peculiar sensation, this double-consciousness, that only lets him see himself through the revelation of the other world. It is a peculiar sensation, this double-consciousness, this sense of always looking at one’s self through the eyes of others, of measuring one’s soul by the tape of a world that looks on in amused contempt and pity.”[^en-ch01-64] These words, written by W. E. B. Du Bois almost a century earlier, helped her navigate the splintering condition of daily life in Beijing. They spoke of art as decolonial method: a means of becoming, in Du Bois’s words, “co-creators in the kingdom of culture.”[^en-ch01-65]

当王和另外两位头被翻制的朋友聊起这个流程时，他们分享了自己的艺术尝试和故事。他们位于低矮单层铁皮顶砖楼里的两居室小公寓，摆满了油画和水彩风景画，以及小型抽象和具象雕塑。王的女友在一家广告公司工作，用业余时间和钱上设计与绘画课。她谈起艺术如何为她提供专注、挑战和创造能量的空间，也谈到被城市人——甚至她的绘画老师——仅仅视为“乡下人”的痛苦。她说自己感觉被夹在两种存在之间，然后跑到另一间屋，从墙上扯下一张纸。纸上抄录的话出自她最近读的一本从英文译成中文的书：“这是一种奇特的感觉，这种双重意识，总是通过另一个世界的揭示来看自己。这是一种奇特的感觉，这种双重意识，总是透过他人的眼睛看自己，用一个带着讥讽的轻蔑与同情的世界的尺子来衡量自己的灵魂。”[^zh-ch01-64] 这些由W. E. B. 杜波依斯在近一个世纪前写下的文字帮助她应对北京日常生活分裂的状况。这些文字阐明了作为去殖民方法的艺术：成为杜波依斯所说的“文化王国中的共同创造者”的途径。[^zh-ch01-65]


〔原书 74〕

Museum

博物馆


〔原书 74〕

By the turn of the twentieth century, the museum had become a worldly emblem of national modernity. In the West, public institutions assumed the art of exhibition as a form of civilizational distinction. World’s Fairs in Euro-American metropoles staged the world for the viewing public, displaying it in a way that naturalized a hierarchy of nations and races. Chinese reformers, in their encounters with such expositions, learned their exhibitory logic and potential to develop a modern, national consciousness and achieve international recognition. With these goals in mind, an official from Jiangsu Province began building the first Chinese museum in 1905. He aimed to transform the small town of Nantong, between Nanjing and Shanghai, into a model of modernity and self-governance. When the Nantong Museum opened in 1912 its buildings and gardens presented a range of objects—paintings, plants, skeletons, tools, industrial machines, furniture, and animals—displayed and classified under the categories of nature, history, and art.[^en-ch01-66]

到20世纪初，博物馆已成为国家现代性的世界性象征。在西方，公共机构把展览艺术视为一种文明区隔形式。欧美大都市的世界博览会为观看公众上演世界，其展示方式使国家与种族的等级自然化。中国改革者在与这类博览会的相遇中，学会了它们的展览逻辑及其发展现代民族意识、获得国际承认的潜能。怀着这些目标，一位江苏官员于1905年开始建造中国第一座博物馆。他要把南京与上海之间的南通小城改造成现代性与自治的模范。1912年南通博物苑开放时，其建筑和园林展示了一系列物品——绘画、植物、骨骼、工具、工业机械、家具和动物——按自然、历史和艺术分类陈列。[^zh-ch01-66]


〔原书 74, 75〕

The national and global legacy of exhibitory politics took on a new millennial life as China bid to host the 2008 Olympics and 2010 World Expo. Museum politics also structured the experiences of Chinese contemporary artists as they exhibited work abroad and at home. The artist Zhu Jia expressed with unsettling candor the dissonance he felt with being put on display. I first met Zhu while helping translate for a U.S.-based curator during his research visit to Beijing for an exhibit of non-Western contemporary art. Zhu Jia worked as a design editor at *Beijing Youth News*, the job assignment he received after graduating from the Central Academy of Fine Arts in 1988. Trained as an oil painter, he moved into photography and video. For *Passage*, a video installation just completed when we met in 2001, he pedaled a video camera strapped to the bed of worker’s bicycle-drawn cart to film various routes through the city.[^en-ch01-67] He projected these journeys onto three long vertical panels, the size and shape of traditional Chinese scrolls. The resulting montage of partial and disjunctive movement refuses a singular view of the city. Since the late 1990s, his work had been included in several international exhibits, but Zhu expressed misgivings about this attention. He told the visiting curator he suspected his nationality mattered more than his art, as curators sought third-world tokens. He described with chagrin a sense of alienation from Chinese audiences. China’s underdeveloped museum system for contemporary art had pushed him to “go global,” but the foreign narrative of surprise and discovery framing Chinese avant-garde art had become tiring. It accentuated the condition of being cut off from audiences who shared similar experiences of passage through Beijing’s social and historical landscape.

展览政治的民族与全球遗产，在中国申办2008年奥运会和2010年世博会时获得了新的千禧年生命。博物馆政治也结构着中国当代艺术家在国内外展出的经验。艺术家朱加以令人不安的坦率，表达了自己被置于展示之中时感到的不协调。我最初遇到朱加，是在为一位常驻美国的策展人担任翻译时，他来北京考察，筹备一个非西方当代艺术展。朱加在《北京青年报》做设计编辑，这是1988年从中央美术学院毕业后分配的工作。他受的是油画家训练，后来转向摄影和录像。我们2001年见面时，他刚完成录像装置《通道》：他把摄像机绑在工人使用的自行车拖车车板上，自己蹬车拍摄穿越城市的各条路线。[^zh-ch01-67] 他把这些旅程投影在三块长竖屏上，尺寸和形状类似中国传统卷轴。由此产生的局部、断裂运动的蒙太奇，拒绝单一的城市视角。自90年代末以来，他的作品已参加若干国际展览，但朱加对这种关注表示疑虑。他告诉来访的策展人，他怀疑自己的国籍比艺术更重要，因为策展人寻求第三世界点缀。他懊恼地描述自己与中国观众的疏离感。中国不发达的当代艺术博物馆体系迫使他“走向全球”，但外国叙事以惊异与发现来框定中国前卫艺术，已令他厌倦。这加剧了他与观众相隔绝的状态——那些观众共享着穿越北京社会和历史景观的类似经验。


〔原书 75〕

When I met with Zhu Jia several months later, the situation and his assessment of it had shifted.[^en-ch01-68] He had recently returned from trips to Berlin and New York, where his work had showed in separate exhibits. *Living in Time* at Berlin’s Hamburger Bahnhof Museum featured twenty-nine Chinese contemporary artists as part of *China Fest*, a showcase of Chinese culture sponsored by the Berlin Senate Administration for Science, Research and Culture and the State Council Information Office of the People’s Republic of China. Zhu explained that the Chinese Ministry of Culture had originally suggested a show of early twentieth-century ink painters. Their German counterparts, however, insisted on contemporary art by young artists. The Chinese conceded, according to Zhu, because with their application to join the WTO still pending, they wanted to present a modern and moderate face.

几个月后我再见到朱加时，情况和他对情况的判断都变了。[^zh-ch01-68] 他刚从柏林和纽约回来，作品在那里的不同展览中展出。柏林汉堡火车站博物馆的《生活在此时》展出了二十九位中国当代艺术家，属于“中国节”的一部分；这个中国文化展示活动由柏林参议院科学、研究与文化部以及中华人民共和国国务院新闻办公室资助。朱加解释说，中国文化部最初建议展出20世纪初的水墨画家。德国方面却坚持要年轻艺术家的当代艺术。朱加说，中方让步了，因为当时加入世贸组织的申请仍待批准，他们想展现现代而温和的面貌。


〔原书 75〕

The curators chosen for the show included Hou Hanru, a Chinese specialist in contemporary art living in Paris, and Fan Di’an, the vice president of the Central Academy of Fine Arts.[^en-ch01-69] Of the artists they selected, roughly one-third had exhibited the previous year in a controversial show staged by Ai Weiwei to coincide with the 2000 Shanghai Biennale. The exhibit title in English, *Fuck Off*, reflected more blatantly Ai’s in-your-face attitude than the Chinese title, *Bu hezuo fangshi* (Uncooperative approach).[^en-ch01-70] The exhibit, together with several others containing artworks that used animals, blood, or human corpses, prompted the Ministry of Culture to issue a public memorandum about the illegality of artworks that “violate state laws, upset social order and damage people’s mental and physical health.”[^en-ch01-71] Association with *Fuck Off* did not, however, prevent nine of its artists from being sponsored by the Ministry of Culture for an exhibition in Beijing’s German sister city.[^en-ch01-72]

展览选定的策展人包括旅居巴黎的中国当代艺术专家侯瀚如和中央美术学院副院长范迪安。[^zh-ch01-69] 在他们选出的艺术家中，大约三分之一参加了前一年艾未未为配合2000年上海双年展举办的有争议展览。展览英文标题“Fuck Off”比中文标题“不合作方式”（Bu hezuo fangshi）更直白地反映了艾未未肆无忌惮的态度。[^zh-ch01-70] 这个展览，连同其他几个包含使用动物、血液或人体尸体作品的展览，促使文化部发布公开通告，称“违反国家法律、扰乱社会秩序、损害人们身心健康”的艺术作品违法。[^zh-ch01-71] 然而，与“不合作方式”的关联并未阻止其中九位艺术家获得文化部赞助，参加在北京的德国姐妹城市举办的展览。[^zh-ch01-72]


〔原书 75, 76〕

Zhu Jia described experiencing profoundly mixed emotions during his trip to Berlin. He felt satisfaction that, for the first time ever, the Chinese government paid for his travel to an exhibit abroad. As the artists installed their pieces in the museum, Ministry of Culture officials came by to congratulate them on a successful show. With a sardonic smile, embarrassed by his own pleasure at the moment, Zhu said he had finally received the national recognition the patriotic education of his youth had taught him to desire. When the same officials spoke at a banquet after the opening about bringing the exhibit back to a museum in Beijing, Zhu judged their talk as a performance well suited for the moment. Not long after our conversation, however, two other *Living in Time* participants told a dinner gathering of artists that they’d heard it would open at the Millennium Monument in 2002. While they viewed this possibility as a good opportunity, they questioned their embrace of state institutionalization and launched into a discussion of the shifting cultural milieu.

朱加描述他在柏林之行中经历了极其复杂的情绪。他感到满足，因为这是中国政府第一次支付他出国参展的旅费。艺术家们在博物馆安装作品时，文化部官员前来祝贺他们展出成功。朱加带着讥讽的微笑，为自己的片刻喜悦感到尴尬；他说自己终于得到了少年时代爱国主义教育教他渴望的国家承认。同一批官员在开幕后的宴会上谈到要把展览带回北京一家博物馆时，朱加认为他们的讲话是适合当时场合的表演。然而，我们谈话后不久，另外两位《生活在此时》参展者在一个艺术家晚餐聚会上说，他们听说展览将于2002年在中华世纪坛开幕。他们把这看作好机会，却又质疑自己对国家制度化的拥抱，并展开关于文化环境变化的讨论。


〔原书 76〕

As they ate and drank, they narrated a diagram of triangulation. In the immediate post-1989 geography of Chinese avant-garde art, the receiving or buying end was generally *xifang* (the West). Beijing buzzed with energy generated by the tension between a desiring West and an image-anxious Chinese state. The interplay between *guanfang* (Chinese officialdom) and xifang allowed for what they called *minjian* (popular or folk) activities.[^en-ch01-73] As they held onto an idea of minjian as nonstate forms of social critique, they simultaneously struggled with anxieties of co-optation by increasing collaborations between xifang and guanfang, as in the *Living in Time* exhibit. While some believed in the development of local museums to bring Chinese contemporary art home, others worried that state institutionalization would limit their ability to creatively play xifang and guanfang off of each other, thereby shutting down cultural critique of both.

他们边吃边喝，讲述了一张三角关系的图式。在1989年之后的中国前卫艺术地理中，接收或购买的一端通常是“西方”（xifang）。北京充斥着由渴望的西方与形象焦虑的中国国家之间的张力所产生的能量。“官方”（guanfang）与“西方”之间的互动，为他们所谓的“民间”（minjian）活动提供了空间。[^zh-ch01-73] 他们一方面坚持民间作为非国家社会批判形式的观念，一方面又因西方与官方日益合作（如《生活在此时》展览）而焦虑被收编。有些人相信发展本地博物馆能把中国当代艺术带回家，另一些人则担心国家制度化会限制他们创造性地利用西方与官方之间矛盾的能力，从而关闭对两者的文化批判。


〔原书 76〕

Another twist on the museum in Beijing appeared as real estate developers adopted the cultural capital of “world-class” art districts and museums as a branding strategy. soho China led the trend, becoming Beijing’s largest real estate company and making its chairman Pan Shiyi and ceo Zhang Xin one of the nation’s wealthiest power couples. The moma Modern Land Group cultivated an even more obvious connection between cosmopolitan art, architecture, and privatized housing by naming successive developments after New York’s Museum of Modern Art. New York architect Steven Holl designed their Grand moma project, an award-winning complex of eight mixed-use towers linked by a sky ring completed in 2009.[^en-ch01-74] When I visited the site in 2007, a sales associate took me on a “virtual” tour that included a presentation in front of an illuminated city map; passage through a corridor of vitrines displaying architectural models of the project; and a walk through a sample unit appointed with modernist furniture. At the end, I received a bag full of promotional materials.
