In an uncooperative and uncompromising way, it self-consciously resists the threat of assimilation and vulgarization.” Ai and Feng, *Fuck Off*, 9.

[^zh-ch01-70]: 在图录中，艾未未与联合策展人冯博一摆出挑衅姿态："在今天的艺术中，'另类'位置意味着挑战和批判权力话语与流行惯例。它以不合作、不妥协的方式，自觉地抵抗同化与庸俗化的威胁。" Ai and Feng, *Fuck Off*, 9。

[^en-ch01-71]: Merewether, “The Spectre of Being Human,” 58.

[^zh-ch01-71]: Merewether, "The Spectre of Being Human," 58。

[^en-ch01-72]: Articles like Sun, “Shenghuo zai cishi,” in the *People’s Daily* reported that the exhibit “let people see that Chinese contemporary art is an art blazing new trails [*chuangxin de yishu*].”

[^zh-ch01-72]: 《人民日报》上 Sun 的 "Shenghuo zai cishi" 等文章报道说，这场展览"让人们看到中国当代艺术是创新的艺术"（chuangxin de yishu）。

[^en-ch01-73]: This use of *minjian* as a term of opposition to *guanfang* contrasted with its Maoist referent, folk traditions of the revolutionary rural peasantry. They used *minjian* instead as a synonym for “unofficial” to describe exhibits, such as *Fuck Off*, that did not bear the imprimatur of the state, and artist or curator-financed catalogues without ISBN numbers that could not officially be sold in bookstores.

[^zh-ch01-73]: 这里把"民间"（minjian）用作与"官方"（guanfang）对立，与毛泽东时代指涉革命农村农民民俗传统的"民间"不同。他们把"民间"当作"非官方"的同义词，用来描述《不合作方式》等未获国家批准举办的展览，以及艺术家或策展人自费印刷、没有书号、无法在书店正式销售的图录。

[^en-ch01-74]: While the complex is referred to in English as Grand moma, in Chinese it is *Dangdai* (contemporary) moma.

[^zh-ch01-74]: 这个建筑群在英文中称为 Grand MOMA，中文名则是"当代MOMA"。

[^en-ch01-75]: Full-page spreads provide details on New York’s Rockefeller and Time Warner Centers, Tokyo’s Roppongi Hills, and Paris’s La Défense District.

[^zh-ch01-75]: 跨页版面详细介绍了纽约洛克菲勒中心与时代华纳中心、东京六本木新城以及巴黎拉德芳斯区。

[^en-ch01-76]: Dangdai zhiye, *Dangdai moma by Steven Holl Architects*.

[^zh-ch01-76]: Dangdai zhiye, *Dangdai moma by Steven Holl Architects*。

[^en-ch01-77]: *La Danse* is part of the New York MoMA permanent collection.

[^zh-ch01-77]: 《舞蹈》（*La Danse*）是纽约现代艺术博物馆永久收藏的一部分。

[^en-ch01-78]: Tweedie, “Delirious Cities and Their Cinema,” 386–87.

[^zh-ch01-78]: Tweedie, "Delirious Cities and Their Cinema," 386–87。


## 第二章　展示北京


〔原书 79〕

Two: Showcase Beijing

第二章　展示北京


〔原书 79, 80〕

At dusk on August 23, 2001, a migrant worker’s voice echoed through the expansive space of a textile factory recently converted into Beijing’s East Modern Art Center (*Yuanyang yishu zhongxin*). The center served as a point of attraction within Ocean Paradise, a real estate development of high-rise apartment buildings still under construction. Lao Wei belted out the opening lines of a folk song from his village in Sichuan Province: “Flowers are covering the branches.... I am the only one alone.”[^en-ch02-1] As he sang, he wandered through an audience of art world cognoscenti, real estate publicists, and print and television reporters. The crowd had first gathered outside in the humid summer air, as a thunderstorm brewed. After entering the long interior space, they stood expectantly. On cue, dancers perched atop steel support beams began to descend. When the lights were thrown on, their bodies appeared in silhouette against the art center’s translucent glass walls. They picked up the refrain of Lao Wei’s tune as they dropped to the floor and began their performance against a backdrop of industrial salvage architecture and installation art: clusters of metal barrels, dangling fluorescent tube lighting, a row of manual sewing machines, piles of bricks, and architectural scale models half-buried in sand on the concrete floor. In the weeks that followed, diverse news outlets reported what transpired that evening with headlines like “A Difficult-to-Define Performance” and “Dancing with Another Kind of Body.”[^en-ch02-2] The art journal *Next Wave* stated matter-of-factly, “The performance astonished the audience, not only because it took place in this kind of real environment, but also because the performers unexpectedly included thirty rural migrant construction workers.”[^en-ch02-3] The review in the Guangzhou newspaper *Southern Weekly* opened with a more evocative description: “Two clusters of people: one whose posture resembled that of prisoners squatted in the distance, some wore no shirts, revealing dark, gleaming skin; another group wore cheap clothing, so that at a glance one could ascertain their identity—migrant worker [*mingong*]. They started to move, horizontally, pushing close to one another. Then those clothed and bare-chested interwove, two heterogeneous elements mixing freely together.” [^en-ch02-4] A rare shower of hail fell as audience members later dispersed, punctuating the evening’s drama.

2001年8月23日黄昏，一名民工的声音在一座不久前改造成北京远洋艺术中心（Yuanyang yishu zhongxin）的纺织厂宽阔空间里回荡。该中心是“远洋天地”内的一个吸引点——这是一个仍在施工中的高层公寓楼盘。老魏放声唱起他四川老家一首民歌的开头：“花儿盖满了枝头……只有我孤身一人。”[^zh-ch02-1] 他一边唱，一边在由艺术界行家、楼盘宣传人员和报刊电视记者组成的观众中游走。人群起初聚集在潮湿的夏日空气里，雷雨正在酝酿。进入狭长的室内空间后，他们满怀期待地站着。信号一到，栖在钢梁上的舞者开始下降。灯光亮起，他们的身体在艺术中心半透明玻璃墙的映衬下显出剪影。他们接续老魏曲调的叠句，落到地面，在利用旧工业建筑改造而成的空间和装置艺术的背景前开始表演：成簇的金属桶、悬垂的日光灯管、一排脚踏缝纫机、成堆的砖块，以及半埋在混凝土地面沙堆里的建筑模型。随后几周，多家新闻媒体以《一场难以定义的演出》《与另一种身体共舞》之类的标题报道了当晚发生的事。[^zh-ch02-2] 艺术杂志《新潮》直言：“这场演出令观众震惊，不仅因为它在这样一种真实环境中发生，还因为表演者中竟有三十名农村来的建筑民工。”[^zh-ch02-3] 《南方周末》的评论以更具感染力的描写开篇：“两群人：一群人的姿态像蹲在远处的囚犯，有些人没穿上衣，露出黝黑发亮的皮肤；另一群人穿着廉价衣服，一眼便可认出身份——民工（mingong）。他们开始移动，横向地、彼此紧挨着推挤。然后，穿衣服的和光膀子的交织在一起，两种异质元素自由混合。”[^zh-ch02-4] 观众后来散去时，一场罕见的冰雹落下，为当晚的戏剧性添上标点。


〔原书 80〕

*Dancing with Mingong* marked the opening and eventual demise of the East Modern Art Center, which would be torn down just over two years later.[^en-ch02-5] This multimedia happening—produced by a choreographer, Chinese and foreign modern dancers, a documentary filmmaker, a photographer, and two visual artists—presents a conundrum. What do we make of so-called avant-gardes working together with migrant construction workers, aged sixteen to forty-five, and real estate entrepreneurs from the spin-off corporation of a state-owned enterprise, attended by a full press of Beijing’s cultural elite and media outlets? How did a factory building in the middle of a commodity apartment development, the only remnant of an enormous socialist work unit that once provided workers with housing, become an art center? The brief efflorescence of the East Modern Art Center represents a turning point in the role of art museums in China.

《与民工共舞》标志着远洋艺术中心的开幕，也预示着它的终结——仅仅两年多后，它便被拆除。[^zh-ch02-5] 这场多媒体事件由一位编舞、中外现代舞者、一位纪录片导演、一位摄影师和两位视觉艺术家共同制作，呈现出一个难解的问题。所谓先锋与十六岁到四十五岁的建筑民工，以及国有企业衍生公司的房地产企业家共同合作，北京文化精英与媒体几乎倾巢出席，这该如何理解？一座位于商品房楼盘中央的厂房——一个曾为工人提供住房的庞大社会主义单位的唯一遗存——如何变成艺术中心？远洋艺术中心的短暂绽放，标志着中国美术馆角色的一次转折。


〔原书 80〕

The reform-era coalition of government and private interests invested in remaking Beijing created new opportunities for contemporary artists. It altered their relationship to a previously censorious state and broadened domestic viewership of their work. The intersection of urban planning, real estate, and art shaped their lives and sometimes became the subject of their art. Market-reform exhibition spaces gradually surpassed state-controlled museums exhibiting the art of proletarian revolutionary nationalism. Museums, increasingly supported by private funds, simultaneously became a model for real estate projects premised on a “desiring China,” Lisa Rofel’s characterization of a postsocialist reimagination of social life prioritizing “the individual who operates through sexual, material, and affective self-interest.”[^en-ch02-6] These projects capitalized on the desire for a worldly cultural milieu, in which the cosmopolitan art museum served as a modernizing, elevating brand.

改革时期政府与私人利益结成的联盟致力于重塑北京，为当代艺术家创造了新机会。它改变了艺术家与先前充满审查的国家之间的关系，也扩大了其作品在国内的观众群。城市规划、房地产与艺术的交汇塑造了他们的生活，有时也成为他们艺术的主题。市场改革的展览空间逐渐超越那些展示无产阶级革命民族主义艺术的国家控制博物馆。与此同时，越来越多由私人资金支持的博物馆，成为以“欲望中国”为前提的房地产项目的榜样——罗丽莎（Lisa Rofel）用这一说法概括后社会主义语境中对社会生活的重新想象，其中优先考虑“通过性的、物质的和情感的自利来运作的个人”。[^zh-ch02-6] 这些项目利用了人们对一种世界性文化氛围的渴望，在其中，世界主义的艺术博物馆成为一种现代化、提升品位的品牌。


〔原书 80, 81〕

Art centers created as part of commodity apartment enterprises emerged as a trend during the first years of new millennium Beijing. In ventures such as the East Modern Art Center, Left Bank Gallery, One World Art Center, X-Ray Art Center, and Today Art Gallery, urban planners and real estate developers became collaborators with artists and curators. Many of these experiments were ephemeral. Ten years later, only the Today Art Gallery remained. Their fleeting existence highlights conflicting ideas about the purpose of art exhibition in China’s capital as global showcase. Was art meant to express social critique, display national modernity, create class distinction, or maximize the value of newly commodified property? These experiments also reflected large-scale social restructuring throughout the 1980s and 1990s, in which urban housing reform contributed to increasing privatization of real estate and dismantling of socialist public housing and land management.[^en-ch02-7] Intensive demolition and relocation schemes turned the city over. Appropriated land was largely used for commercial development, including new commodity apartments (*shangpin fang*), leading to property speculation and skyrocketing prices. Bulldozers and construction cranes, as well as residents’ complaints and protests, pervaded Beijing and set the scene for contemporary art production.

作为商品房开发项目的一部分而创建艺术中心，在新千年最初几年的北京成为潮流。在远洋艺术中心、左岸画廊、一世界艺术中心、X光艺术中心、今日美术馆等项目中，城市规划者和房地产开发商成为艺术家与策展人的合作者。许多实验都是短暂的。十年后，只有今日美术馆仍在。它们的昙花一现凸显了关于艺术展览目的的相互冲突的观念——在中国首都作为全球展示窗口之际：艺术是要表达社会批判、展示国家现代性、制造阶级区隔，还是最大化刚刚商品化的房产价值？这些实验也反映了整个1980年代和1990年代的大规模社会重组，其中城市住房改革推动了房地产的日益私有化，并拆解了社会主义的公共住房与土地管理制度。[^zh-ch02-7] 密集的拆迁安置计划把城市翻了个底朝天。征用的土地大多用于商业开发，包括新的商品房，导致房地产投机和价格飞涨。推土机和建筑起重机，以及居民的抱怨与抗议，遍布北京，为当代艺术生产搭起了舞台。


〔原书 81〕

In the intertwining of public and private characteristic of late socialist China, real estate developers who ventured into art center construction and management represented one unexpected outcome, an externality of the nationwide reform of state-owned enterprises (soes). As soes developed into quasi-private, semi-independent entities, their leaders took land from downsized or shuttered factories and entered the expanding commercial property market. Members of the emergent real estate profession explored various marketing strategies; those who incorporated art galleries into their plans saw the promotion of contemporary art as a marker of taste that could attract potential homebuyers. An ironic situation arose for contemporary art. Critics and curators from the West understood Chinese officials to be repressive and disapproving of local contemporary art; they often found this belief confirmed by Chinese artists who complained about the dearth of domestic exhibition space for avant-garde expression. At the same time, new exhibition spaces for contemporary art, some created by branches of China’s largest and most influential soes, began opening. For example, within the same year that “*Canceled”: Exhibiting Experimental Art in China* was shown at the Smart Museum of Art in Chicago, one of its featured artists, Song Dong, participated in the large-scale experimental art project *Dancing with Mingong* at the East Modern Art Center, developed in Beijing by the state-owned China Ocean Shipping Company (cosco).[^en-ch02-8]

在晚期社会主义中国特有的公与私的交织中，冒险进入艺术中心建设与管理的房地产开发商，代表了一个出人意料的结果——国有企业（SOEs）全国性改革的外部性。随着国企发展为准私人、半独立的实体，其领导层从裁员或倒闭的工厂取得土地，进入不断扩张的商业地产市场。新兴房地产业的人士探索各种营销策略；将艺术画廊纳入计划者，把推广当代艺术视为品位标志，以吸引潜在购房者。当代艺术由此陷入一种讽刺处境。西方批评家和策展人认为中国官员压制、不赞成本土当代艺术；他们常常发现，抱怨国内缺乏先锋表达展览空间的中国艺术家印证了这一看法。与此同时，一些当代艺术的新展览空间开始开放，其中有的正由全中国最大、最具影响力的国企的分支机构创建。例如，在《“取消”：中国实验艺术展》于芝加哥斯马特艺术博物馆展出的同一年，其参展艺术家之一宋东参加了大型实验艺术项目《与民工共舞》——演出场地是国有的中国远洋运输公司（COSCO）在北京开发的远洋艺术中心。[^zh-ch02-8]


〔原书 81, 82〕

Part of artists’ distinction as interlocutors of cosmopolitan culture included engagement with globally circulating forms such as site-specific art, with its goal of exploring physical and social space outside museum walls. This marked a significant shift from the 1990s, during which official hostility to avant-garde art, particularly the unpredictable mediums of installation and performance art, prevailed. During that period, some artists turned to site-specific art in reaction to the conservatism of official exhibit spaces, and more importantly as a way of responding to the massive changes wrought by urban renewal.[^en-ch02-9] They moved out of the studio to engage their social environment in new ways. They roved the streets with spray paint can, camera, or camcorder in hand. They created installation and performance pieces in apartments, courtyards, and alleyways as well as in public spaces—parks, factories, and historical locations like the Great Wall. Documentary photographs and videos of performance pieces sometimes ended up in museums, but gallery exhibition was not necessarily originally intended. This situation changed as display in new quasi-public, quasi-private art spaces presented artists with opportunities for increased exposure to local audiences, as well as international art world observers. The practice of site-specific art then ran the risk of becoming tamed and commercialized as artists created pieces in and specifically for these new spaces.

艺术家作为世界性文化对话者的独特地位，部分来自他们对全球流通的艺术形式的参与，例如以探索博物馆围墙之外的物理与社会空间为目标的场域特定艺术。这标志着与1990年代的重大转变——当时官方对先锋艺术，尤其是装置和行为艺术这类不可预测的媒介，普遍持敌对态度。在此期间，一些艺术家转向场域特定艺术，以回应官方展览空间的保守主义，更重要的是以此回应城市更新带来的巨变。[^zh-ch02-9] 他们走出画室，以新的方式介入社会环境。他们手持喷漆罐、相机或摄像机在街头游走。他们在公寓、庭院、胡同以及公园、工厂和长城等历史场所创作装置和行为作品。行为作品的纪实照片和录像有时最终出现在博物馆里，但画廊展览未必是最初意图。随着新的准公共、准私人艺术空间中的展示为艺术家提供更多接触本地观众以及国际艺术界观察者的机会，这种情况发生了变化。场域特定艺术的实践于是面临被驯化和商业化的风险，因为艺术家开始在这些新空间中、并专门为这些空间创作作品。


〔原书 82〕

The story of the East Modern Art Center demonstrates how artists got caught up in the nexus of urban planning, real estate, and art. After the center opened in August 2001, it quickly became a hotspot for contemporary art exhibition, although a short-lived one. Its rise and fall reflects tensions over the role of art: to highlight growing forms of inequality and alienation in showcase Beijing; or to smooth them over in the promotion of commodity value, cultural capital, and middle-class sensibility as a form of global achievement.[^en-ch02-10]

远洋艺术中心的故事展示了艺术家如何卷入城市规划、房地产与艺术的交织网络。该中心于2001年8月开放后，迅速成为当代艺术展览的热点，尽管短暂。它的兴衰反映了围绕艺术角色的紧张：是凸显展示北京日益增长的不平等与异化形式，还是在推广商品价值、文化资本和中产阶级感性作为全球成就形式的过程中将其抹平。[^zh-ch02-10]


〔原书 82, 83〕

To provide the larger context for this case study, this chapter first presents an analysis of the nested relationship of state-led urban renewal, privatized real estate, art exhibition spaces, and art. Zooming in from the level of the city to Ocean Paradise to the East Modern Art Center to individual artworks exhibited there illuminates the various interests involved in the redefinition of what a museum is meant to do. Thinking about the linkages between these different scales sets up questions about how they influence one another in top-down or bottom-up ways. I begin, on the macro level, with how Beijing itself became a showcase in the city’s Olympic bid to go global, with spectacular urban planning initiatives meant to symbolize China’s cosmopolitan modernity and widespread demolition of historical neighborhoods leading to pseudo-preservation and museumification. I turn next to the reform-era phenomenon in China of commodity housing as part of a “growth-machine” ethic and an overall increase in consumption, and examine developers’ leveraging of art as a civilizing commodity. These sections culminate in an exploration of the historical layers, classed and gendered social relations, and ways of thinking that came together in the East Modern Art Center.

为给这一案例研究提供更大背景，本章首先分析国家主导的城市更新、私有化房地产、艺术展览空间与艺术之间的嵌套关系。从城市层面推进到远洋天地，再到远洋艺术中心，再聚焦到在那里展出的单件作品，可以揭示重新界定博物馆应有功能所涉及的各种利益。思考这些不同尺度之间的联系，会引出关于它们如何以自上而下或自下而上的方式相互影响的问题。我先从宏观层面开始，考察北京本身如何在申奥走向全球的过程中成为展示窗口，包括旨在象征中国世界性现代性的壮观城市规划举措，以及历史街区的大规模拆除如何导致伪保存和博物馆化。接下来，我转向改革时期中国商品房现象，把它作为“增长机器”伦理与整体消费增长的一部分，并考察开发商如何把艺术用作文明化的商品。这些部分最终汇聚到对远洋艺术中心的历史层次、阶级化与性别化的社会关系，以及在此交汇的各种思维方式进行探讨。


〔原书 83〕

Beijing as Museum

北京作为博物馆


〔原书 83〕

After Beijing won the 2008 Olympic bid on July 13, 2001, a second wave of urban renewal, even more intense than that of the 1990s, engulfed the city.[^en-ch02-11] In addition to large-scale demolition and relocation, the government hired star international architects to design key monuments: Paul Andreu’s National Grand Theater, Rem Koolhaas’s China Central Television headquarters, and Herzog and de Meuron’s Beijing National Stadium.[^en-ch02-12] Capital development led to a new place of prominence for the architectural scale model, as officials and residents alike debated monumental designs and future projections of the city’s layout. These three-dimensional visualizations became part of everyday life, displayed as works of art and commodities in new museums and real estate offices, and in advertisements that filled newspapers and appeared plastered on walls and billboards throughout the city.[^en-ch02-13]

2001年7月13日北京赢得2008年奥运会主办权后，第二波城市更新吞没了这座城市，比1990年代更为猛烈。[^zh-ch02-11] 除了大规模拆迁，政府还聘请国际明星建筑师设计标志性建筑：保罗·安德鲁的国家大剧院、雷姆·库哈斯的中央电视台总部大楼、赫尔佐格和德梅隆的北京国家体育场。[^zh-ch02-12] 首都建设使建筑模型获得新的突出地位，官员和居民都在辩论纪念性设计和城市布局的未来想象。这些三维可视化成为日常生活的一部分，作为艺术品和商品陈列在新的博物馆和售楼处，也出现在充斥报纸、张贴于全城墙面和广告牌的广告中。[^zh-ch02-13]


〔原书 83〕

This obsession with planning and the symbolic importance of the capital’s built environment can be traced to the premodern era. The legacy of imperial city planning persists in the conflict between spatial expressions of power and functionality.[^en-ch02-14] The Beijing Urban Planning Museum, which opened in 2004 on the southeast corner of Tiananmen Square, celebrates planning as a legitimizing act, underwritten in part by new real estate development companies, including Sino-Ocean (cosco’s subsidiary) and soho China. Its spectacular projections of the city’s future elided social hierarchies intensified by urban renewal: the displacement of long-term residents from the city center to less desirable, peripheral locations and the temporary labor force of rural migrants brought in to build the city’s new buildings. The architectural model on display became a fetish object on which audiences were mobilized to project collective dreamworlds—of the private, aestheticized space of the commodity apartment and of China’s global arrival. In Susan Buck-Morss’s formulation, such dreamworlds of modernity “are expressions of a utopian desire for social arrangements that transcend existing forms,” but that become dangerous “when their enormous energy is used instrumentally by structures of power, mobilized as an instrument of force that turns against the very masses who were supposed to benefit.”[^en-ch02-15]

对规划的痴迷以及首都建成环境的象征重要性，可追溯到前现代时期。帝国城市规划的遗产延续在空间权力表达与功能之间的冲突中。[^zh-ch02-14] 2004年在天安门广场东南角开放的北京市规划展览馆，把规划颂扬为一种赋予合法性的行为，其部分资金来自新的房地产开发公司，包括远洋（中远的子公司）和SOHO中国。它壮观的城市未来投影抹去了因城市更新而加剧的社会等级：长期居民从市中心被迁往条件较差的外围地区，以及为建造城市新楼而引入的农村流动劳动力。展出的建筑模型成为拜物教对象，观众被动员在其上投射集体梦想世界——商品公寓私密的、审美化的空间，以及中国的全球登场。用苏珊·巴克-莫斯的话说，这类现代性梦想世界“表达了对超越现有形式的社会安排的乌托邦欲望”，但当“其巨大能量被权力结构工具性地利用，被动员为一种暴力工具，转而针对本应受益的群众”时，便变得危险。[^zh-ch02-15]


〔原书 84〕

![图2.01　参观者与按比例制作的三维北京地图合影。前景为奥林匹克公园，其南北轴线与首都传统的中轴线对齐。北京市规划展览馆，2007年。作者摄。](web/assets/ch02-b012.jpg)

FIG 2.01 Visitors taking a photograph with a to-scale, three-dimensional map of Beijing. The Olympic Green, whose north-south axis aligns with the traditional imperial meridian line of the capital, is pictured in the foreground. Beijing Urban Planning Museum, 2007. Photograph by author.

图2.01　参观者与按比例制作的三维北京地图合影。前景为奥林匹克公园，其南北轴线与首都传统的中轴线对齐。北京市规划展览馆，2007年。作者摄。


〔原书 84, 85〕

In 2007, the four stories of the exposed steel beam and glass-encased Beijing Urban Planning Museum presented an orchestrated chronology of the city from its founding in the Yuan Dynasty to its Olympic triumph. From a ground-floor reception area, visitors proceeded to second-floor exhibits of Beijing’s eighteen districts and counties and a third-floor narrative of the capital’s development through the Yuan, Ming, Qing, and Republican periods, with socialist planning by and large skipped over. History then gave way to the museum’s largest and most popular exhibit: a scale map of the contemporary city that spread across the floor under dramatic lighting. Three-dimensional architectural models represented the urban core surrounding the Forbidden City. This area was cordoned off, but the map continued well beyond with aerial photographs, under glass and illuminated from below, which visitors walked over as they searched for familiar locations (figure 2.01). Side exhibits displayed areas of architectural distinction, such Beijing’s new high-rise-filled Central Business District (cbd). The fourth floor included models of Beijing’s Olympic sports facilities, illuminated maps of global cities such as Paris, Tokyo, London, Moscow, and New York, and a multimedia hall where visitors could watch a double feature of *The Immortal City* and *The New Beijing*. The second 3-D animation offered a visual ride through a vertiginous cityscape that mixed together existing buildings with future designs, such as the Rem Koolhaas cctv tower.[^en-ch02-16]

2007年，北京市规划展览馆的四层空间以裸露钢梁和玻璃幕墙构成，呈现了一部精心编排的城市编年史，从元代建城到奥运胜利。从底层接待区开始，参观者前往二层观看北京十八个区县的展览，再到三层观看元、明、清和民国时期首都发展的叙述，社会主义规划大体被跳过。历史随后让位于博物馆最大、最受欢迎的展品：一张在戏剧性灯光下铺满地面的当代城市比例地图。三维建筑模型代表紫禁城周边的城市核心区。该区域被围栏隔开，但地图远远延伸出去，以航空照片的形式置于玻璃之下、从下方照亮，参观者一边走在其上，一边寻找熟悉的地点（图2.01）。侧展厅展示具有建筑特色的区域，如北京布满新高楼的中央商务区（CBD）。四层包括北京奥运体育设施的模型、巴黎、东京、伦敦、莫斯科、纽约等世界城市被照亮的地图，以及一个多媒体厅，观众可以在那里观看《不朽之城》和《新北京》双片连映。第二部三维动画提供了一次穿越令人眩晕的城市景观的视觉之旅，将现有建筑与未来设计混合在一起，例如雷姆·库哈斯的央视大楼。[^zh-ch02-16]


〔原书 85〕

If the museum encouraged visitors to understand Beijing as a world metropolis that represented the past and future grandeur of China, with its socialist history strategically erased, it also linked this vision to a progrowth, commercialized mode of urban dwelling. Nestled next to the third-floor historical exhibits, a model commodity apartment half-hidden behind white plastic walls beckoned visitors to enter a space of modern domestic fantasy, in which they could aspire to become part of, to inhabit on a personal level, the museum showcase of Beijing. Oversize, ornate, vaguely Victorian chairs dominated the living room. A mannequin of a young girl lay on a velvet-draped bed in a darkened room on whose walls a dreamy, flowery projection flickered. Mod red café stools in a living room looked out on a picture window/screen that showed a video-loop view of the Olympic Green with fireworks exploding over it to a syncopated soundtrack. Discrete white raised characters on the outside wall of the exhibit informed visitors that it was “donated by soho China.”

如果博物馆鼓励参观者把北京理解为一个代表中国过去与未来辉煌的世界大都市，并策略性地抹去其社会主义历史，它也将这一愿景与一种亲增长、商业化的城市居住方式联系起来。在三层历史展览旁边，一套半掩在白色塑料墙后的样板商品房邀请参观者进入一个现代家庭幻想空间，在那里他们可以渴望成为北京博物馆展示的一部分，在个人层面上栖居其中。客厅里摆着超大、华丽、隐约带有维多利亚风格的椅子。一个年轻女孩的人体模型躺在铺着天鹅绒的床上，房间昏暗，墙上闪烁着梦幻的花卉投影。客厅里的现代红色咖啡凳朝向一扇画窗/屏幕，屏幕上循环播放奥林匹克公园的影像，烟花在切分音配乐中绽放。展品外墙上的独立白色凸起字告诉参观者，它“由SOHO中国捐赠”。


〔原书 85, 86〕

A corollary of the move to turn the city into a site of display was the growth of museums. The widespread demolition caused by urban planning spurred efforts to preserve the cultural heritage of quickly disappearing historic neighborhoods. Museumlike spaces displayed protected fragments or theme-park-like re-creations, ranging from the Red Gate Gallery’s exhibiting of contemporary art in the Dongbianmen watchtower of the old city wall to rickshaw alleyway tours of the Houhai neighborhood to the shopping mall re-creation of the Qing Dynasty Qianmen commercial district. The development of museums became an important sector of China’s growing culture industry. From 2001 to 2010, the number of registered museums in Beijing grew from 110 to 156, a 42 percent increase.[^en-ch02-17] These numbers include private museums, the first of which was registered in Beijing in 1996, and large state projects such as the China Millennium Monument (2000), Beijing Urban Planning Museum (2004), China National Film Museum (2005), and the new Capital Museum (2006). In Beijing, the temporal and ideological relationship between urban renewal and museum development conferred on museums a double mandate of memorializing certain pasts and imagining certain futures, thereby muting debate over the catastrophic effects of the Communist dreamworld or of the market-reform dreamworld rapidly replacing it.

把城市变成展示场所的另一个结果是博物馆的增长。城市规划导致的大规模拆除，促使人们努力保护迅速消失的历史街区的文化遗产。类似博物馆的空间展示受保护的碎片，或像主题公园一样的再造景观，从红门画廊在老城墙东便门城楼展示当代艺术，到后海街区的人力车胡同游，再到购物中心对清代前门商业区的再造。博物馆的发展成为中国不断增长的文化产业的重要部门。从2001年到2010年，北京注册博物馆的数量从110座增长到156座，增幅42%。[^zh-ch02-17] 这些数字包括私人博物馆（北京首家私人博物馆于1996年注册），以及大型国家项目，如中华世纪坛（2000）、北京市规划展览馆（2004）、中国电影博物馆（2005）和新首都博物馆（2006）。在北京，城市更新与博物馆发展之间的时间与意识形态关系，赋予博物馆双重使命：纪念某些过去，想象某些未来，从而压制关于共产主义梦想世界或迅速取代它的市场改革梦想世界之灾难性后果的辩论。


〔原书 86〕

Museum display practices create frames for understanding and interacting with the world that extend beyond institutional walls. Barbara Kirshenblatt-Gimblett describes this “museum effect”: “Not only do ordinary things become special when placed in museum settings, but also the museum experience itself becomes a model for experiencing life outside its walls.... An ethnographic bell jar drops over the terrain. A neighborhood, village, or region becomes for all intents and purposes a living museum in situ.”[^en-ch02-18] The “museum effect” was at work in contemporary Beijing, to the extent that visiting foreigners or Chinese whose own lives were sufficiently buffered from the material and social ruptures of urban renewal could explore the city as a museum of a disappearing past. A form of what Marilyn Ivy calls “discourses of the vanishing,” leisured consumption of a suspended past held on the verge of disappearing assuaged anxieties about the loss of cultural identity while also demonstrating the achievement of global modernity.[^en-ch02-19] In Beijing, the museum effect also encouraged residents who aspired to cosmopolitan parity with global cities like New York and Paris to see new commodity homes as modern art objects, a future under construction in which China is recognized as a place in the process of accumulating widely acknowledged forms of privilege and beauty. The museum could be as much a dreamy snow globe as an ethnographic bell jar.

博物馆展示实践创造了理解和与世界互动的方式，其框架延伸至机构围墙之外。芭芭拉·柯申布拉特-金布莱特将这种“博物馆效应”描述为：“不仅普通物品被置于博物馆环境中时变得特殊，博物馆经验本身也成为在围墙之外体验生活的模式……一个民族志玻璃钟罩罩在地形上。一个街区、村庄或地区实际上就成了一座原地保存的活态博物馆。”[^zh-ch02-18] “博物馆效应”在当代北京发挥了作用，以至于来访的外国人，或自身生活与城市更新的物质和社会断裂有足够缓冲的中国人，都可以把这座城市当作一座展示正在消失的过去的博物馆来探索。这是玛丽琳·艾维所称“消逝的话语”的一种形式：对悬置在消失边缘的过去的悠闲消费，缓解了文化认同丧失的焦虑，同时也展示了全球现代性的成就。[^zh-ch02-19] 在北京，博物馆效应还鼓励那些渴望与纽约、巴黎等全球城市平起平坐的居民，把新的商品房视为现代艺术品，视其为正在建设中的未来——中国在其中被认可为一个正在积累广泛承认的特权与美的形式的地方。博物馆可以既是梦幻的雪花玻璃球，也是民族志的玻璃钟罩。


〔原书 86〕

Apartment Art

公寓艺术


〔原书 86, 87〕

State urban planning initiatives coincided with a new housing regime. City residents once received affordable housing through the socialist work unit, but beginning in the 1990s this basic resource became commoditized, with new apartments built and sold by progrowth coalitions of private and public entities.[^en-ch02-20] Scholars of Chinese urban planning have taken up the “growth machine” as a comparative heuristic for thinking about China’s rapid urbanization during economic reform. This concept theorizes the value transactions that drive urban redevelopment: the everyday use value of a particular site—community cohesion, everyday sociality, local history, small-scale commerce—is usurped by a quest for exchange value in which land is commoditized for wealth accumulation. In the city as growth machine, “the pursuit of exchange values so permeates the life of localities that cities become organized as enterprises devoted to the increase of aggregate rent levels through the intensification of land use.”[^en-ch02-21] This process, while often protested by residents in the neighborhoods it threatens to obliterate, “pervades virtually all aspects of local life, including the political system, the agenda for economic development, and even cultural organizations like baseball teams and museums.”[^en-ch02-22]

国家城市规划举措与新的住房制度同时发生。城市居民曾经通过社会主义工作单位获得负担得起的住房，但从1990年代开始，这一基本资源被商品化，新公寓由亲增长的公私实体联盟建造和出售。[^zh-ch02-20] 中国城市规划学者把“增长机器”作为比较性启发工具，用来思考经济改革期间中国快速城市化。这一概念从理论上阐释了驱动城市再开发的价值交易：特定地点的日常使用价值——社区凝聚、日常社会性、地方历史、小规模商业——被对交换价值的追求所取代，土地被商品化以积累财富。在以增长机器为组织方式的城市中，“对交换价值的追求如此渗透地方生活，以至于城市被组织成企业，通过土地使用的集约化来增加总地租水平”。[^zh-ch02-21] 这一过程虽然常遭面临被抹除的社区居民抗议，却“几乎渗透地方生活的所有方面，包括政治制度、经济发展议程，甚至棒球队和博物馆之类的文化组织”。[^zh-ch02-22]


〔原书 87〕

In an article titled “Is History Repeating Itself?” Yan Zhang and Ke Fang compare the U.S. federal urban redevelopment program of the 1950s and 1960s with contemporary Chinese efforts and conclude that a city like Beijing is a “growth machine in the making.”[^en-ch02-23] They point out many similarities between the two cases, including destruction of tradition and tricks employed by elite coalitions of government and business interests that turn the stated beneficiaries of development into victims. They also identify ways in which the Chinese case reflects a different political and socioeconomic context. Under market reform, increased decentralization of government conferred to local government much of the power to control the exchange value of once publically held land; and their business dealings included involvement with both domestic and foreign partners. The unclear line between public and private in entities like local soes and their spin-off companies facilitated the tight networking of government and business elites in redevelopment schemes; these networks, with the power to enact ideological visions of spatial modernity and to accumulate disproportionate wealth for those at the top, constitute late-socialist progrowth coalitions.[^en-ch02-24] Finally, in contrast with sporadic success in the United States of grassroots activism to protect neighborhoods from being bulldozed, tight social control in China meant that in spite of isolated, often well-publicized protests, popular resistance did little to change the course of urban renewal.

在《历史是否在重演？》一文中，Yan Zhang 和 Ke Fang 将1950至1960年代美国联邦城市再开发计划与当代中国实践相比较，得出结论：像北京这样的城市是“形成中的增长机器”。[^zh-ch02-23] 他们指出两个案例之间有许多相似之处，包括对传统的破坏，以及政府与商业利益精英联盟所采用的伎俩——把宣称的开发受益者变成受害者。他们还指出中国案例反映不同政治与社会经济背景的方式。在市场改革下，政府权力日益下放，使地方政府获得控制曾经公有土地交换价值的大部分权力；其商业往来包括与国内外合作伙伴的接触。在地方国企及其衍生公司等实体中，公私界限模糊，促进了政府与商业精英在再开发计划中的紧密网络；这些网络拥有实施空间现代性的意识形态愿景、并为上层积累不成比例财富的权力，构成晚期社会主义的亲增长联盟。[^zh-ch02-24] 最后，与美国草根行动在保护社区免遭推土机方面偶尔取得成功不同，中国严密的社会控制意味着，尽管有孤立的、往往被广泛报道的抗议，民众抵抗对城市更新的进程几乎无所改变。


〔原书 87, 88〕

Beijing as a growth machine in the making opens up questions about the tenuous interpellation of artists by progrowth coalitions. On the one hand, with state stipends for artists a thing of the socialist past, they sought new ways to survive in an increasingly market-driven environment: through sales of artwork, patronage by wealthy individuals, participation in primarily overseas artist residencies, design work, teaching, or other jobs that supported their ability to make art. On the other hand, not all artists fully embraced the commoditization of their work. In fact, doing so could conflict with their own philosophies of art as a form of social observation and critique. The counterpractices developed by artists like those who created *Dancing with Mingong* at the East Modern Art Center destabilized visions of growth-machine cities as inevitable or desirable.[^en-ch02-25] At the same time, the difficulty they experienced in integrating public involvement in their site-specific experiments drew attention to the social context of weak community power detailed by urban planning scholars.

把北京视为形成中的增长机器，引出关于亲增长联盟与艺术家之间不稳固的询唤关系的问题。一方面，在艺术家国家津贴已成为社会主义过去之后，他们在日益由市场驱动的环境中寻求新的生存方式：出售作品、富裕个人赞助、参加主要在海外的艺术家驻留项目、设计工作、教学或其他支持其创作的工作。另一方面，并非所有艺术家都完全接受其作品的商品化。事实上，这样做可能与他们自己的艺术哲学相冲突，即艺术是一种社会观察和批判的形式。像在远洋艺术中心创作《与民工共舞》的艺术家们所发展出的反实践，动摇了把增长机器城市视为不可避免或可取的愿景。[^zh-ch02-25] 同时，他们在把公众参与融入场域特定实验时经历的困难，也引起人们对城市规划学者所详述的社区权力薄弱这一社会背景的关注。


〔原书 88〕

A genealogy of the term *apartment art* demonstrates the turn in Chinese contemporary art from a subversive underground activity to a form of cultural capital with new domestic market value. Gao Minglu coined this term while writing about Chinese avant-garde art in the 1990s:

“公寓艺术”一词的谱系，展示了中国当代艺术从颠覆性的地下活动向在国内市场上获得新价值的文化资本的转变。高名潞在1990年代论述中国先锋艺术时创造了这个词：


〔原书 88〕

Facing many difficulties during the nineties—such as a lack of acceptance of the avant-garde by both official and commercial galleries in China, being ignored by the media, lack of attention by the organizers of some Chinese avant-garde exhibitions overseas, and a paucity of financial resources—conceptual artists have had to retreat to confined spaces. They have been forced to do or keep their work at home; to employ inexpensive materials in small-scale work that can be displayed in a private space; and to communicate only with a small audience of artists and interested persons. Thus I call this phenomenon Apartment Art (Gongyu yishu).[^en-ch02-26]

在九十年代面临重重困难——先锋艺术在中国既不被官方画廊也不被商业画廊接受，被媒体忽视，一些中国先锋艺术海外展览的组织者不予关注，且资金匮乏——观念艺术家不得不退回到狭小的空间。他们被迫在家中创作或保存作品；使用廉价材料制作可在私人空间展示的小型作品；只能与由艺术家和感兴趣者组成的小圈子交流。因此我把这一现象称为公寓艺术（Gongyu yishu）。[^zh-ch02-26]


〔原书 88〕

Just a few years later, this definition would come to seem outdated as some of the very artists Gao named as exemplary of the category began to exhibit their work in a widening ambit of domestic and international contexts. By the early 2000s, the term could be repurposed to describe a new traffic between art and commodity apartment that pulled artists into its sphere of influence.

仅仅几年后，高名潞列为该范畴范例的一些艺术家开始在国内和国际不断扩展的范围内展出作品，这一定义便显得过时了。到2000年代初，这个词可以被重新用来描述艺术与商品房之间新的流通，这种流通把艺术家拉入其影响范围。


〔原书 88〕

As an emerging urban middle class in China embraced the privatization of property and lifestyle, they sought ways to establish their class distinction, against the historical backdrop of a once putatively classless society.[^en-ch02-27] As real estate developers advertised their new private housing projects, they circulated images marketing different types of middle-class distinction. One popular strategy in Beijing was an association with art, not for social revolution but for art’s sake. These images promoted art as a desired form of cosmopolitan leisure. They asserted the following proposition: one starts with an empty apartment and learns to design and decorate this private space as an expression of personal aesthetics that can be developed through the proper art of consumption.

随着中国新兴城市中产阶级拥抱财产和生活方式的私有化，他们寻求确立自身阶级区隔的方式，而背景是一个曾经被宣称无阶级的社会。[^zh-ch02-27] 当房地产开发商宣传新的私宅项目时，他们传播推销不同类型中产阶级区隔的图像。在北京，一种流行的策略是与艺术建立联系——不是为了社会革命，而是为艺术而艺术。这些图像把艺术推崇为一种令人向往的世界性休闲方式。它们提出如下主张：从一间空公寓开始，学习设计和装饰这个私人空间，作为个人审美的表达，而这种审美可以通过掌握恰当的消费之道来培养。


〔原书 88, 89〕

A campaign for the Beautiful Garden housing estate incorporated imagery drawn from Western masterpieces, works that would have been declared bourgeois and decadent during the height of Chinese socialism. Half-page newspaper ads featured a rendering of the apartment complex in various European styles of modernist painting. Paul Gaugin’s 1894 *Nave Nave Moe (Sacred Spring*) inspires their nod to postimpressionist symbolism. In an ingenious reworking of the original (figure 2.02), the foreground features an almost exact copy of two Tahitian women seated on the ground, while the middle ground turns two bathers into apartment residents clad in white, and the background replaces totemic stone sculptures with an apartment block. The accompanying slogan, “Return to Beautiful Garden,” plays on the double meaning of coming home to one’s private oasis and achieving a position of worldly privilege in which one can recognize this art historical reference and appreciate Gaugin’s primitivizing, feminizing exoticism as an expression of one’s own progress. Beautiful Garden residents, the ad promises, wander through a lush, color-drenched landscape (a figment of the imagination in the polluted megacity of Beijing) like tourists from the developed world while going to and from a modern luxury apartment on the horizon.

“美丽园”住宅小区的广告运动融入了取自西方名作的图像——这些作品在中国社会主义鼎盛时期会被宣判为资产阶级和颓废的。半版报纸广告以不同欧洲现代主义绘画风格呈现该公寓楼群的渲染图。保罗·高更1894年的《纳韦·纳韦·莫埃（神圣的春天）》启发了他们对后印象派象征主义的致意。在对原作的巧妙改造中（图2.02），前景几乎原样复制了两名坐在地上的塔希提妇女，中景把两个沐浴者变成身穿白衣的公寓居民，背景则用一栋公寓楼取代图腾石雕。伴随的广告语“重返美丽园”玩的是双重含义：回到自己的私人绿洲，以及达到一种世界性特权位置——在那里，人们能够辨认这一艺术史典故，并把高更那种原始化、女性化的异国情调欣赏为自身进步的体现。广告承诺，美丽园居民将像来自发达世界的游客一样，漫步于郁郁葱葱、色彩浓郁（在这座污染严重的北京巨型城市中纯属想象）的风景中，同时往返于地平线上一套现代豪华公寓。


〔原书 89〕

![图2.02　“美丽园”房地产广告，《北京青年报》，2000年11月15日。](web/assets/ch02-b026.jpg)

FIG 2.02 Beautiful Garden real estate advertisement, *Beijing Youth News*, November 15, 2000.

图2.02　“美丽园”房地产广告，《北京青年报》，2000年11月15日。


〔原书 89, 90〕

The traffic between art and commodity apartment exerted a pull on artists as they forged paths for themselves in an emerging market economy, but it also became a problem for them to explore through the medium of art. I examine the encounters that ensued when artists discovered in Ocean Paradise’s East Modern Art Center an intriguing opportunity for creating and exhibiting work. My mode of investigation is archaeological to the extent that I describe the substrata—ways of thinking, forms of sociopolitical organization, and elements of the built environment—that made up this particular Beijing location. These substrata structured what could be expressed artistically. They did not, however, exist in discrete layers that could be easily isolated. Instead they impinged on one another. What appears as a radical shift—the socialist factory razed to make way for the commodity apartments of globalization—also harbored shared qualities of vision. The art created and exhibited in this nested context of Showcase Beijing–Ocean Paradise–East Modern Art Center mixes and plays on the mass utopian grandiosity of socialism and capitalism, participating in but also calling into question the bankruptcy of the dreams they trade on.

艺术与商品房之间的流通在艺术家于新兴市场经济中为自己开辟道路时对他们产生拉力，但也成为他们通过艺术媒介加以探讨的问题。我考察当艺术家在远洋天地的远洋艺术中心发现创作和展出作品的有趣机会时，随之而来的相遇。我的考察方式可以说是考古式的：描述构成这一特定北京地点的基底——思维方式、社会政治组织形式，以及建成环境的要素。这些基底结构了艺术上可以表达的东西。然而，它们并非存在于可轻易分离的离散层次中，而是相互冲撞。看似激进转变的东西——社会主义工厂被夷平，为全球化的商品房让路——也蕴含相通的愿景特质。在这个展示北京—远洋天地—远洋艺术中心的嵌套语境中创作和展出的艺术，混合并戏耍社会主义与资本主义的群众乌托邦宏大幻想，参与其中，也质疑其所交易的梦想的破产。


〔原书 90〕

Ocean Paradise’s East Modern Art Center

远洋天地的远洋艺术中心


〔原书 90〕

At the turn of the twenty-first century, Ocean Paradise developers broke ground just outside Ciyun Temple Bridge on Beijing’s East Fourth Ring Road. Although the location would soon adjoin the cbd, at the time it remained on the city’s edge. The border zone between rural and urban represents a long twentieth-century Chinese history of social debate, in which the city and the country have served as politically demarcated spaces, temporalities, and ideologies. This debate played out in the layers of change made to the site as it was cleared, constructed, razed, gutted, and eventually remade as Ocean Paradise.

二十一世纪之交，远洋天地的开发商在慈云寺桥外、北京东四环路破土动工。虽然该地点很快将与中央商务区毗邻，当时仍在城市边缘。城乡交界地带代表着二十世纪中国漫长社会辩论的历史，城市与乡村在其中充当政治上划定的空间、时间和意识形态。这场辩论体现在该地点历经的层层变化中：清理、建设、夷平、拆空，最终改建为远洋天地。


〔原书 90, 91〕

In 1919, Li Dazhao, the intellectual who two years later cofounded the Chinese Communist Party, denounced the corrupting influence of China’s semicolonial cities: “My young friends drifting about in the cities! You should know that the cities are full of crime, and that great contentment is to be found in the villages; that life in the city is more or less the life of a ghost, but that the work going on in the villages is the work of people; that the air in the city is foul and the air in the villages is pure.”[^en-ch02-28] Thirty years later, Mao Zedong, Great Helmsman of the new state, announced a vision that would stand in tension with Communist commitment to the peasantry for decades to come. He stood atop the Gate of Heavenly Peace and expressed his hope that one day this vantage point would afford a view of hundreds of smokestacks symbolizing China’s industrial modernization.[^en-ch02-29] On a 1950 street map of Beijing, the area outside of the Second Ring Road remained virtually blank. That would soon change. The rhetorical revolutionary potential of the peasantry laid the ground for the rise of the state industrial sector, with those officially classified as rural citizens provided less access to public goods, such as education and health care, than the urban proletariat. Central planners collectivized land ownership and enacted the *hukou* (household registration) system that bound farmers to agricultural areas. They simultaneously incorporated key tracts of farmland, once empty spaces on the margins of the city map, into their vision of a factory-studded urban landscape.

1919年，两年后参与创建中国共产党的知识分子李大钊谴责中国半殖民地城市的腐蚀性影响：“我的青年朋友们在城市里漂泊！你们应当知道，城市充满了罪恶，最大的满足在乡村；城市生活或多或少是鬼的生活，而乡村进行的工作是人的工作；城市的空气污浊，乡村的空气纯净。”[^zh-ch02-28] 三十年后，新国家的伟大舵手毛泽东宣布了一个愿景，它在此后数十年里将与共产党对农民的承诺形成紧张关系。他站在天安门城楼上，表达了他的希望：有朝一日，从这个制高点望去，能看到数以百计象征中国工业现代化的烟囱。[^zh-ch02-29] 在1950年的一张北京街道地图上，二环路以外的地区几乎是空白。这种情况很快将改变。农民在修辞上的革命潜力为国家工业部门的兴起奠定基础，而官方划为农村公民的人获得教育和医疗等公共物品的机会少于城市无产阶级。中央计划者将土地所有制集体化，并实施把农民束缚在农业地区的户口制度。他们同时把主要农田——曾经是城市地图边缘的空白空间——纳入工厂林立城市景观的愿景中。


〔原书 91〕

To the southeast of Ciyun Temple, work teams cleared agricultural fields and traced the ground with the lines of a modernist grid. Foundations were poured for spinning and weaving workshops and worker dormitories of what would become China’s three largest state-run textile factories, the No. 1, No. 2, and No. 3 Cotton Mills. At the height of production, each factory employed approximately eight thousand workers, more than 80 percent of whom were female. In “Talking of Women’s Liberation,” a correspondent for *Peking Review*, an official foreign-language weekly, recounts a 1973 visit to the No. 3 Cotton Mill. Deputy Secretary Wang, a veteran cadre and member of her work unit’s party standing committee, proudly stated that in 1955 she had helped build the factory.[^en-ch02-30] Some three decades later, *China Textile News* reported the financial challenges faced by the Beijing Cotton Textile Group, the conglomerate name assigned to the three mills after their incorporation in the 1990s.[^en-ch02-31]

在慈云寺东南方，工作队清理农田，并以现代主义网格的线条在地面上划出轮廓。他们为将成为中国三大国营纺织厂——国棉一厂、二厂、三厂——的纺纱织布车间和工人宿舍浇筑地基。在生产高峰期，每家工厂雇佣约八千名工人，其中80%以上是女性。官方外文周刊《北京周报》的一位记者在《谈妇女解放》中记述了1973年访问国棉三厂的经历。王副书记是一位老干部，也是她所在工作单位的党委常委，她自豪地说，1955年她曾参与建造这座工厂。[^zh-ch02-30] 大约三十年后，《中国纺织报》报道了北京棉纺织集团面临的财务挑战——该集团是三家工厂在1990年代合并后所冠的企业名称。[^zh-ch02-31]


〔原书 91〕

When Deng Xiaoping advocated for opening and reform to *chuang shijie* (break a path to the world), the related phrase *xia hai* ( jump into the ocean) emerged as a 1990s buzzword. Figuratively meaning to abandon socialist work affiliations and go into private business, it became the organizing logic of the Ocean Paradise brand. The land under the No. 3 Cotton Mill was sold to the state-owned cosco, whose containers fill cargo ships in ports worldwide and whose leaders had diversified into real estate. cosco’s commercial real estate ventures, which began in the port cities of Shanghai, Dalian, Qingdao, Guangzhou, and Nantong, expanded and joined forces with Sinochem, one of China’s four major state-owned oil companies. This merger gave rise to cosred (cosco Real Estate Development), eventually known as Sino-Ocean Land Limited, and in 2000 they received permission to begin construction in the capital. A policy enacted after Beijing won its Olympic bid in 2001 mandated that all industrial enterprises move outside of the Fifth Ring Road, in part to control air pollution. The No. 3 Cotton Mill workers were laid off or transferred to other units, and bulldozers quickly reduced rows of workshops and dormitories to rubble.

当邓小平倡导改革开放、闯世界（chuang shijie）时，相关说法“下海”（xia hai）作为1990年代流行语出现。它比喻放弃社会主义工作归属、进入私营商业，成为远洋天地品牌的运作逻辑。国棉三厂所在的土地被出售给国有的中远公司（COSCO）——其集装箱装满世界各港口的货轮，其领导层已多元化进入房地产。中远的商业房地产业务始于上海、大连、青岛、广州和南通等港口城市，随后扩张并联合中国四大国有石油公司之一的中化。这一合并催生了中远房地产开发公司（COSRED），最终称为远洋地产有限公司；2000年，他们获准在首都开始建设。北京2001年申奥成功后颁布的一项政策规定，所有工业企业迁至五环路以外，部分原因是为了控制空气污染。国棉三厂的工人被下岗或调往其他单位，推土机很快把一排排车间和宿舍化为瓦砾。


〔原书 91, 92〕

The Ocean Paradise developers hired hok (Hellmuth, Obata + Kassabaum), a transnational architecture firm based in St. Louis, to design the new commodity apartment complex. One of the project architects explained that their commissioned work never went beyond the conceptual stage: “hok produced marketing brochures including images and text, and eventually they will do what they want with it.” She confessed to a personal moral crisis after it became apparent the client simply wanted to buy “a picture or an ideology of American-ness.”[^en-ch02-32] Ocean Paradise advertisements in the Beijing subway stated that the “famous U.S. architecture firm hok” had designed their plans. In 2002, a billboard next to the Ocean Paradise sales office announced in English: “Built on Lifestyle.” Slogans on the walls around the construction site included: “We like the floating life. We enter this city at any time, and depart at any time. We like to be surrounded by art. We like the simple life.”[^en-ch02-33] Behind these walls, rural migrants, members of the “floating population,” worked around the clock on apartment structures rising toward the sky.

远洋天地的开发商聘请总部位于圣路易斯的跨国建筑事务所 HOK（Hellmuth, Obata + Kassabaum）设计新的商品房小区。该项目的一位建筑师解释说，他们的委托工作从未超越概念阶段：“HOK制作了包含图像和文字的营销手册，最终他们会按自己的意愿处理。”她承认，当客户显然只是想购买“一幅美国性的图景或意识形态”时，她经历了个人道德危机。[^zh-ch02-32] 北京地铁里的远洋天地广告称，其规划由“美国著名建筑事务所 HOK”设计。2002年，远洋天地售楼处旁的一块广告牌用英文宣布：“Built on Lifestyle（建筑于生活方式之上）。”工地四周墙上的标语包括：“我们喜欢浮游的生活。我们随时进入这座城，随时离开。我们喜欢被艺术环绕。我们喜欢简单的生活。”[^zh-ch02-33] 在这些墙后，“流动人口”中的农村移民夜以继日地建造着向天空升起的公寓楼。


〔原书 92〕

The marketing team faced the challenge of attracting homebuyers to an area still considered the city’s industrial outskirts. The cosred assistant general manager in charge of marketing, Xu Qian, had started out as an architect and interior designer. On an early visit to the Ocean Paradise site, Xu took photographs as bulldozers knocked over factory walls. He was moved by the emotional response of female textile workers witnessing the demolition: “I felt that perhaps this history was in our hands, at least that this piece of land would be rewritten by us.”[^en-ch02-34] This transformation was necessary, Xu explained. The fabric produced in the No. 3 Cotton Mill was too coarse and had no market value. “We must now link tracks again with the world and participate in global competition. With the contradictions that unfold, many interesting things also emerge.” He thought about filming a documentary or scripting a television drama based on the social change he oversaw or continuing his photographic documentation as a study in contrasts. Believing in the necessity of economic readjustment, he yet pondered what cultural or humanizing elements might come out of the process. He harbored an affective attachment to past forms of sociality, but even more so to the epic melodrama of inevitability.

营销团队面临的挑战是吸引购房者来到仍被视为城市工业郊区的地区。负责营销的中远房地产开发公司总经理助理 Xu Qian 最初是建筑师和室内设计师。在早期一次造访远洋天地工地时，Xu Qian 拍下了推土机推倒工厂围墙的照片。他被女纺织工目睹拆除时的情感反应所打动：“我觉得也许这段历史掌握在我们手中，至少这片土地将被我们改写。”[^zh-ch02-34] 他解释说，这一转变是必要的。国棉三厂生产的布料太粗糙，没有市场价值。“我们现在必须重新与世界接轨，参与全球竞争。随着矛盾展开，许多有趣的事物也出现了。”他考虑过拍摄纪录片或根据自己所见证的社会变化编写电视剧，或继续以摄影记录为对比研究。他相信经济调整的必要性，却也在思考这一过程可能产生什么文化或人性化元素。他对过去的社会交往形式怀有情感依恋，但更依恋那种不可避免性的史诗情节剧。


〔原书 92, 93〕

On a tour of the United States, Xu Qian and his colleagues had been impressed by New York’s soho and other urban industrial zones turned into art districts. Standing in front of the remaining shell of the No. 3 Cotton Mill’s New Great Factory, Xu had the vision to preserve it as a cultural attraction. He considered the possibility of public works projects such as a textile factory museum or a school for the children of laid-off workers, but these proved too complicated in terms of government bureaucracy. His team also had to convince cosred leaders, who saw only a dilapidated factory building, of its value. They debated transforming it into a restaurant, disco, supermarket, dance school, or furniture showroom.[^en-ch02-35] Xu’s vision of cultural cultivation as an indirect benefit won out.

在一次美国之行中，Xu Qian 和同事对纽约苏荷区及其他由城市工业区改造而成的艺术区印象深刻。站在国棉三厂“新大厂房”的残壳前，他产生了将其保留为文化吸引物的愿景。他考虑过纺织厂博物馆或下岗工人子女学校之类的公共工程，但就政府官僚程序而言，这些过于复杂。他的团队还必须说服只看到一栋破旧厂房的远洋地产领导层认识到它的价值。他们争论过把它改造成餐厅、迪斯科舞厅、超市、舞蹈学校还是家具陈列室。[^zh-ch02-35] 他把文化培育视为间接收益的愿景胜出。


〔原书 93〕

They decided to create the East Modern Art Center, which would provide space to Chinese contemporary artists for large-scale exhibitions of the sort that traditional museums did not support. Generating audiences for their work would increase the artists’ visibility and value of their work. The center would also elevate the cultural milieu surrounding Ocean Paradise. In their logic, it would be a boon to both new homeowners and laid-off factory workers still residing in the area by providing them with an opportunity to learn about art and thereby raise their quality (*suzhi*). An expansive spirit of idealism shaped the guiding principles they outlined for a noncommercial organization: they would take and make no money from artists, and they would set no limits on the style of art exhibited. They even attempted to set up a cross-cultural exchange with MoMA in New York. They admired the fiscal management, channeling of corporate sponsorship, and international programming of the museum, although the complexity of MoMA’s inspection and oversight guidelines and the high rate of insurance they required prevented any collaboration.[^en-ch02-36]

他们决定创建远洋艺术中心，为中国当代艺术家提供空间，举办传统博物馆不支持的此类大型展览。为他们的作品创造观众，将提高艺术家的可见度和作品价值。该中心也会提升远洋天地周边的文化氛围。按照他们的逻辑，这对新购房者和仍住在该地区的下岗工人都有好处，因为它为他们提供了了解艺术的机会，从而提高其素质。一种宽广的理想主义精神塑造了他们为一个非商业组织制定的指导原则：不从艺术家那里收取或赚取任何费用，也不对展出的艺术风格设限。他们甚至试图与纽约现代艺术博物馆（MoMA）建立跨文化交流。他们钦佩该博物馆的财务管理、企业赞助渠道和国际项目策划，尽管MoMA审查监督准则的复杂性和高额保险要求使任何合作都无法实现。[^zh-ch02-36]


〔原书 93〕

As excitement about the idea grew, city officials informed them of traffic codes requiring the Ocean Paradise entrance road to cut through the location of the New Great Factory. Yung Ho Chang, the internationally recognized Chinese architect who had already created a preliminary design for the art center, came up with a solution (figure 2.03): “An art center and a real estate office are to be located in an old textile factory building. However, a newly planned road slices right through the structure. The only way to avoid total demolition was to cut off half the existing building. As a consequence, a section of the industrial architecture is revealed as the elevation on the south side. To emphasize this explicit reality the rugged edge of the water drill surgery is left as it is; in other words the process of mutilation is preserved.”[^en-ch02-37]

随着对这一想法的热情高涨，城市官员通知他们，交通法规要求远洋天地入口道路穿过新大厂房的位置。已经为艺术中心完成初步设计的国际知名中国建筑师张永和提出了解决方案（图2.03）：“艺术中心和房地产售楼处将位于一座旧纺织厂建筑内。然而，新规划的道路正好从建筑中间穿过。避免完全拆除的唯一办法是切掉现有建筑的一半。结果，工业建筑的一个剖面显露出来，成为南立面。为了强调这一明确的现实，水钻手术留下的粗糙边缘保持原样；换言之，残损的过程被保留下来。”[^zh-ch02-37]


〔原书 93, 94〕

The Ocean Paradise marketing staff invited artists and reporters to a “salon” to generate ideas for the East Modern Art Center. Living Dance Studio choreographer Wen Hui proposed a dance performance for the center’s opening. She initially thought about using female dancers dressed as textile workers. Artists Song Dong and Yin Xiuzhen, who are husband and wife, also attended the gathering. Wen Hui phoned them afterward to ask if they wanted to work together with her and her husband, documentary filmmaker Wu Wenguang. As the four of them discussed ideas, Song Dong thought of involving mingong from the Ocean Paradise construction site. He wanted to set up an encounter between rural migrants and urban art enthusiasts, in which the line between audience and spectacle was unclear. Thinking about this idea in terms of a choreographic response to Beijing’s transformation, Wen Hui decided she wanted to bring its cultural and manual workers into physical contact.[^en-ch02-38] *Dancing with Mingong*, the multimedia event that evolved from their collaboration, represents a momentary crystallization of these artists’ ongoing thought processes and experiments with particular media. It also represents a shift in logics of display. Once exemplary creators of what Gao Minglu termed “apartment art,” Song Dong and Yin Xiuzhen now found themselves creating pieces specifically for the site of a real estate development, in a way that involved critical reflection on their part but also supported developers’ marketing need for a media spectacle.

远洋天地的营销人员邀请艺术家和记者参加“沙龙”，为远洋艺术中心出谋划策。生活舞蹈工作室的编舞文慧提议为中心开幕做一场舞蹈演出。她最初想用打扮成纺织女工的女舞者。艺术家宋东和尹秀珍夫妇也参加了这次聚会。文慧后来打电话给他们，问他们是否愿意与她和丈夫、纪录片导演吴文光合作。四人讨论想法时，宋东想到让远洋天地建筑工地的民工参与进来。他想促成农村移民与城市艺术爱好者之间的相遇，其中观众与奇观之间的界限模糊不清。从以编舞回应北京转变的角度思考这一想法，文慧决定要让文化工作者和体力劳动者进行身体接触。[^zh-ch02-38] 《与民工共舞》正是从他们合作中发展出的多媒体事件，代表这些艺术家持续思考过程与特定媒介实验的短暂结晶。它也代表了展示逻辑的转变。宋东和尹秀珍曾是高名潞所谓“公寓艺术”的典范创作者，如今却发现自己专门为房地产开发的场所创作作品，这种方式既包含他们的批判性反思，也支持了开发商对媒体奇观的营销需求。


〔原书 94〕

![图2.03　远洋天地售楼处（一层）、远洋艺术中心（二层），2002年。作者摄。](web/assets/ch02-b039.jpg)

FIG 2.03 Ocean Paradise sales offices (first floor), East Modern Art Center (second floor), 2002. Photograph by author.

图2.03　远洋天地售楼处（一层）、远洋艺术中心（二层），2002年。作者摄。


〔原书 94, 95〕

The East Modern Art Center supplied the four artists with funds for materials and wages to hire thirty construction workers at thirty yuan per day, to rehearse for one week with Wen Hui’s dancers, six Chinese and three foreign. They were told that the workers on the Ocean Paradise site were too busy, so Wu Wenguang contacted photographer Mao Ran, who had once worked as a subcontractor, and he found a group of mingong for hire. These men, largely from rural counties across Sichuan, stripped off their shirts and, following direction in improvisational exercises, moved through an empty space once filled with female textile workers (figure 2.04). Yin Xiuzhen assembled an installation piece that consisted of hanging lights and foot-pedal sewing machines, each sewing through one of Beijing’s daily newspapers. Song Dong brought in piles of sand, on top of which he arranged architectural models borrowed from the Ocean Paradise sales office to create a miragelike diorama.[^en-ch02-39] He photographed the workers’ identity cards and temporary residence permits for a projection on the night of the performance.[^en-ch02-40]

远洋艺术中心为四位艺术家提供了材料费和工资，以每人每天三十元雇佣三十名建筑工人，与文慧的舞者——六名中国人和三名外国人——排练一周。他们被告知远洋天地工地的工人太忙，于是吴文光联系了曾做过分包工的摄影师毛然，他找到了一群待雇的民工。这些男子大多来自四川各县农村，他们脱掉上衣，在即兴练习的指导下，穿过一个曾经挤满女纺织工的空旷空间（图2.04）。尹秀珍组装了一件装置作品，由悬吊的灯和脚踏缝纫机构成，每台缝纫机缝穿一份北京的日报。宋东运来成堆的沙子，把从远洋天地售楼处借来的建筑模型摆在上面，营造出幻影般的立体布景。[^zh-ch02-39] 他拍摄了工人的身份证和暂住证，用于演出当晚的投影。[^zh-ch02-40]


〔原书 95〕

![图2.04　2001年在北京远洋天地楼盘远洋艺术中心的《与民工共舞》排练。图底一排缝纫机属于尹秀珍的装置；后方成排的砖堆标记宋东装置作品的位置。吴文光，《和民工跳舞》，2001年。影像截帧。](web/assets/ch02-b041.jpg)

FIG 2.04 *Dancing with Mingong* rehearsal at Beijing’s East Modern Art Center in the Ocean Paradise real estate development, 2001. The line of sewing machines at the bottom of the image are for Yin Xiuzhen’s installation; the line of brick piles in back mark where an installation piece by Song Dong will be placed. Wu Wenguang, *Dance with Farm Workers*, 2001. Film still.

图2.04　2001年在北京远洋天地楼盘远洋艺术中心的《与民工共舞》排练。图底一排缝纫机属于尹秀珍的装置；后方成排的砖堆标记宋东装置作品的位置。吴文光，《和民工跳舞》，2001年。影像截帧。


〔原书 95, 96〕

Wu Wenguang filmed the rehearsals and final performance.[^en-ch02-41] The resulting documentary records the demand of a worker on the first day: “Why are we here?” Wen Hui responded with a speech about how they, as artists, were interested in the former factory space as emblematic of a changing urban environment. On camera, she asserted that Beijing was being built by mingong, but very few Beijingers had a chance to actually talk to them. “You are at the very bottom of the social hierarchy, but Beijing has been built by you. You can give us advice. This performance gives you a chance to express your experience.” The workers had a lot to express: “We came to Beijing to work, to make money, but sometimes people in Beijing hire us and then refuse to pay up after we’ve done the work. Will this performance help us get back these unpaid wages or get us residence permits or stop the police from arresting us? Since Beijing has gotten the Olympics, you really need us, but how will this performance help?” Flustered, Wen Hui turned to her assistants, “Is someone taking notes on this? I can’t solve these problems.”

吴文光拍摄了排练和最终演出。[^zh-ch02-41] 由此产生的纪录片记录了第一天一个工人的质问：“我们为什么在这里？”文慧回答时讲到，他们作为艺术家对旧厂房空间作为变化中的城市环境的象征感兴趣。她在镜头前断言，北京是由民工建造的，但很少有北京人有机会真正与他们交谈。“你们处在社会最底层，但北京是你们建起来的。你们可以给我们建议。这场演出给你们一个机会表达你们的经历。”工人们有许多话要说：“我们来北京干活，挣钱，但有时候北京人雇了我们，干完活却不肯付钱。这场演出能帮我们要回工钱吗，能给我们暂住证吗，能让警察不抓我们吗？北京申奥成功了，你们确实需要我们，可这场演出有什么用？”文慧慌了神，转向助手：“有人在做记录吗？这些问题我解决不了。”


〔原书 96〕

When cosred officials learned about the details of the performance, they feared it would bring the wrong kind of attention to Ocean Paradise. They tried to get those involved to remove mingong from the title, but it had already been publicized to the media.[^en-ch02-42] When the performance took place, on August 23, 2001, several hundred people turned out to join the divergent energies and intentions that intermingled that evening.

当远洋地产的官员得知演出的细节后，他们担心这会给远洋天地带来不利关注。他们试图让参与者把“民工”从标题中去掉，但消息已经向媒体公布。[^zh-ch02-42] 演出于2001年8月23日举行，数百人到场，加入了当晚相互交织的不同能量与意图。


〔原书 96, 97〕

As the performers, thirty rural migrant men joined by nine professional dancers, moved through the space, audience members ebbed and flowed around them. The dancers ran sporadically through the space, as if going through the paces of frenetic urban life. They came to a halt en masse. As a recording announced the arrival of a subway train, their heads slowly lifted together as they gazed upward. They formed two long parallel lines and threw bricks back and forth up the length of the building. They noisily rolled metal barrels across the concrete floor and over other dancers who had fallen to the ground.[^en-ch02-43] Slides taken by Mao Ran of the messages of hope and despair that migrant workers write on construction site walls were projected on a column. Song Dong’s video *Broken Mirror* (1999) was screened on a corner wall. Each segment of this piece opens with a Beijing street scene—an old alleyway, local market, or park. As a hammer hits the surface, the viewer realizes it is a reflection in a mirror. With each strike of the hammer, the scene ripples until the mirror finally shatters, revealing what lies across the street, or behind the mirror: the high-rise buildings of a rapidly modernizing Beijing. In another corner, the shirtless mingong formed a human screen with their bodies onto which Song Dong’s video of their identity documents was projected. They formed human chains, each with hands on the back of the person in front of them, with the lead person pushing a newspaper through one of the sewing machines in Yin Xiuzhen’s installation. Their interaction with these material objects conveyed a sense of history in the making, and the destruction and displacement involved in the process. The predominantly male corporeality of the performance reinforced the marginalization of demobilized women whose labor had once built and run the factory.[^en-ch02-44] The event ended with the sung call and response of Lao Wei’s village tune: “Flowers are covering the branches.... I am the only one alone.” The mingong presented bricks to random members of the audience, who received them with a mixture of laughter, puzzlement, graciousness, and discomfort.

表演者——三十名农村来的男子和九名职业舞者——在空间中移动时，观众在他们周围潮汐般流动。舞者不时狂乱地跑过空间，仿佛经历着疯狂城市生活的步伐。他们集体停下。录音宣布地铁列车进站，他们的头一起缓缓抬起，向上凝视。他们排成两条长长的平行线，沿着整栋建筑来回扔砖。他们喧闹地把金属桶滚过混凝土地面，滚过已经倒地的其他舞者。[^zh-ch02-43] 毛然拍摄的民工在工地墙上写下希望与绝望话语的幻灯片被投射到一根柱子上。宋东的录像《破镜子》（1999）在角落墙面上放映。这件作品的每一段都以北京街景开场——旧胡同、本地市场或公园。当锤子击打表面时，观众意识到那是镜子中的倒影。锤子每敲一下，景象便泛起涟漪，直到镜子最终碎裂，露出街对面或镜子后面的景象：迅速现代化的北京的高楼大厦。在另一个角落，光膀子的民工用身体组成人屏，宋东拍摄的他们的身份证件录像被投射其上。他们组成人链，每个人把手搭在前面那人的背上，领头者把一份报纸送入尹秀珍装置中的一台缝纫机。他们与这些物品的互动传达出一种历史正在形成的感觉，以及过程中涉及的破坏与流离失所。演出以男性为主的身体性强化了下岗女工的边缘化——她们的劳动曾经建造并运转这座工厂。[^zh-ch02-44] 演出在老魏村歌的唱和呼应中结束：“花儿盖满了枝头……只有我孤身一人。”民工把砖头送给随机选中的观众，观众以笑声、困惑、礼貌和不安混合回应。


〔原书 97〕

The Limits of Art Center Site Specificity

艺术中心场域特定性的限度


〔原书 97〕

In coverage of the East Modern Art Center’s inaugural event, reporters struggled to describe its overall effect, even as the messy chaos of it captured the oversized, hardscrabble ethos of contemporary Beijing; they described the mingong as earnest and moving; they lauded the status artists had granted them, while recognizing it would be as ephemeral as the hail that fell that night.[^en-ch02-45] The physical contact between worldly urbanites and exploited migrant workers disrupted any easy romanticization of rural folk. The responses of various stakeholders in the project revealed tensions over the purpose of art exhibition in showcase Beijing. Xu Qian conceded that the performance expressed contradictions between people from different classes and backgrounds but concluded, “What effect did it have? It didn’t make me feel relaxed or happy.” [^en-ch02-46] Song Dong reflected on the limits of artists to effect social change: “Although you could say that we employed mingong and also touched, moved, and mixed with mingong, we’re certainly no saviors.... I felt that after it was over, they still had their lives, and we had ours. It’s not like what a lot of the media reported, that we had given mingong dignity, or raised them to that level. They already had dignity.” [^en-ch02-47] Xu Qian’s assistant in charge of art center logistics quit her job two months after *Dancing with Mingong*. She compared her departure, to work for a transnational software company, to breaking up with a lover who had laid waste to her passion. If she had it all to do over, she would focus more on the relationship between art and economics, in terms of cultivating sustainable patronage, instead of using the center simply as a means of generating publicity.[^en-ch02-48] Graphic designer Wei Lai, a principal consultant on the project, placed blame on the artists who failed to thank or even mention Ocean Paradise Real Estate in their press interviews: “In the company we were suddenly seen as having bad judgment. The voices of everyone’s criticism flew. Why did you want to preserve that factory? Why did you want to create an art center in that factory? Why did you create this kind of performance in that art center?” [^en-ch02-49]

在关于远洋艺术中心首展的报道中，记者们难以描述其整体效果，尽管其中混乱的喧闹抓住了当代北京那种过度、艰辛的精神；他们把民工描述为真挚感人；他们称赞艺术家赋予民工的地位，同时意识到那将像当晚落下的冰雹一样短暂。[^zh-ch02-45] 世界性城市居民与被剥削的外来民工之间的身体接触，打破了任何对农村人的轻松浪漫化。项目各方利益相关者的反应，揭示了围绕展示北京艺术展览目的的紧张。Xu Qian 承认，这场演出表达了不同阶级和背景的人之间的矛盾，但总结道：“它有什么效果？它没让我感到轻松或快乐。”[^zh-ch02-46] 宋东反思艺术家推动社会变革的限度：“虽然你可以说我们雇用了民工，也接触、感动并与民工混合在一起，但我们当然不是救世主……我觉得演出结束后，他们仍有他们的生活，我们有我们的。事情不像许多媒体报道的那样，说我们给了民工尊严，或把他们提升到那个层次。他们本来就有尊严。”[^zh-ch02-47] Xu Qian 负责艺术中心后勤的助理在《与民工共舞》两个月后辞职。她把自己去一家跨国软件公司工作，比作与一个毁掉了自己激情的情人分手。如果能重来，她会更关注艺术与经济的关系，培养可持续的赞助，而不是仅仅把中心当作制造宣传的手段。[^zh-ch02-48] 平面设计师 Wei Lai 是项目主要顾问，他把责任归咎于艺术家——他们在媒体采访中没有感谢、甚至没有提到远洋天地房地产：“我们在公司里突然被认为判断力糟糕。大家的批评声四起。你们为什么想保留那座工厂？为什么想在工厂里建艺术中心？为什么在艺术中心做那种演出？”[^zh-ch02-49]


〔原书 98〕

Was the goal for art to foster a humanizing aura of culture that would confer commodity value to real estate, and in the process to Chinese contemporary artworks? To dissolve museum walls and call into question their power to create and conflate economic and aesthetic value? Or to incite debate and change related to issues of social inequality and segregation created by urban renewal projects? In the aftermath of *Dancing with Mingong*, cosred leaders refused to fund any more art activities. They simply rented the space to interested parties. Eight subsequent exhibitions and performances took place at the East Modern Art Center: *Trip to Kunlun*, a performance by the Beijing Modern Dance Group; *Fantasia*, an exhibit of contemporary art from China, Japan, and Korea; *What a Wonderful World*, an exhibit and performance created by artist Wang Nengtao; *Run, Jump, Crawl, Walk*, an exhibit of Chinese contemporary art; *Witness to Growth*, a solo exhibit of paintings by Yu Hong; *DV Life*, a youth digital video exhibit; *The New Middle Class: Germany 1989–2000*, an exhibit of photographs by Regina Schmeken sponsored by the Goethe Institute in Beijing; and *Synthetic Reality*, an exhibit of Chinese video art.

艺术的目的是培养一种人性化的文化光环，赋予房地产以商品价值，并在此过程中赋予中国当代艺术以商品价值吗？是消解博物馆的围墙，质疑其创造并混淆经济与审美价值的力量吗？还是激发关于城市更新项目造成的社会不平等与隔离问题的辩论和改变？《与民工共舞》之后，远洋地产领导层拒绝再资助任何艺术活动。他们只是把空间出租给有兴趣的各方。此后在远洋艺术中心举办了八场展览和演出：《昆仑之旅》，北京现代舞团演出；《幻想曲》，中国、日本和韩国当代艺术展；《多么美好的世界》，艺术家王能涛创作、演出；《跑、跳、爬、走》，中国当代艺术展；《目击成长》，喻红油画个展；《DV生活》，青年数字影像展；《新中产阶级：德国1989—2000》，歌德学院（北京）赞助的雷吉娜·施梅根摄影展；以及《合成现实》，中国录像艺术展。


〔原书 98, 99〕

None of these exhibits were site-specific in the way *Dancing with Mingong* had been, with the artists creating work that responded directly to the physical and historical space. The East Modern Art Center did, however, attract ambitious independent curators because it provided them with a large, museumlike space where experimental artworks could be displayed without the official imprimatur or level of oversight associated with staid institutions like the National Art Museum of China Art. A primary goal for Zhang Li, curator of *Run, Jump, Crawl, Walk*, was to develop a local audience for Chinese contemporary artists’ embodied explorations of their social environment.[^en-ch02-50] It would be an oversimplification of the many factors involved in curatorial decision-making to claim the space alone influenced the selection of artwork exhibited there, but the mixed nature of the site, the mutilated and unfinished feel of the center’s architecture, the layers of its history still exposed and being struggled over, heightened the representational politics explored by many of the works shown. I highlight a few of these pieces to demonstrate how the intersection of urban planning, real estate, and art in new millennium Beijing shaped the lives of artists and sometimes became the subject of their art. These works reflect the encounter of socialist and market aesthetics, as well as the positions and desires within them of urbanites, the historical proletariat, and rural migrants. Several of these pieces have been exhibited in other locations, from commercial galleries to international museums, but in the East Modern Art Center they resonated with the space in a particular way. Not yet assigned a price or a place in an authorized narrative of China, poised at the edge of critique *and* co-optation, they contextualized the space as much as it contextualized the art.

这些展览都不像《与民工共舞》那样具有场域特定性，艺术家创作直接回应物理和历史空间的作品。然而，远洋艺术中心确实吸引了雄心勃勃的独立策展人，因为它为他们提供了一个大型、类似博物馆的空间，可以在那里展出实验性作品，而不必获得官方批准，也不受中国美术馆等沉闷机构那种监督。张离作为《跑、跳、爬、走》策展人的主要目标之一，是为中国当代艺术家对其社会环境进行具身探索发展本地观众。[^zh-ch02-50] 声称仅凭空间便影响了展出作品的选择，会过度简化策展决策涉及的诸多因素，但该场所的混合性质、艺术中心建筑被切割和未完成的感觉、仍暴露在外并处于争夺中的历史层次，都强化了展出的许多作品所探索的表征政治。我着重介绍其中几件作品，以展示新千年北京城市规划、房地产与艺术的交汇如何塑造艺术家的生活，有时又成为其艺术主题。这些作品反映了社会主义与市场美学的相遇，以及城市居民、历史无产阶级和农村移民在其中的位置与欲望。其中几件作品曾在其他场所展出，从商业画廊到国际博物馆，但在远洋艺术中心，它们以特殊方式与空间产生共鸣。它们尚未被赋予价格或在被认可的中国叙事中的位置，徘徊于批判与被收编的边缘，它们既使空间语境化，也被空间语境化。


〔原书 99〕

Artist Wang Nengtao’s *What a Wonderful World* staged a larger-than-life party over the weekend of April 20–22, 2002. Through a cacophonous assemblage of people and materials, Wang explored the market-era maxim of material indulgence: *chi he wan le* (eat, drink, play, enjoy). The spectacle consisted of sixteen different sections—theater and music performances, on-the-spot food preparation, installations, documentary films, photographs, and paintings—arranged as a maze of excess through which audience members could wander.[^en-ch02-51] For *What a Wonderful Life*, roast duck chefs carved meat for partygoers to enjoy. The discarded carcasses placed atop a mound of construction rubble mimicked Prospect Hill in central Beijing’s Jingshan Park. A 360-degree, grey-toned panorama of the urban landscape, pieced together from photographs taken on Prospect Hill, surrounded the mountain of consumed ducks. In another scene, female performers in gold robes stood on tables draped in white and pumped their fists around a king in metallic pink. Behind them hung large digitally altered reproductions of propaganda posters from the Great Leap Forward. A young female collective farm worker grasps a stalk of wheat and smiles above the slogan “Circle the globe to take root, sprout, blossom, yield fruit.” The steely sweat-beaded face of a male factory worker is paired with the slogan “We will certainly surpass America.”[^en-ch02-52] In an installation titled *Met Old Chap Marx in Paris*, a poster of Karl Marx, an old camera, spilled wine, a student desk, a burned out hearth, and a poster with the lyrics to the Internationale sets a scene of cosmopolitanism different from that epitomized by Ocean Paradise. The bedroom scene in Wang’s *Dream World Music* (figure 2.05) installation provides a similarly striking contrast with that in the soho model apartment at Urban Planning Museum. The clutter of old photographs, advertising images from the 1920s, socialist propaganda posters, work unit merit certificates, toys, and musical instruments that surround the plain white mattress on the floor presents a historical archive of dreams and emotions antithetical to the contemporary commodity apartment advertising image. The installation’s affective pull on a certain generation of viewers accentuates the hollowness of the wonderful world of pursuing material pleasure.

艺术家王能涛的《多么美好的世界》在2002年4月20日至22日的周末举办了一场超乎现实的派对。通过人与物的喧闹组合，王能涛探讨了市场时代的物质放纵信条：吃喝玩乐（chi he wan le）。这场奇观由十六个不同部分——戏剧与音乐表演、现场备餐、装置、纪录片、照片和绘画——组成，排布成一座过剩的迷宫，观众可以在其中游荡。[^zh-ch02-51] 为《多么美好的生活》，烤鸭厨师为派对客人片鸭肉。被丢弃的鸭骨架堆在建筑瓦砾堆上，模仿北京市中心景山公园的景山。由在景山上拍摄的照片拼接而成的360度灰调城市全景，环绕着这座被吃掉的鸭子堆成的小山。在另一个场景中，身穿金色长袍的女性表演者站在铺着白布的桌子上，围绕一位金属粉色的国王挥舞拳头。她们身后挂着大幅数字修改的“大跃进”宣传画复制品。一位年轻的女性集体农庄社员握着一根麦穗微笑，下方标语是“围绕全球扎根、发芽、开花、结果”。一位男性工人满面汗水、神情坚毅的脸庞，配上标语“我们一定要超过美国”。[^zh-ch02-52] 在一件题为《在巴黎遇见马克思老兄》的装置中，卡尔·马克思的海报、一台旧相机、泼洒的葡萄酒、一张学生书桌、烧尽的壁炉，以及一张印有《国际歌》歌词的海报，布置出一个不同于远洋天地所象征的世界主义场景。王能涛《梦幻世界音乐》（图2.05）装置中的卧室场景，与城市规划展览馆SOHO样板间形成同样鲜明的对比。旧照片、1920年代广告图像、社会主义宣传画、单位奖状、玩具和乐器杂乱地环绕着地板上的素白床垫，呈现出一个与当代商品房广告形象相悖的梦想与情感历史档案。这件装置对某一代观众的情感引力，凸显了追求物质享乐的“美好世界”的空洞。


〔原书 99, 100, 101〕

The other Chinese solo show held at the East Modern Art Center was Yu Hong’s *Witness to Growth*, a series of thirty-four oil paintings, all self-portraits or intimate scenes with family and friends, one and sometimes two painted for each year of her life. While individual paintings from the series had appeared in group exhibits, this marked the first time they were exhibited as a complete series and with each painting juxtaposed with a media representation from the same year. For 1966, Yu pairs *China Pictorial* color photographs of Chairman Mao waving to soldiers in Tiananmen Square at the start of the Cultural Revolution with a painting after a black-and-white photograph of herself at six months, bundled and lying asleep in a pram outside in the sun. Twelve years later, the chosen *China Pictorial* photograph features Yu herself, sketching outside with three other students from the Beijing Children’s Palace; in the paired painting, she poses in a park with her parents and younger sister for a family photograph. In *1996, Thirty Years Old* (figure 2.06), the *China Pictorial* image has shifted to a dreamscape of mass consumer prosperity, a grid of identical new villas in suburban Beijing. In the accompanying paintings, the artist sits lost in thought in her studio, her two-year-old daughter napping on the sofa next to her; or just her daughter slumped asleep in an office chair in front of a large-than-life but seemingly inconsequential Mao portrait hanging on the studio wall. Yu’s technically deft yet loose brushwork reflects her academy training in socialist realist painting. (She is the artist whose sketch of the head of David remained legendary among the next generation of cafa students.) Her paintings, however, depict melancholic introspection rather than idealized working class-struggle or hagiographic hero worship. They also present a contrast to the crisp media images, challenging the realism of photographic representation. The overall series represents historical reflection and interjects individual subjectivity into collective history and fantasy. The woman in these paintings does not, in heroic worker, mother, or consumer pose, represent the nation or promote a real estate developer’s vision of domestic bliss. She conveys the philosophical ambivalence of a witness. Her auratic presence is heightened by the layers of history overturned and memorialized in the very architecture of the East Modern Art Center.

在远洋艺术中心举办的另一场中国艺术家个展是喻红的《目击成长》，由三十四幅油画组成，全部是自画像或与家人朋友的亲密场景，为她生命中的每一年画一幅，有时两幅。虽然该系列的个别画作曾在群展中出现，但这是首次作为完整系列展出，且每幅画都与同年的媒体图像并置。1966年，喻红将《人民画报》那幅文化大革命开始时毛泽东在天安门广场向士兵挥手的彩色照片，与她根据自己六个月大、裹着襁褓在户外婴儿车中熟睡的黑白照片所绘的画并置。十二年后，选用的《人民画报》照片中是喻红本人和另外三名北京市少年宫的学生在户外写生；在配对画作中，她和父母、妹妹在公园里摆姿势拍全家福。在《1996，三十岁》（图2.06）中，《人民画报》图像已转向大众消费繁荣的梦想景象——北京郊区一排排一模一样的新别墅。在相配的画作中，艺术家坐在画室里陷入沉思，两岁女儿在她旁边的沙发上打盹；或者就只有女儿瘫睡在办公椅上，面前是一幅超大却似乎无关紧要的毛泽东画像，挂在画室墙上。喻红技法娴熟而松弛的笔触反映她在学院接受的社会主义现实主义绘画训练。（她就是在中央美院后辈学生中传说的大卫头像素描作者。）然而，她的画作描绘忧郁的内省，而不是理想化的工人阶级斗争或圣徒式的英雄崇拜。它们也与清晰的媒体图像形成对比，挑战摄影再现的现实主义。整个系列代表历史反思，把个体主体性插入集体历史与幻想之中。这些画中的女人没有摆出英雄工人、母亲或消费者的姿态，不代表国家，也不宣传开发商对家庭幸福的愿景。她传达出一位见证者在哲学层面上的矛盾心态。她的灵光式存在感，因远洋艺术中心建筑本身所掀翻并纪念的层层历史而增强。


〔原书 100〕

![图2.05　王能涛，《梦幻世界音乐》，2002年。装置现场，《多么美好的世界》，远洋艺术中心，2002年4月。艺术家惠允。](web/assets/ch02-b051.jpg)

FIG 2.05 Wang Nengtao, *Dream World Music*, 2002. Installation view, *What a Wonderful World*, East Modern Art Center, April 2002. Courtesy of the artist.

〔原书 101〕

![图2.06　喻红，《1996，三十岁》，2002年。布面丙烯，100厘米×100厘米×2厘米。画作与一幅《人民画报》1996年第6期的照片一同展出；该期画报用夹子固定在一张跨页照片处，照片由 Hu Dunzhi 拍摄，呈现城市住宅建设——北京大兴县半壁店别墅街区，66厘米×100厘米。所有图像©喻红2016，长征空间惠允。摄影©顾小波/喻红2016。](web/assets/ch02-b052.jpg)

All images © Yu Hong 2016, Courtesy of Long March Space. Photographs © Gu Xiaobo/Yu Hong 2016.
