By turning around American depictions of Japanese social relations as not transparent enough, especially in business negotiations—insinuating that Japanese needed to learn the American practice of “saying no when you mean no”—Sony chairman Akio Morita and politician Shintaro Ishihara critiqued U.S. business practices and advocated greater Japanese independence. *The Japan That Can Say No* then led to *The Asia That Can Say No*, coauthored by Ishihara and the prime minister of Malaysia.[^en-ch03-31] The book’s title in English, *The Voice of Asia: Two Leaders Discuss the Coming Century*, toned down its claim to sovereignty and rejection of the West. The translation of “saying no” into Chinese represents what linguists call a Sino-Japanese-English loanword. Uncertainty about where and how cultural and political nationalism overlap, which caused the laughter at my use of the loan word, troubled the artists’ response to Joo’s insistence on more translators at the table of international art over simply “saying no.”

它追随了亚洲“说不”书籍的潮流，始于1989年的《日本可以说不》。这本书在日本的畅销在美国国会引起极大关注，有人用它作为对日贸易制裁的理由，于是它被译成英文。[^zh-ch03-30] 日语中的“say no”借自英语，“no”未加翻译。索尼董事长盛田昭夫和政治家石原慎太郎反过来利用美国对日本社会关系——尤其在商业谈判中——不够透明的描绘（暗示日本人需要学习“想拒绝时就拒绝”的美国做法），批评美国商业实践，主张日本更大的独立性。《日本可以说不》随后催生了石原慎太郎与马来西亚总理合著的《亚洲可以说不》。[^zh-ch03-31]该书的英文版标题《亚洲之声：两位领袖纵论即将到来的世纪》淡化了其主权主张和对西方的拒绝。“说不”译入中文，代表语言学家所称的汉日英借词。文化与政治民族主义在何处、如何重叠的不确定性——正是这种不确定性让我使用借词时引来笑声——困扰着艺术家对 Joo 坚持在国际艺术桌上增加口译员、而非仅仅“说不”的回应。


〔原书 129〕

Wei Cheng

围城


〔原书 129〕

Wang Yin nodded at my summary in Chinese of Joo’s comments, but then noted with an exhalation of cigarette smoke and raised eyebrows that things were not so easy. Recruiting his teacup as explanatory tool, he laid out his working metaphor for translation as a process that always exceeds the standard tropes of fidelity or natural equivalency that can be discovered between languages, suggesting that more translation may not solve their dilemma. Pointing to his teacup, Wang described any object of translation as a boat, which—he slid the teacup from one spot on the table to another—crosses a river. When tethered to one shore the boat means something different than when docked on the other shore. Even though the materiality of the teacup/boat remains the same, people view it differently, just as Chinese and Western audiences will inevitably “place” his paintings through different conceptual and experiential frameworks.[^en-ch03-32] What the boat means changes because of the journey. He concluded, “It’s like *Wei Cheng*,” indicating for me to explain this reference to the 1947 novel by Qian Zhongshu popularized by the 1991 television adaptation. In Wang’s invocation of this novel, he reached back to China’s semicolonial past. His besieged city is early-2000s Beijing, with its embassy districts and art galleries catering to expatriate clients, where artists at the table with curators from the United States sought international recognition while remaining wary of inevitable misreadings and accusations of selling out.

王音听我用中文概括 Joo 的评论后点了点头，但随后吐出一口烟、扬起眉毛说，事情没那么简单。他借茶杯作解释工具，摆出自己关于翻译的工作隐喻：翻译是一个总会超出惯常的忠实隐喻、或语言之间存在可发现的天然对等这一观念的过程，这意味着更多翻译未必解决他们的困境。王音指着茶杯说，任何翻译对象都像一只船——他把茶杯从桌上一个位置滑到另一个位置——渡过一条河。系在此岸时，船的意义不同于停泊在对岸时。尽管茶杯／船的物质性保持不变，人们看待它的方式不同，正如中西方观众不可避免地会通过不同概念和经验框架来“放置”他的画作。[^zh-ch03-32] 船的意义因旅程而改变。他最后说：“这就像《围城》。”示意我向在场者解释这部钱锺书1947年的小说——1991年电视剧改编使其广为人知。王音援引这部小说，回望中国的半殖民过去。他的围城是2000年代初的北京，有使馆区和迎合外籍客户的画廊；艺术家与来自美国的策展人同桌交谈，寻求国际承认，同时警惕不可避免的误读和“卖身”指控。


〔原书 129, 130〕

The artist at his side further explained, “It’s like the saying about marriage at the beginning of *Wei Cheng*. Unmarried people want to get married. Married people want to get divorced.” In *Wei Cheng*, Qian Zhongshu uses marriage as a symbol of kinship or fidelity doomed to failure. His female characters embody in turn moribund tradition; whorish, superficial treaty-port culture; and corrupt, materialistic class-based society. The protagonist Fang Hongjian is the bewildered, satirized, individual hero who bounces between them, with the novel’s women in the supporting roles of representing China in all its possible failed incarnations. The gendered logic underlying this extended metaphor is that contemporary (male) artists identify with the protagonist of *Wei Cheng*.

他身旁的艺术家进一步解释：“就像《围城》开头关于婚姻的那句话。没结婚的人想结婚。结了婚的人想离婚。”在《围城》中，钱锺书用婚姻象征注定失败的亲缘或忠诚。他的女性人物依次化身垂死的传统；娼妓式的、肤浅的通商口岸文化；以及腐败、物质至上的阶级社会。主人公方鸿渐是在她们之间弹跳的困惑、被讽刺的个体英雄，而小说中的女性则承担配角角色，代表中国种种可能失败的化身。这一延伸隐喻底层的性别逻辑是：当代（男性）艺术家认同《围城》的主人公。


〔原书 130〕

In our banquet room, someone returned to the teacup, stating that if it represented Chinese artwork in international circulation, then Huang Du was the boatman. Huang protested this comparison of him to a middleman, as if it might reduce him to the pidgin of treaty-port compradors like Jimmy Chang in *Wei Cheng*, who sprinkles his speech with foreign words. When asked, for example, if he collects porcelain, Jimmy responds: “*Sure! Have a look-see.... Sure*! Worth quite a lot of money, *plenty of dough*. Besides, these things aren’t like calligraphy or paintings. If you can buy calligraphy or paintings which turn out to be fakes, they aren’t worth a cent. They just amount to *wastepaper*. If the porcelain is fake, at least it can hold food” (italics are in English in the original).[^en-ch03-33] For Huang Du, the cultural capital of his cosmopolitan profession resided in the vocabulary of foreign theory: *discourse, hybridity, performativity*.

在我们的包间里，有人回到茶杯，说如果它代表国际流通中的中国艺术品，那么黄笃就是船夫。黄笃抗议把他比作中间人，仿佛这会把他贬低为《围城》里吉米·张那种通商口岸买办的洋泾浜语——说话时点缀外文词。例如，有人问吉米是否收集瓷器，他回答：“*Sure! Have a look-see… Sure!*（当然！去看一看……当然！）值不少钱，*plenty of dough*（大把钞票）。再说，这些东西不像书法或画。你要是买了书法或画，结果是假的，一文不值，就是 *wastepaper*（废纸）。瓷器是假的，至少还能盛东西。”（斜体部分在中文原作中即为英文；括号内为本译稿所附释义）[^zh-ch03-33] 对黄笃而言，他世界性职业的文化资本存在于外国理论的词汇中：话语、杂糅、述行性。


〔原书 130〕

After so much talk of metaphorical boats and movement of porcelain across the table, Joo asserted that as Asian American curators, she and her colleagues represented a new West, intent on resisting the orientalism she felt their comments suggested. Pointing at her face, she said, “The West looks like this now too.” The Chinese artists did not respond; this suggestion of racial alliance or minority cosmopolitanism did not bridge the gap for them. Doryun Chong, the one curator born and educated in Asia before attending university in the United States, interjected to express hesitancy over the idea of being somehow more authentic culture brokers: “In the United States, I’m called upon as a native expert of Korea or Asia. In Korea, I’m granted certain respect or privilege because of my education in the United States. Can I really exploit both situations and stay honest with myself?”

谈了这么多关于隐喻之船和瓷器在桌上移动的话之后，Joo 断言，作为亚裔美国策展人，她和同事代表一个新的西方，决心抵抗她感到他们评论中暗示的东方主义。她指着自己的脸说：“西方现在也长这样。”中国艺术家没有回应；这种种族联盟或少数者世界主义的提议，并未为他们弥合鸿沟。Doryun Chong 是唯一在亚洲出生并接受教育、后赴美读大学的策展人，他插话说，对成为某种更本真的文化中介的想法感到迟疑：“在美国，我被当作韩国或亚洲的本土专家；在韩国，我又因为在美受教育而获得某种尊重或特权。我真的能同时利用这两种处境，又对自己保持诚实吗？”


〔原书 130〕

Insides and Outsides

内部与外部


〔原书 130, 131〕

All of the arts professionals present at lunch that day were bicultural in their own right. In everyday experience they drew on cultural vocabularies of both Asia and the West and could do so with relative ease. As a group, they arguably had more in common with each other—the global culture of contemporary art and access to its cosmopolitan resources—than with most citizens of their respective nations.[^en-ch03-34] They were all invested in thinking outside the ideological categories of the nation-state. The artists often felt at odds with the Chinese state and its vacillating policies of censorship and sponsorship. The Asian American curators struggled against U.S. institutions of citizenship and national identity framing them as the “unassimilable alien” and worked to create sites of cultural production that remind the nation of its historical ties with Asia in economics, labor, and war.[^en-ch03-35] Yet the different discourses of cultural nationalism that informed their participation in global art led to a subtle polarization over the course of the conversation so that the two sides seemed more in tension than sympathy.

那天午餐时在场的所有艺术专业人士本身都是双文化的。在日常经验中，他们调用亚洲和西方的文化词汇，并能相对自如地这样做。作为一个群体，他们彼此之间的共同点——当代艺术的全球文化及其世界主义资源的可及性——可以说多于与各自国家大多数公民的共同点。[^zh-ch03-34] 他们都投身于超越民族国家意识形态范畴的思考。艺术家常感到与中国国家及其摇摆不定的审查与赞助政策相冲突。亚裔美国策展人则与美国公民身份和国族认同制度抗争——这些制度把他们框定为“无法同化的异族”——并努力创造文化生产场所，提醒国家其与亚洲在经济、劳动和战争中的历史联系。[^zh-ch03-35] 然而，塑造他们参与全球艺术的不同文化民族主义话语，在对话过程中导致了微妙的两极分化，使双方显得更紧张而非同感。


〔原书 131〕

The conversation had entered uncertain terrain, where the borders of Asia (as a geopolitical and cultural region) and Asian America (as a geographically based political coalition that deploys notions of a common culture) abraded one other, and where the translation of identity could only be uttered haltingly. For Huang Du, Wang Yin, and the other artists, a sense of fidelity to or kinship with China grew out of a shared language and historical experience of being Third World in relation to the United States or even other parts of Asia such as Japan; theirs was a heroic *liumang* (hooligan) nationalism apropos the international stage, where they felt they must prove China worthy of inclusion and by doing so might increase the opportunities currently available to them as culture workers at home. They became comrades in discomfort with their dependency on the West (and its interpreters) for this recognition, even if it is a West with an Asian face. Eungie Joo, Doryun Chong, and René de Guzman, however, might be said to advocate a Pan-Asian fidelity or kinship born of the racialized politics of the United States, where they too felt besieged in relation to a contemporary art world whose exclusivity they challenged. These different versions of who is inside or outside, speaking nearby, represent a moment of coauthorship, but also of fractious claims to oppositionality that strain to recognize one another.

对话进入了不确定的地带：亚洲（作为地缘政治和文化区域）与亚裔美国（作为基于地理的政治联盟，运用共同文化的观念）的边界相互摩擦，而身份认同的翻译只能结结巴巴地说出。对黄笃、王音和其他艺术家而言，对中国保持忠诚或亲缘感，源于共同语言和作为第三世界相对于美国，甚至日本等亚洲其他地区的共同历史经验；他们的民族主义是面对国际舞台时英雄式的流氓（liumang）民族主义——他们觉得自己必须证明中国配得上被纳入，并借此增加他们作为国内文化工作者目前可获得的机会。他们对依赖西方（及其阐释者）给予这种承认感到同样的不安，并因此成为同志，即便那是一个长着亚洲面孔的西方。然而，也可以说 Eungie Joo、Doryun Chong 和勒内·德古兹曼倡导一种源自美国种族化政治的泛亚忠诚或亲缘感；在美国，他们同样感到被一个他们质疑其排他性的当代艺术世界围困。这些关于谁在内、谁在外的不同说法在彼此近旁言说，代表一个共同书写的时刻，也代表对对立立场的好斗主张——这些主张艰难地试图相互承认。


〔原书 131, 132〕

In my blurred role as ethnographer-interpreter, I found myself positioned in different contextual ways: as an imperfect speaker of Chinese who had spent enough time in China to get cultural references like *Wei Cheng*; as an Asian American intimately aware of racial hierarchies and the fraught politics of inclusion; as a feminist critic of power dynamics in the art world; and as an anthropologist of cultural translations of value. I was aware from the start of disciplinary tensions between art and anthropology. I often tried to reinforce this divide because I did not want to be seen within my research community as an arbiter of aesthetic distinction with the power to provide entrée to Western art spaces. I frequently felt called on by artists to attempt this role, but I resisted it because I lacked institutional art world connections and for fear of seeming partisan to certain individuals. My one attempt to breach this divide, by advocating for more women to be included in the curators’ studio visits, had backfired. The ybca curators’ project description seemed to equate anthropology with orientalism in the following statement: “Wary of the limiting effects of anthropological approaches to contemporary art, we want to disrupt our complicity in the neo-orientalist gaze.” I understood this wariness as emerging from an ethnic studies demand that art be read as art in a universal sense rather than ethnography, for otherwise the Asian in America remains the “unassimilable alien,” a case study in foreign culture rather than cocreator in the kingdom of culture. As an ethnographer of the cultural encounters that produce what is recognized as global contemporary art, and of the aesthetic conventions that shape how those encounters unfold, my goal is not to provide a more historically or culturally accurate way to interpret artworks, but to examine the encounter of conventions as producing art world practices of meaning-making, evaluation, selection, and resistance.[^en-ch03-36] I also remain compelled to account for those art world participants who fell out of the picture. Transnational efforts to speak a shared language of art produce exclusions, the anonymous folk painter in Wang Yin’s studio or the virtually invisible Chinese woman artist.[^en-ch03-37]

在我作为民族志学者兼口译员的模糊角色中，我发现自己以不同方式被语境定位：作为中文不完美、却在中国待得够久、能领会《围城》之类文化指涉的言说者；作为深谙种族等级和包容政治之艰险的亚裔美国人；作为艺术界权力动态的女性主义批评者；作为研究价值之文化翻译的人类学家。我从一开始就意识到艺术与人类学之间的学科张力。我常试图强化这一分界，因为我不想在研究群体中被视为审美区分的仲裁者，有权提供进入西方艺术空间的入场券。艺术家经常要求我尝试这一角色，但我拒绝了，因为我缺乏艺术界机构人脉，也害怕显得偏袒某些个人。我唯一一次试图打破这一分界，是主张让策展人参观更多女性艺术家的工作室，结果适得其反。YBCA策展人的项目说明似乎把人类学等同于东方主义：“由于警惕人类学方法对当代艺术可能产生的限制，我们希望打破自身与新东方主义凝视的共谋。”我理解这种警惕源于族裔研究的要求：艺术应被当作普遍意义上的艺术来阅读，而非民族志；否则，在美国的亚洲人仍将是“无法同化的异族”，是异国文化的案例研究，而非文化王国的共同创造者。作为研究生产所谓全球当代艺术之文化相遇的民族志学者，也作为研究塑造这些相遇如何展开之审美惯例的学者，我的目标不是提供一种在历史上或文化上更准确地阐释艺术品的方式，而是考察惯例的相遇如何生产艺术界意义制造、评价、选择和抵抗的实践。[^zh-ch03-36] 我也仍感到有责任说明那些从画面中掉落的艺术界参与者。用共同艺术语言言说的跨国努力制造排斥：王音工作室里匿名的民间画师，或几乎隐形的中国女性艺术家。[^zh-ch03-37]


〔原书 132〕

One World Art Center

一世界艺术中心


〔原书 132〕

After the curators departed, they proceeded to select artists, develop exhibit themes, and arrange for artwork to be shipped to their gallery spaces. The conversation also continued on the other side of the Pacific, where their hosts transformed the interaction into global assertions of their own. Huang Du, for example, published a series of dialogues between curators—himself and colleagues from Cuba, Germany, Japan, and the United States—in the Chinese journal *Jinri xianfeng* (Avant-garde today). His introduction to the published interviews asserts that curatorial work necessitates nothing less than the globe as its playing field: “In fact, prominent art curators, no matter whether they work from theory to realization, or from realization to theory, must have a macroscopic and global visual field.... Curators play a bridge-like role of enabling dialogue and exchange between artist, the exhibit, and its audience.”[^en-ch03-38]

策展人离开后，他们继续挑选艺术家、发展展览主题，并安排作品运往画廊空间。对话也在太平洋彼岸继续，那里的主人把互动转化为自身的全球主张。例如，黄笃在中文杂志《今日先锋》上发表了一系列他与古巴、德国、日本和美国同行策展人的对话。他为访谈所写的导言断言，策展工作必须以全球为竞技场：“事实上，杰出的艺术策展人，无论从理论到实现，还是从实现到理论，都必须具有宏观的全球视野……策展人扮演着促成艺术家、展览及其观众之间对话与交流的桥梁角色。”[^zh-ch03-38]


〔原书 133〕

Beijing under the mandate to become a global city that would attract the world’s attention also suggests one final translation. The urban redevelopment model that led to the creation of the Yerba Buena Center, in which art symbolizes a city’s urbane distinction but also critiques the wreckage created in the attainment of this goal, was transplanted across the Pacific to sites like the East Modern Art Center described in chapter 2. Some months before *Time After Time: Asia and Our Moment* opened at the ybca, Wang Yin became curator for the first exhibit held at Beijing’s One World Art Center, housed within a commodity apartment complex of the same name.

在受命成为吸引世界目光的全球城市这一背景下，北京还提示出最后一次翻译。催生耶尔巴布埃纳中心的城市再开发模式，被跨越太平洋移植到第二章所述远洋艺术中心等地。在这一模式中，艺术象征城市的文雅区隔，却也批判达成这一目标过程中制造的废墟。在《一次又一次：亚洲与我们此刻》于YBCA开幕前几个月，王音成为北京一世界艺术中心首展的策展人，该中心位于同名商品房小区内。


〔原书 133, 134〕

I had gone to the center to meet another artist for an interview, but we got waylaid by a group of Belgian university students who had arranged to talk to Wang and several of the artists from his exhibit. The students had funding from their national ministry of culture to investigate contemporary art in China and develop cultural contacts between the two countries but had sparse language skills to do so. I was cajoled into interpreting what was, by now, a fairly familiar conversation. One of the first questions asked by the Belgians was why Chinese contemporary art borrowed so much from the West. The question, in the same breath that it expressed a Western desire for art untainted by the traffic of the world, waiting only to be discovered, also framed Chinese contemporary art as lacking in originality. In the midst of the ensuing discussion, in which several artists took the students to task for their naïve assumption of overwhelming Western influence and Chinese derivativeness, a latecomer, the artist He An, walked in and was brought up to speed. He immediately replied, with a deadpan expression on his face, “I don’t really know anything about Belgium except that you make good guns and now you sell them to the Chinese military.” The students were completely thrown by this display of willful disdain for their country’s culture, which is what they thought they’d come to exchange in the One World Art Center, and the seeming accusation that their nation’s military industry fueled Chinese nationalism. He An’s form of “saying no” underlined the historical legacy that lurks behind Chinese-Western cultural and economic exchange. As the Belgian students scrambled to defend the peaceful ambitions of their small country and the good will behind their visit, He An watched his work of reversals unfold, with a complex intentionality of its own that also had the artists feinting with the shadow of a question that still lingered: Is there a difference between colonization and self-colonization? They had, after all, consented to spend their afternoon hosting a group of curious but uninformed students sent by the Belgian Ministry of Culture.

我去中心是为采访另一位艺术家，但我们被一群比利时大学生耽搁了——他们安排与王音及其展览的几位艺术家交谈。这些学生获得本国文化部资助，来考察中国当代艺术、发展两国文化联系，却几乎没有相应的语言能力。我被劝说为一场如今已相当熟悉的对话担任口译。比利时人最先问的问题之一是，为什么中国当代艺术从西方借鉴了这么多。这个问题在表达西方渴望未受世界流通污染、只待被发现的艺术的同时，也把中国当代艺术框定为缺乏原创性。在随后的讨论中，几位艺术家责备学生天真地假定西方影响压倒一切、中国只会模仿；这时，迟到的艺术家何岸走进来，被告知了前情。他立刻面无表情地回答：“我对比利时真不太了解，只知道你们枪造得好，现在又卖给中国军队。”学生们被这种对本国文化的故意轻蔑完全打乱了阵脚——他们以为来到一世界艺术中心是为了交流文化——也被那看似指控其国家军工助长中国民族主义的话打乱。何岸的“说不”形式，强调了中西文化与经济交换背后潜伏的历史遗产。当比利时学生匆忙捍卫小国的和平抱负和此行的善意时，何岸看着自己的逆转作品展开，其中自有复杂的意图性，也让艺术家们与一个仍然萦绕的问题之影过招：殖民与自我殖民之间是否存在差异？毕竟，他们同意花一下午接待一群由比利时文化部派来的好奇却无知的学生。


〔原书 134〕

In a 1957 speech addressed to China’s youth, Mao Zedong declared, “The world is yours, but it is also ours.” His use of “the world” in relation to who defines it marks a distinction between generations, between the revolutionary founders of the nation and the youthful inheritors of this vision. As a phrase appropriated by contemporary artists, it also registers the difference between world visions, and of what art represents within them, held by various art world participants.[^en-ch03-39] In the next chapter, a monumental art project following the historical route of the Red Army’s Long March demonstrates an ongoing preoccupation with this discrepancy between art worldings. Its curators resurrected Mao Zedong’s revolutionary nationalism to reverse the status quo directionality of art translation efforts. Instead of sending Chinese artists into the Western world, they attempted to draw global attention to Chinese contemporary art by hosting well-known Western artists in China, within the cultural context of world communism. This reconfiguration of global-local relations also nested feminist art encounters within the global-local and East-West encounters that shaped Chinese contemporary art. Again, I found myself drawn in as an interpreter and witness, this time to Chinese female artists finding their own way of “saying no.”

在1957年对中国青年的讲话中，毛泽东宣布：“世界是你们的，也是我们的。”他对“世界”的用法，以及谁界定世界，标志着代际区分——国家的革命奠基者与这一愿景的青年继承者之间。作为当代艺术家挪用的说法，它也记录了各种艺术界参与者所持世界愿景的差异，以及艺术在这些愿景中所代表之物的差异。[^zh-ch03-39] 下一章将展示一个沿红军长征历史路线行进的大型艺术项目，它以持续的方式关注艺术世界营造之间的这种差异。其策展人复活毛泽东的革命民族主义，以逆转艺术转译活动既有的流动方向。他们不是把中国艺术家送往西方世界，而是试图通过在世界共产主义的文化语境中邀请知名西方艺术家来中国，把全球注意力吸引到中国当代艺术上。这种对全球—地方关系的重新配置，也把女性主义艺术相遇嵌套在塑造中国当代艺术的全球—地方与东西方相遇之中。再一次，我发现自己作为口译员和见证者被拉入其中，这一次是中国女性艺术家寻找自己的“说不”方式。

## 第四章　女性主义艺术的腹地


〔原书 135〕

Four: The Hinterlands of Feminist Art

第四章　女性主义艺术的腹地


〔原书 135〕

A revolution is not a dinner party.

—MAO ZEDONG, 1927

革命不是请客吃饭。

——毛泽东，1927年


〔原书 135〕

The Long March is the first of its kind. It is a manifesto, a propaganda force, a seeding machine.

—MAO ZEDONG, 1935

长征是历史纪录上的第一次。它是宣言书，是宣传队，是播种机。

——毛泽东，1935年


〔原书 135, 136〕

On July 28, 2002, fourteen Chinese artists traveled on foot and in cars along a rain-washed dirt and gravel road from the village of Luoshui to a new wooden guesthouse on the shore of Lugu Lake. Upon arriving, the artists gathered in the courtyard of the two-story inn, built to resemble a traditional Mosuo dwelling, and examined the art proposals hung on the walls of the first floor. Two camera crews set up their equipment beneath flimsy hand-held umbrellas and began filming the artists as they heatedly discussed the whereabouts of Judy Chicago, icon of the U.S. feminist art movement, with whom they were to meet that morning. They had traveled to this remote corner of Yunnan Province in southwestern China in response to an online call issued by Chicago three months earlier (figure 4.01). Her proposal, organized around the theme “What If Women Ruled the World,” suggested a feminist art gathering in this location of renown among anthropologists, Lonely Planet backpackers, and tourists seeking either sexual titillation or feminist inspiration, all attracted by the matrilineal culture of the Mosuo, a Chinese ethnic minority. Chicago had been invited by Lu Jie, chief curator of *The Long March: A Walking Visual Display*, to serve as guest curator for this site, one of twenty planned for an art project following the route of the Communist Red Army’s 1934 Long March. Once all participants finally converged at Lugu Lake, any utopian expectation of transnational feminist collaboration quickly faded. After a group meeting with Chicago, many of the Chinese artists worried their work would be appropriated. Hours of internal debate led them to issue a manifesto, and on that morning in the guesthouse courtyard, they waited for her to emerge and respond.

2002年7月28日，十四位中国艺术家徒步或乘车，沿着一条被雨水冲刷的土石路，从落水村前往泸沽湖畔一座新建的木制客栈。到达后，艺术家们聚集在这座仿摩梭传统民居建造的两层客栈院子里，查看一楼墙上挂着的艺术方案。两个摄制组在单薄的手持雨伞下架好设备，开始拍摄艺术家们热烈讨论朱迪·芝加哥（Judy Chicago）的下落——这位美国女性主义艺术运动的偶像，本应在那天上午与他们见面。三个月前，芝加哥在网上发出征集，他们因此来到中国西南云南省这个偏远角落（图4.01）。她的方案围绕“如果女人统治世界”这一主题组织，提议在这个人类学家、《孤独星球》背包客，以及寻求性刺激或女性主义灵感之旅的游客都熟悉的地方，举行一次女性主义艺术聚会——吸引他们的都是中国少数民族摩梭人的母系文化。芝加哥受《长征：一个行走中的视觉展示》总策展人卢杰邀请，担任这一地点的客座策展人；该地点是计划中二十个地点之一，整个艺术项目沿共产党红军1934年长征路线行进。当所有参与者最终汇聚泸沽湖时，任何乌托邦式的跨国女性主义合作期待都迅速消退。在与芝加哥举行小组会议后，许多中国艺术家担心自己的作品会被挪用。数小时内部辩论使他们发表了一份宣言；那天早晨，他们在客栈院子里等她出来回应。


〔原书 136〕

![*图4.01　长征泸沽湖站的艺术家，在落水村与朱迪·芝加哥所住客栈之间的路上；该客栈是拟议中的“中国女人屋”选址。从左至右，前排：宋雁萍、雷燕；第二排：苏亚碧、黄引、Sasha Welland、孙国娟、庞璇、黄茹、张伦、付丽雅、Shen Yu、苏茹娅。James Tweedie 摄。*](web/assets/ch04-b004.jpg)

FIG 4.01 Artists at the Lugu Lake site of *The Long March*, on the road between Luoshui and Judy Chicago’s guesthouse, proposed site for a Chinese Womanhouse. From left to right, first row: Song Yanping, Lei Yan; second row: Su Yabi, Huang Yin, Sasha Welland, Sun Guojuan, Pang Xuan, Huang Ru, Zhang Lun, Fu Liya, Shen Yu, Su Ruya. Photograph by James Tweedie.

*图4.01　长征泸沽湖站的艺术家，在落水村与朱迪·芝加哥所住客栈之间的路上；该客栈是拟议中的“中国女人屋”选址。从左至右，前排：宋雁萍、雷燕；第二排：苏亚碧、黄引、Sasha Welland、孙国娟、庞璇、黄茹、张伦、付丽雅、Shen Yu、苏茹娅。James Tweedie 摄。*


〔原书 136, 137〕

Lu Jie and Qiu Zhijie, the chief and assistant curators of *The Long March*, conceived of the Lugu Lake exhibit as site six on an ambitious five-month traveling art show to follow the route of the original Long March. In 1934, the Communist Red Army, under attack by the Guomindang in the southeast, began a six-thousand-mile trek to the northwest. They abandoned prior attempts to revolutionize the urban proletariat and shifted their propaganda efforts toward a rural population, lecturing to peasants and garnering support for their guerrilla tactics as they marched through the interior to an eventual base in Yan’an, Shaanxi Province. This grueling yearlong ordeal serves as a foundational story about the consolidation of the Chinese Communist Party and its maxim “to serve the people” through teaching and learning from them. This tenet of Maoist praxis rejected colonial stagist history.[^en-ch04-1] The peasantry, rather than relegated to a period of development before they could become new citizen-subjects, were called on to play a vital and immediate role in shaping national revolutionary consciousness. In his 1942 “Talks at the Yan’an Conference on Literature and Art,” Mao Zedong cemented this mode of political consciousness-raising to cultural production. He borrowed Lenin’s phrase to describe art and literature as “a screw in the whole machine” of proletarian revolution and asserted their goals of exposing imperialist and class enemies, reaching a wider audience, and raising standards. He declared that cultural workers must prioritize “the task of understanding people and getting to know them properly,” in order to create literature and art that would be the result of “the revolutionary’s mind reflecting and processing popular life.”[^en-ch04-2]

《长征》总策展人卢杰和助理策展人邱志杰把泸沽湖展览构思为这个雄心勃勃、为期五个月的行进展览的第六站，该项目沿原始长征路线行进。1934年，共产党红军在东南部遭受国民党进攻，开始向西北进行六千英里的跋涉。他们放弃先前使城市无产阶级革命化的尝试，把宣传工作转向农村人口，在向内陆行军、最终抵达陕西延安根据地的途中向农民演讲，为其游击战术争取支持。这场长达一年的艰苦磨难，成为关于中国共产党巩固及其“为人民服务”信条——通过教育人民并向人民学习——的基础故事。这一毛泽东实践原则拒绝殖民主义的阶段论历史观。[^zh-ch04-1]农民不再被归入必须经历一个发展阶段才能成为新公民主体的位置，而是被号召在塑造国家革命意识中发挥至关重要而直接的作用。毛泽东在1942年《在延安文艺座谈会上的讲话》中，把这种政治觉悟提升模式与文化生产牢固结合。他借用列宁的说法，把文艺描述为无产阶级革命“整个机器上的螺丝钉”，并宣称其目标是揭露帝国主义和阶级敌人、触及更广泛受众、提高水准。他宣布，文化工作者必须优先考虑“了解人、熟悉人的工作”，以便创作出“革命者的头脑反映和加工人民生活”所产生的文学艺术。[^zh-ch04-2]


〔原书 137〕

With Yan’an planned as the final site for the 2002 “walking visual display,” Lu Jie, who holds a master’s degree in curatorial studies from Goldsmiths College, University of London, revisited this moment of artistic manifesto-making in the sixtieth anniversary year of Mao’s “Talks,” not with the aim of advocating world revolutionary socialism but of integrating China with the global art system. His self-professed goals were to introduce international contemporary art to China’s “peripheral population” and to draw international attention to Chinese contemporary art. Financed by a foundation set up in New York and headquartered in Beijing, *The Long March* was launched in Ruijin, Jiangxi Province, starting point of the original Long March and host now to “red tourism” pilgrims. His curatorial team organized several events here, including a screening of *La Chinoise* in Mixi village, site of the first Red Army headquarters. The projection of Jean Luc-Godard’s 1967 film about young Maoist revolutionaries in Paris on a makeshift fabric screen hung in a village ancestral hall emblematized Lu’s overall effort to revisit and instigate cross-cultural artistic dialogue. His restaging of the march was partial, highly interpretive, and designed to provoke. The “comrades” he mobilized traveled with a media entourage of camera people by plane, train, and bus. They did not become involved in any sustained learning from rural communities, but their strategic resuscitation of the Long March as political praxis demanded recognition of Chinese cultural production as worth learning from, as innovative rather than derivative. Lu Jie invited and funded Western artists to join their endeavor, to work and learn alongside Chinese artists.

由于延安被计划为2002年“行走中的视觉展示”的终点，拥有伦敦大学金匠学院策展研究硕士学位的卢杰，在毛泽东《讲话》发表六十周年之际重新回到这个艺术宣言制作的时刻——不是为了倡导世界革命社会主义，而是为了把中国融入全球艺术体系。他自称的目标包括把国际当代艺术介绍给中国“边缘人群”，并把国际注意力吸引到中国当代艺术上。《长征》由一家在纽约成立、总部设在北京的基金会资助，在江西省瑞金启动——原始长征的起点，如今是“红色旅游”朝圣者的目的地。他的策展团队在此组织了数场活动，包括在红军第一个总部所在地密溪村放映《中国姑娘》。把让-吕克·戈达尔1967年这部关于巴黎青年毛主义革命者的影片，投放到挂在村庄祠堂里的临时布幕上，象征了卢杰重新造访并激发跨文化艺术对话的整体努力。他对长征的重演是局部的、高度阐释性的，且意在挑衅。他动员的“同志们”带着摄影摄像媒体团队，乘飞机、火车和大巴行进。他们没有参与任何持续向农村社区学习的过程，但他们把长征战略性地复活为政治实践，要求承认中国文化生产值得学习，是创新的而非派生的。卢杰邀请并资助西方艺术家加入他们的行动，与中国艺术家一起工作和学习。


〔原书 137, 138〕

This promotion of cosmopolitan Chinese culture via a return to the socialist past demonstrates the hybrid hallmarks of the reform-era culture industry. Its promoters aimed to integrate with global capitalism but in a way that drew on culturally specific legacies and differentiated them from the West.[^en-ch04-3] Lu Jie played on the cultural distinction of the Long March, while simultaneously loosening it from its socialist referent and rejection of individual authorship. His *Long March* intermingled different orders of worldliness—the global 1960s circulation of Maoism and the neocolonial hierarchies of contemporary global art—to chart an art worlding in which Chinese socialist modernity serves as a living historical resource, in which China is not catching up, but was already avant-garde. This embrace of Maoist culture highlighted the instability of one of its key signs, that of “woman.” What was it, is it to be a woman, a Chinese woman, or a new woman? Who has the power to author her? What resources do female cultural producers draw on in their struggle to be recognized as authors of their own sign? Responses to these questions arose in dissonant ways at site six of the Long March.

这种通过回归社会主义过去来推广世界性中国文化的做法，展示了改革时期文化产业的混合特征。其推动者旨在融入全球资本主义，但方式要利用文化特有的遗产，并使之区别于西方。[^zh-ch04-3] 卢杰利用长征的文化区隔性，同时把它从其社会主义指涉和对个人作者身份的拒绝中松动开来。他的长征混合了不同世界性秩序——毛泽东主义在1960年代的全球流通与当代全球艺术的新殖民等级——以绘制一种艺术世界营造：其中中国社会主义现代性是活生生的历史资源，中国不是在追赶，而是早已先锋。这种对毛泽东文化的拥抱，凸显了其关键符号之一“女人”的不稳定性。过去以及现在，身为女人、中国女人或新女人意味着什么？谁有权书写她？女性文化生产者在自己争取被承认为自身符号作者的斗争中，动用了什么资源？对这些问题的回答在《长征》第六站以不和谐的方式出现。


〔原书 138, 139〕

Although none of the Red Army troops actually reached Lugu Lake, Lu and his assistant curator Qiu Zhijie, a well-known conceptual artist based in Beijing, deemed it close enough to the original Long March route to include on their itinerary. With its well-documented matrilineal Mosuo culture, Lugu Lake seemed the perfect locale for a feminist theme. Their original prospectus for site six ranged broadly: it proposed projects on the lives of Grandma Xiao, a Mosuo supporter of the Red Army in the 1930s, and Yang Erche Namu, a Mosuo pop sensation who transformed a brief music career into a industry of self-promotion that has included the publication of nine memoirs; as well as public on-site readings of Julia Kristeva’s *About Chinese Women* and Simone de Beauvoir’s *The Second Sex*.[^en-ch04-4] Of these two French feminists, Kristeva in particular provided a conceptual bridge; in 1974, she had traveled to China with editorial members of the literary journal *Tel Quel*, which for several years embraced Maoism. In spite of stated curatorial plans to include Mosuo women in the project, the necessary work of building local connections was never carried out. Over a year in advance, however, Lu convinced Chicago to join the project. Excited by what she learned about the Mosuo from materials Lu sent her, Chicago felt compelled to spread the word about their alternative sexual and kinship practices, especially to Chinese women who might not know of this culture within their own national borders. Lu translated her call for submissions of artworks to exhibit or create at Lugu Lake and posted it on a popular Chinese art website. Chicago asked artists to consider Mosuo society as a feminist inspiration: “Just like in the Lugu Lake area, ‘if women ruled the world,’ what would the world be like?”[^en-ch04-5] The announcement suggested that Chicago, twelve selected artists, and twelve local Mosuo women would convene at Lugu Lake to explore the history, imaginary, myth, and reality of matriarchal society through an art exhibition. This alteration of the original curatorial plan presaged what would become a continually evolving art happening.

尽管红军部队实际上并未到达泸沽湖，卢杰和助理策展人、北京知名观念艺术家邱志杰认为这里足够接近原始长征路线，可以列入行程。泸沽湖有记载详备的摩梭母系文化，似乎是女性主义主题的完美地点。他们为第六站撰写的最初策划书范围宽泛：提议以1930年代支持红军的摩梭人肖奶奶，以及摩梭流行明星杨二车娜姆的生平为项目——杨二车娜姆把短暂的歌唱生涯转变为自我推销产业，包括出版九部回忆录；还提议在泸沽湖现场公开朗读朱莉娅·克里斯蒂娃的《中国妇女》和西蒙娜·德·波伏娃的《第二性》。[^zh-ch04-4] 在这两位法国女性主义者中，克里斯蒂娃尤其提供了概念桥梁；1974年，她与文学杂志《原样》（Tel Quel）编辑成员一起访华，该杂志曾拥护毛泽东主义数年。尽管策划书声称要让摩梭女性参与项目，建立本地联系的必要工作从未落实。然而，卢杰提前一年多就说服芝加哥加入。芝加哥从卢杰寄给她的材料中了解到摩梭人，兴奋不已，觉得自己必须传播他们另类的性与亲属实践，尤其是告诉那些可能不知道自己国境内存在这种文化的中国女性。卢杰把芝加哥征集在泸沽湖展出或创作作品的呼吁翻译成中文，发布在一个流行的中国艺术网站上。芝加哥请艺术家把摩梭社会视为女性主义灵感：“就像在泸沽湖地区那样，‘如果女人统治世界’，世界会是什么样？”[^zh-ch04-5] 公告称芝加哥、十二位入选艺术家和十二位本地摩梭女性将在泸沽湖聚集，通过一场艺术展览探索母权社会的历史、想象、神话与现实。对原策划的这种改动，预示着它将成为一场不断演变的艺术事件。


〔原书 139〕

My participation began in Beijing, with meetings and phone calls with Lu Jie, Qiu Zhijie, and Beijing-based artists. Many of these artists eventually decided not to become involved, but after communicating with artists in Sichuan and Yunnan, two of them chose to go to Lugu Lake. They convinced me to join them because they knew I had a video camera. Lu Jie had arranged for a television crew to follow *The Long March*, and the artists who planned to meet with Judy Chicago at Lugu Lake worried that these “official” cameras wouldn’t record whatever might transpire from their perspective. They pulled me in as an ethnographer of the project, although at the moment I became witness to it, I also mediated it: through how I wielded my camera, weighed in on erupting debates, and served as interpreter for their interactions with Judy Chicago.

我的参与始于北京，与卢杰、邱志杰和北京艺术家们开会、通电话。他们中许多人最终决定不参与，但在与四川和云南的艺术家沟通后，其中两人选择前往泸沽湖。他们说服我同行，因为他们知道我有摄像机。卢杰已安排电视摄制组跟拍《长征》，而计划在泸沽湖与朱迪·芝加哥会面的艺术家担心，这些“官方”镜头不会从他们的视角记录可能发生的一切。他们把我拉进来，作为项目的民族志学者；然而在我成为其见证者的那一刻，我也中介了它：通过我如何运用摄像机、如何介入爆发的辩论，以及如何为他们与朱迪·芝加哥的互动担任口译。


〔原书 139, 140〕

This chapter tells several stories, or a story of several layers. The first is one of emergent worlds, which argues for the role of ethnography in understanding art as more than a collection of stable objects reflecting the world. On the shore of Lugu Lake, visions of the world collided. The artworks created out of the encounter represent momentary crystallizations of artists’ ongoing thought processes and material experiments with particular media, technologies of image making, and the gendered histories of both. The next layer of the story explores this encounter in relation to questions about cultural globalization. It demonstrates the unstable relations between “global” and “local” and how sociocultural forms labeled global and considered universal, like contemporary art or feminism, are multiply produced through uneven global encounters. The impulse to craft a common or even a shared narrative can instead create fractures. Another layer of the story asks how this fracturing or decentering of globality necessitates a reassessment of institutionalized narratives of global feminist art. What it means for Chinese contemporary art to go global demands feminist attention to questions of gender, power, and aesthetic form immanent in social worlds of visual production. The nesting of feminist art encounters within global–local and East–West encounters forces a rethinking of conventional center-periphery relations and therefore of discourses about global art and global feminism. The struggles that occurred at Lugu Lake revolved around the question of feminism in Chinese contemporary art repeatedly raised in the capital. In this off-center location, female artists asserted a demand for equity often lost or overshadowed in Beijing’s race for recognition. Finally, this is a story of rural–urban relations in China, the flipside of artists depicting rural migrants in Beijing, in which artists go down to the countryside, a longstanding socialist practice. While the road espoused by Mao Zedong beginning with the Long March envisioned the countryside as the foundation of Communist China that would encircle and revolutionize the semicolonial, parasitic city, the rapid urbanization of the economic-reform era reversed this ideological geography. The development of a postsocialist urban aesthetics, what Robin Visser describes as “cities surround the countryside,” was deeply part of emerging Chinese art worlds in which cities were understood as the motor of culture even as affective attachments often still lay in past socialist privileging of rural people and places.[^en-ch04-6]

本章讲述几个故事，或一个有多重层次的故事。第一个是关于涌现中的世界，论证民族志在理解艺术——不只是反映世界的稳定物品集合——方面的作用。在泸沽湖畔，各种世界愿景相互碰撞。从相遇中产生的艺术作品，代表艺术家持续思考过程与特定媒介、图像生产技术，以及两者性别化历史之物质实验的短暂结晶。故事的下一层结合文化全球化问题考察这场相遇，展示“全球”与“地方”之间的不稳定关系，以及被标为全球、被视为普遍的当代艺术或女性主义等社会文化形式，如何通过不均等的全球相遇多重生成。塑造共同、甚至共享叙事的冲动，反而可能制造裂隙。故事的又一层追问：全球性的这种碎裂或去中心化，如何要求重新评估全球女性主义艺术的制度化叙事？中国当代艺术走向全球意味着什么，要求女性主义关注视觉生产之社会世界中内蕴的性别、权力和审美形式问题。女性主义艺术相遇嵌套在全球—地方和东西方相遇之中，迫使人们重新思考传统的中心—边缘关系，从而重新思考关于全球艺术和全球女性主义的话语。泸沽湖发生的斗争，围绕中国当代艺术中的女性主义问题展开——这个问题在首都不断被提出。在这个偏离中心的地点，女性艺术家提出了在北京争取承认的竞赛中常常失落或被掩盖的平等要求。最后，这是一个关于中国城乡关系的故事，是艺术家描绘北京外来民工的背面：艺术家下乡，一种历史悠久的社会主义实践。毛泽东从长征开始倡导的道路，把乡村设想为共产主义中国的基础，它将包围并使半殖民地、寄生的城市革命化；而经济改革时期的快速城市化逆转了这一意识形态地理。后社会主义城市美学的发展——罗宾·维瑟（Robin Visser）所谓“城市包围农村”——深深属于新兴中国艺术世界；在其中，城市被理解为文化引擎，尽管情感依恋往往仍寄托于社会主义过去对农村人民和地方的优先。[^zh-ch04-6]


〔原书 140〕

Long March as Seeding Machine

长征作为播种机


〔原书 140, 141〕

Lei Yan’s curiosity was sparked when she read Judy Chicago’s online call for proposals on her home computer in Kunming one day after it was posted on April 28, 2002. A former soldier, she was intimately acquainted with the story of the Red Army’s Long March. Questions about gender difference raised by her experience in a male-dominated military family also made Chicago’s thematic proposition intriguing. That night Lei Yan called her friend Sun Guojuan, an artist who splits her time between Beijing and her hometown of Kunming, and told her that she wanted to join this activity. Although Sun did not feel the same inherent interest in the proposal, she agreed to accompany her friend on an advance scouting trip to Lugu Lake. Before their departure on May 3, their discussion of possible pieces turned to the idea of leaving something at Lugu Lake to return to later. Suddenly a famous historical dictum popped out of Lei’s mouth: “The Long March is a manifesto, a propaganda force, a seeding machine.” They decided to take hempseed to scatter on the bank of Lugu Lake. The action of scattering, conceived of as a performance piece, drew on the history of the Long March as means of ideological dissemination and suggested symbolic possibilities. The first was the potential of the artworks produced as part of *The Long March* Lugu Lake exhibit to spread out and transmit new ideas about art and gender. The second conceptualized hemp or marijuana seeds as symbolic of capitalism’s bourgeois way of life and conjectured that when scattered in a field of “plain, modest, proletarian” corn, the two plants would grow strong together as in “socialism with Chinese characteristics.” Both artists kept journals of their trip in the form of battlefield reports (figure 4.02), decorated with drawings by Lei Yan that referenced hand-produced military unit newspapers. A side column declared, “By recording our ideas for participating in the Long March plan, we employ the most primary propaganda tactic of the Red Army’s Long March. We use the idea of sowing seeds to transmit the beliefs and ideas of our creative work.”[^en-ch04-7] Their avant-garde, in the literal sense, action provides a metaphor for the larger encounter that took place almost three months later. Along with Lei and Sun, artists from around China, to whom Chicago was generally well known, began to submit proposals. *Sowing Hempseed* might also represent the various individuals and aspirations set in motion by the Long March project: a seeding machine that mixed different elements in a strategically chosen field, yielding unpredictable results.

朱迪·芝加哥的网上征集于2002年4月28日发布，次日，雷燕在昆明家中的电脑上读到它，好奇心被点燃。她当过兵，对红军长征的故事非常熟悉。她在男性主导的军人家庭中的经历所引发的性别差异问题，也使芝加哥的主题提议显得有趣。当晚，雷燕给朋友孙国娟打电话——这位艺术家在北京和家乡昆明之间往来——告诉她自己想参加这个活动。孙国娟对此提议并无同样的内在兴趣，但仍同意陪朋友先去泸沽湖探路。5月3日出发前，她们讨论可能的作品时，想到在泸沽湖留下什么东西，日后再回来。雷燕突然脱口说出一句著名的历史格言：“长征是宣言书，是宣传队，是播种机。”她们决定带大麻籽，撒在泸沽湖岸边。这一撒种行为被构想为一件行为作品，借鉴长征作为意识形态传播手段的历史，并提示多种象征可能。第一，是作为《长征》泸沽湖展览一部分创作的作品有潜力传播关于艺术与性别的新观念。第二，是把大麻籽象征为资本主义资产阶级生活方式，并推测把它撒在“朴素、谦逊、无产阶级”的玉米地里，两种植物会像“中国特色社会主义”那样一起茁壮成长。两位艺术家都以战地报道的形式记录此行（图4.02），并配以雷燕参照手工制作部队报纸所作的绘画。侧栏宣称：“通过记录我们参与长征计划的构想，我们采用红军长征最原始的宣传工作方式。我们用播种的观念来传递创作工作的信念与思想。”[^zh-ch04-7] 她们字面意义上的先锋行为，为近三个月后发生的更大相遇提供了隐喻。与雷燕和孙国娟一起，来自中国各地、普遍熟知芝加哥的艺术家开始提交方案。《播撒大麻籽》也可以代表长征项目所启动的各种个体与愿望：一台在战略选择的地里混合不同元素的播种机，产出不可预测的结果。


〔原书 141〕

![*图4.02　雷燕，《长征前线报道》第1期，2002年5月10日。纸本钢笔墨水，27厘米×38.7厘米。艺术家惠允。*](web/assets/ch04-b013.jpg)

FIG 4.02 Lei Yan, *Long March Battlefront Report, Issue #1*, May 10, 2002. Pen and ink on paper, 27 cm × 38.7 cm. Courtesy of the artist.

*图4.02　雷燕，《长征前线报道》第1期，2002年5月10日。纸本钢笔墨水，27厘米×38.7厘米。艺术家惠允。*


〔原书 141, 142〕

Judy Chicago, originally Judy Cohen, changed her surname to the city of her birth as a protest against patriarchal naming traditions. The reputation of the artist as icon of 1970s feminist art in the United States rests most solidly on her piece *The Dinner Party* (1975–79). Both attacked and celebrated, this large-scale installation has “long been thought of as the feminist art manifesto, par excellence.”[^en-ch04-8] In collaboration with historians and other artists, Chicago created a table in the shape of an equilateral triangle with place settings for thirty-nine women of mythical or historical significance, from the Primordial Goddess to Sojourner Truth to Georgia O’Keefe. The opening in the table’s center reveals a white tile floor painted with the names of 999 additional women. The identity of each woman at the table is crafted through intricately stitched table runners and porcelain plates painted with vulvar motifs, some sculpted in three-dimensional relief.[^en-ch04-9] Chicago rooted this monumental effort to reclaim women’s role in history and art in her belief in premodern matriarchal culture.[^en-ch04-10]

朱迪·芝加哥原名朱迪·科恩，为抗议父权命名传统，她把姓氏改为出生城市的名字。她作为1970年代美国女性主义艺术偶像的声誉，最牢固地建立在其作品《晚宴》（1975—79）之上。这件大型装置既受攻击也受赞颂，“长期以来一直被视为女性主义艺术的宣言书，典范之作”。[^zh-ch04-8] 芝加哥与历史学家及其他艺术家合作，制作了一张等边三角形的桌子，为三十九位神话或历史中的女性设置席位，从原初女神到索杰纳·特鲁思，再到乔治亚·欧姬芙。桌子中央的开口露出铺着白瓷砖的地面，上面绘有另外999位女性的名字。每位女性的身份由精心缝制的桌旗和绘有外阴图案的瓷盘构成，其中一些以三维浮雕塑成。[^zh-ch04-9] 芝加哥把这项重夺女性在历史与艺术中地位的纪念碑式努力，扎根于她对前现代母权文化的信念。[^zh-ch04-10]


〔原书 142〕

While Chicago’s online proposal piqued the interest of many Chinese artists, disputes arose around how to interpret the project’s direction. Were they to consider the largely forgotten history of the some two thousand women who participated in the original Long March; the relationship between the Han majority of China and the southwestern ethnic minority group of the Mosuo; or the power dynamics of an international art world still largely driven by the West and by men? Why were so few women invited to participate in the rest of Lu’s *The Long March*, with Lugu Lake a seeming push to segregate them in a single location? And, why was such a large portion of the budget allocated to host Judy Chicago’s travels in China, when the same amount could support the cost of materials and travel for numerous Chinese women to participate in the exhibit? When questioned about this last executive decision, which the artists had correctly inferred, Lu Jie insisted the presence of such a prominent figure would set the stage for greater debate. He tacked on the statement that he wished to “re-educate Judy Chicago.” In this ambiguous addendum, Lu possibly got carried away with his tongue-in-cheek adoption of Communist political language, or registered the internal contradictions of his own role. He stood aware of the necessity for a big name and a big issue (enter Chicago and her controversial feminism) to garner international attention, yet this need was exactly what he hoped to overturn in the art world.

芝加哥的网上提议激起许多中国艺术家的兴趣，但围绕如何理解项目方向出现了争议。他们是应当考虑参加原始长征的约两千名女性这段大体被遗忘的历史；考虑中国汉族多数与西南少数民族摩梭人的关系；还是考虑仍主要由西方和男性驱动的国际艺术世界的权力动态？为什么卢杰《长征》其余部分邀请的女性如此之少，仿佛泸沽湖是为了把她们隔离在单一地点？为什么预算中有如此大一部分用于接待朱迪·芝加哥在中国旅行，而同样的钱可以支持众多中国女性参展的材料和差旅费用？当被问及这最后一个执行决定——艺术家们正确地推断出了它——卢杰坚称，这样一位显赫人物的到场会为更大辩论搭建舞台。他又补充说，他希望“重新教育朱迪·芝加哥”。在这句含糊的补充中，卢杰或许是对自己半开玩笑挪用共产党政治语言入了迷，或许是无意间暴露了自己角色的内在矛盾。他清楚知道需要一个大名字和一个大议题（于是有了芝加哥及其有争议的女性主义）来吸引国际关注，而这种需要恰恰是他希望在艺术界推翻的。


〔原书 142, 143〕

Ill will began to surface when several Beijing-based artists withdrew after being told the organizers would not help pay their expenses to Lugu Lake, something they asserted had been verbally promised to them when Lu Jie had solicited their participation. They had also grown uncomfortable with what they saw as a male curatorial effort to partition the majority of *The Long March* female participants to a single, marginal site. Three other Beijing women with rising art world profiles—Jiang Jie, Lin Tianmiao, and Yin Xiuzhen—had been invited to display pieces along with male peers at other sites, and the slight felt by the women relegated to the Lugu Lake activity contributed to their eventual boycott. As debate about site six of the project flared, I met in Beijing with Lu Jie and Qiu Zhijie to pursue more information about it. Upon hearing of my research interests in feminist art, they similarly sounded me out and suggested that I should come along as an ethnographic collaborator.[^en-ch04-11] Meanwhile, Lu revised the curatorial plan again. Overwhelmed by the number of submitted proposals and not wanting to reject any of the artists who had responded, he changed the format to a “proposals exhibit.” He informed artists that all proposals would be displayed at Lugu Lake. If they wanted to travel there to exhibit or create original works, they would have to cover their own expenses. When artists tried to clarify how the event would be organized, they were told to just show up with art in hand. When others complained about the financial difficulty of making the journey, they were told that the comrades of the original Long March knew how to “eat bitterness.” In Beijing, word traveled quickly about how the project represented an attempt to exploit Chinese women artists for the international reputation of its male curators. Some promoted boycotting the event as the reproduction of a male power structure unsurprisingly similar to that of the original march. Their criticisms recognized the hierarchies of both global contemporary art and historical Chinese socialism, even as they failed to call into question Lugu Lake as a site for the encounter of these issues. Except for an artist from Sichuan, Zhang Lun, who traveled in advance to Mosuo territory to learn about the issues that mattered to people there, they seemed uncharacteristically uncritical in their consumption of conventional representations of Mosuo.

当几位北京艺术家得知主办方不会帮助支付前往泸沽湖的费用，因而退出时，不满开始显现——他们声称卢杰邀请他们参与时曾口头承诺过。他们也逐渐感到不安，因为在他们看来，这是男性策展努力把《长征》的大部分女性参与者分割到一个边缘地点。另外三位艺术界声望日升的北京女性——姜杰、林天苗和尹秀珍——曾被邀请与其他男性同行一起在其他地点展示作品；被贬到泸沽湖活动的女性所感到的轻慢，促成了她们最终的抵制。随着关于项目第六站的辩论激化，我在北京与卢杰、邱志杰见面，希望了解更多信息。听说我对女性主义艺术的研究兴趣后，他们也同样试探我，并建议我作为民族志合作者同行。[^zh-ch04-11] 与此同时，卢杰再次修改策展计划。他被提交的方案数量压倒，又不想拒绝任何回应的艺术家，于是把形式改为“方案展”。他通知艺术家，所有方案都将在泸沽湖展示。如果他们想前往那里展示或创作原作，必须自负费用。当艺术家试图弄清活动将如何组织时，他们被告知带着作品出现就行。当其他人抱怨旅途的经济困难时，他们被告知原始长征的同志们懂得如何“吃苦”。在北京，消息迅速传开：这个项目代表着利用中国女性艺术家为其男性策展人的国际声望去牟利。一些人推动抵制活动，认为它复制了男性权力结构，与原来的长征相似，这并不令人意外。他们的批评认识到了全球当代艺术和中国历史社会主义的双重等级，却未能质疑泸沽湖作为这些议题相遇之地的选择。除了四川艺术家张伦提前前往摩梭地区，了解当地人关心的问题之外，他们似乎一反常态地不加批判地消费着对摩梭的常规再现。


〔原书 143〕

When Judy Chicago finally arrived in China, stopping first in Beijing to present a slide lecture, frustrated artists greeted her with their questions. She tried to make the best of the situation by insisting on the importance of a joint pilgrimage to a place she described as a kind of feminist utopia, a still existing matriarchal society. She declared that she hadn’t come from so far away to *not* cooperate with Chinese women, but if she had to, she would travel to Lugu Lake and exhibit her work in a solo stand for women’s right to make art as part of *The Long March*. With me as Chinese-English interpreter, she explained to skeptical artists in Beijing that she had also harbored the suspicion that “this was like just this little women’s thing.” But she continued, “I figured that if we all got together we could make so much trouble that they would wish they had never done this. So you know that’s what I was hoping. And for them to boycott it is like the absolute opposite of what should have happened.”[^en-ch04-12]

当朱迪·芝加哥终于抵达中国，先在北京作幻灯片讲座时，沮丧的艺术家们带着问题迎接她。她努力缓和局面，坚持认为共同到访她所描述的某种女性主义乌托邦、一个仍然存在的母权社会至关重要。她宣称，自己远道而来，就是要与中国女性合作；但如果不得不如此，她会前往泸沽湖，在《长征》中独自展出作品，以捍卫女性创作艺术的权利。由我担任中英口译，她向北京持怀疑态度的艺术家解释说，她也曾怀疑“这就像只是件小小的女人事情”。但她接着说：“我想，如果我们都聚在一起，我们可以制造那么多麻烦，让他们后悔做了这件事。所以你知道，这就是我所希望的。而他们抵制它，恰恰是应该发生的事情的绝对反面。”[^zh-ch04-12]


〔原书 144〕

Judy Chicago’s attempt to collaborate with those Chinese counterparts who did make their way to Lugu Lake continued to be a vexed encounter. I interpret this resistance to solidarity not as failure but a form of feminist practice that incites debate over who or what is the subject of feminism and over how different styles of activism interpellate or alienate. The focus on gender at Lugu Lake highlighted contradictions inherent in the project, and the Chinese contemporary art world, which I unravel by exploring the proliferating ironies they produced. I then turn to the events that led Chinese artists to issue a manifesto to Chicago and to the range of art works exhibited and created at Lugu Lake. These works reflect a larger question regarding feminism in Chinese contemporary art and the terminological trouble it created in curatorial practice. Through a review of these politics, I argue that a set of interlocking double binds arises from the art world encounter of Chinese and Western feminisms.

朱迪·芝加哥与那些确实抵达泸沽湖的中国同行合作尝试，仍然是一场棘手的相遇。我不把这种对团结的抵抗解释为失败，而视为一种女性主义实践：它引发关于谁是或什么是女性主义主体、不同行动主义风格如何询唤或疏离他人的辩论。泸沽湖对性别的聚焦，凸显了项目及中国当代艺术世界固有的矛盾；我通过探讨它们产生的不断增殖的讽刺来展开。然后，我转向导致中国艺术家向芝加哥发表宣言的事件，以及泸沽湖展出和创作的一系列作品。这些作品反映了一个关于中国当代艺术中女性主义的更大问题，以及它在策展实践中造成的术语麻烦。通过回顾这些政治，我论证中国与西方女性主义在艺术界的相遇产生了一组相互交织的双重束缚。


〔原书 144〕

Proliferating Ironies

不断增殖的反讽


〔原书 144〕

In *The Long March: A Walking Visual Display*, “women’s art” became subject to exclusionary partition, literally outside of time as the only exhibit site that detoured from the historical route. The conjoining of the Long March and feminism in Mosuo territory was fantastical on multiple levels. Women’s liberation as part of the Chinese Communist Party’s revolutionary platform arguably experienced a step backward at the time of the Long March. While female activists played an important role in early political mobilization, especially in urban factories, they became a liability as the Communists, in their war with the Guomindang, retreated from urban centers and turned toward revolutionizing a rural population.[^en-ch04-13] Party leaders backed off family and marriage reform for fear of alienating what they viewed now as their most important membership, the disenfranchised male peasantry who sought a return to an idealized past of control over family stability and its uninterrupted production of male lineages.[^en-ch04-14]

在《长征：一个行走中的视觉展示》中，“女性艺术”遭到排他性分割，字面上处于时间之外——它是唯一偏离历史路线的展览地点。长征与女性主义在摩梭地区的结合，在多个层面上都是幻想的。作为中国共产党革命纲领一部分的妇女解放，在长征时期可以说经历了一次倒退。女性行动者在早期政治动员中发挥了重要作用，尤其是在城市工厂；但随着共产党在与国民党战争中撤离城市中心、转向使农村人口革命化，她们成了累赘。[^zh-ch04-13] 党的领导人放弃家庭与婚姻改革，因为害怕疏远如今被视为最重要成员的无权男性农民——他们渴望回到理想化的过去，即控制家庭稳定并持续生产男性世系。[^zh-ch04-14]


〔原书 144, 145〕

Once the Red Army had established their guerrilla base at Yan’an, one of the female comrades, well-known writer Ding Ling, published an article in 1942 in the *Liberation Daily* entitled “Thoughts on March 8.”[^en-ch04-15] On the occasion of International Women’s Day, she exposed and satirized the internal *nannü* class system of Communist life at Yan’an. She opens, “When will it no longer be necessary to attach special weight to the word ‘woman’ and raise it specially?” She raises the Communist double bind for women mobilized on the one hand to serve the party and on the other to serve family: they are criticized as either irresponsible for not sacrificing their careers for family, or if they do, as politically backward. On marriage, Ding writes with sarcastic humor: “But women invariably want to get married. (It’s even more of a sin not to be married, and single women are even more of a target for rumors and slanderous gossip.) So they can’t afford to be choosy, anyone will do: whether he rides horses or wears straw sandals, whether he’s an artist or a supervisor.”[^en-ch04-16] In response, party leaders attacked her as an internal dissenter and her views as an expression of “narrow feminism.” Three months later, she published a self-criticism not of her original charges but of the ideological method she had used in “Thoughts on March 8,” declaring, “This article is a bad article.”[^en-ch04-17]

红军在延安建立游击根据地后，一位女同志、著名作家丁玲于1942年在《解放日报》发表《三八节有感》。[^zh-ch04-15] 在国际妇女节之际，她揭露并讽刺延安共产主义生活内部的男女阶级制度。她开篇写道：“‘妇女’这两个字，将在什么时代才不被重视，不需要特别的被提出呢？”她提出共产党动员女性所面临的双重束缚：一方面要服务党，另一方面要服务家庭：如果不为家庭牺牲事业，就被批评为不负责任；如果牺牲了事业，又被批评为政治落后。关于婚姻，丁玲以讽刺幽默写道：“可是女人总是要结婚的。（不结婚就更其罪大，独身女人更是谣言和诽谤的对象。）因此她们不能挑剔，什么人都行：不管他是骑马还是穿草鞋，是艺术家还是总务处长。”[^zh-ch04-16] 作为回应，党的领导人攻击她是内部异见者，称其观点为“狭隘的女性主义”表现。三个月后，她发表自我批评，不是检讨自己原来的指控，而是检讨自己在《三八节有感》中使用的思想方法，宣称：“这篇文章是篇坏文章。”[^zh-ch04-17]


〔原书 145, 146〕

Likewise, for the Mosuo, the Long March effort of ccp consolidation, as prehistory to the party state of the People’s Republic of China, would pose an eventual threat to their matrilineal kinship system and custom of *sese*, “walking marriage.” The ideal-type of Mosuo family differs significantly from that of the traditional Han lineage or modern nuclear family. Children live in their mother’s household, even as adults. Men make night visits to female partners, with sexual relations initiated and continued voluntarily. Some couples form life-long relationships but continue to live separately by day, with children raised by their mothers and maternal uncles.[^en-ch04-18] After the founding of the PRC, state ethnographers in the 1950s used Stalin’s criteria for defining a nation to develop an ethnic classification system that grouped more than four hundred reported ethnic identities into fifty-five officially recognized minority nationalities, or *minzu*. Thomas Mullaney describes this project as “an inventive process of social engineering, not simply an attempt at neutrally reflecting primordial qualities of the non-Han social sphere.”[^en-ch04-19] The Mosuo did not receive recognition as an independent ethnic group—something they have protested to varying degrees over time—and were divided according to provincial borders, with those in Yunnan classified as Naxi, and those in Sichuan as Mongolian. As part of the official classification, ethnographers staged ethnic groups along a scale of classical Marxist evolution characterized by five major production modes: primitive (or primordial communist), slave, feudal, capitalist, and socialist. They placed groups with matrilineal family systems at the primitive end of an evolutionary timeline. Viewed as a “living fossils” who had to be disciplined into modern national norms, the Mosuo were subjected in the late 1960s and early 1970s to an official “one husband, one wife” policy that broke up families, forced them into married household units, and regulated their sexuality and reproduction.[^en-ch04-20] Since economic reform, representations of the Mosuo circulated by domestic and foreign travel writers, journalists, and filmmakers have depicted them as matriarchal and sexually liberated from the strictures of modern life. As Eileen Walsh notes, “In an ironic reversal, the cultural characteristics the Maoist government tried to change became celebrated as markers of Mosuo cultural uniqueness and value.”[^en-ch04-21]

同样，对摩梭人而言，长征中中共巩固的努力作为中华人民共和国党国史前史，最终对其母系亲属制度和“色色”（sese，即走婚）习俗构成威胁。摩梭家庭的理想类型与传统汉人世系或现代核心家庭显著不同。孩子即使成年也住在母亲家中。男子夜间拜访女性伴侣，性关系自愿开始并持续。一些伴侣结成终身关系，但白天仍分开居住，孩子由母亲和舅舅抚养。[^zh-ch04-18] 中华人民共和国成立后，1950年代的国家民族志学者使用斯大林定义民族的标准，发展出一套民族分类体系，把四百多个上报的民族身份归为五十五个官方承认的少数民族（minzu）。托马斯·穆拉尼（Thomas Mullaney）把这一项目描述为“一项创造性的社会工程，而非中立反映非汉社会领域原始特质的尝试”。[^zh-ch04-19] 摩梭人未获承认为独立民族——他们为此在不同时期以不同方式抗议——并按省界划分：云南的划为纳西族，四川的划为蒙古族。作为官方分类的一部分，民族志学者把各民族沿经典马克思主义演化的尺度排列，以五种主要生产方式为特征：原始（或原始共产主义）、奴隶、封建、资本主义和社会主义。他们把具有母系家庭制度的群体置于演化时间线的原始一端。摩梭人被视为必须被规训进现代民族规范的“活化石”，在1960年代末和1970年代初遭受官方“一夫一妻”政策的冲击；该政策拆散家庭，迫使他们进入已婚家庭单位，并管制其性与生育。[^zh-ch04-20] 经济改革以来，国内外旅行作家、记者和电影制作者传播的摩梭再现，把他们描绘成母权制、性自由的，摆脱了现代生活束缚。正如艾琳·沃尔什（Eileen Walsh）指出：“在一个讽刺性的反转中，毛主义政府试图改变的文化特征，反而成为摩梭文化独特性与价值的标志而受到颂扬。”[^zh-ch04-21]


〔原书 146〕

State-sponsored primitivizing and subsequent exotic commodification of the Mosuo were the twin poles that enabled consumers of these representations, including Judy Chicago and Han Chinese artists, to project utopian visions on Luoshui.[^en-ch04-22] After the height of Maoist social engineering passed, Mosuo communities attempted to revive suppressed cultural traditions within a context of marketization. In places like Luoshui, where the primary tourist destination is Lugu Lake, locals capitalized on outsiders’ romanticization of them as a “kingdom of daughters” to develop an economy based primarily on tourism.[^en-ch04-23] While represented as a place on the margins of contemporary life, Luoshui was incredibly cosmopolitan. The descent on the village of Lu Jie, Judy Chicago, a group of Chinese artists, and the camera crews following them represented a regular occurrence, with such interactions core to local livelihood actively influencing what it meant to be Mosuo. Walsh argues that a romanticized idea of a traditional Mosuo past, re-created for tourism, affected the local division of labor between men and women.[^en-ch04-24] Young men imagined a past in which it was not customary for men to do farm work and explained that doing household chores would detract from the image of Mosuo women as strong and capable. Luoshui women trapped in a “myth of matriarchy” shouldered a greater burden, while also becoming the sexualized object of visitors’ desires to experience “walking marriage.” Tami Blumenfield emphasizes that Mosuo is a state construction, whose essentialized and mediated characteristics do not reflect the historical complexity of ethnic identity in the region.[^en-ch04-25] Mosuo is a Chinese term; the indigenous Tibetan-Burmese term of self-identification is Na. Furthermore, members from other ethnic groups sometimes performed as Mosuo as part of the new tourist economy.

国家赞助的原始化以及随后对摩梭的异国情调商品化，构成两个相互关联的极点，使这些再现的消费者——包括朱迪·芝加哥和汉族中国艺术家——得以把乌托邦愿景投射到落水村。[^zh-ch04-22] 毛主义社会工程的高峰过去后，摩梭社区试图在市场化语境中复兴被压制的文化传统。在落水村等地，主要旅游目的地是泸沽湖，当地人利用外来者把他们浪漫化为“女儿国”的想象，发展以旅游为主的经济。[^zh-ch04-23] 落水村虽然被再现为当代生活边缘之地，却极其世界主义。卢杰、朱迪·芝加哥、一群中国艺术家以及跟随他们的摄制组降临村庄，是司空见惯的事；这类互动是当地生计的核心，积极影响着做摩梭人意味着什么。沃尔什论证，为旅游而再造的对摩梭传统过去的浪漫想象，影响了当地男女劳动分工。[^zh-ch04-24] 年轻男子想象出一个按习俗男子不做农活的过去，并解释说做家务会损害摩梭女性强壮能干的形象。被困在“母权神话”中的落水村女性承担更重负担，同时也成为游客体验“走婚”欲望的性化对象。塔米·布鲁门菲尔德（Tami Blumenfield）强调，摩梭是国家建构，其本质化、被中介的特征并不反映该地区民族认同的历史复杂性。[^zh-ch04-25] 摩梭是汉语词；当地藏缅语的自称是“纳”（Na）。此外，其他民族群体成员有时也会在新旅游经济中扮演摩梭人。


〔原书 146, 147〕

When Judy Chicago staged at Luoshui an artwork reflecting her own U.S. second-wave feminist preoccupation with an idea of essential womanhood and universal sisterhood, she privileged the local to promote a universal that then effectively erased local historical and cultural specificity. During her Beijing slide lecture, Chicago introduced the piece she created for *The Long March. What If Women Ruled the World* consists of prayer flags (the Mosuo practice a variant of Tibetan Buddhism), each posing a rhetorical question about how the world might be different if women ruled, paired with black and white drawings of scenes suggesting positive responses: Would god be female? Would men and women be equal? Would sexual freedom prevail? Would there be jealousy? Would there be equal parenting? Would children go hungry? Would old women be revered? Would buildings resemble wombs? Would there be private property? Would there be war? These questions in Chinese appeared on the reverse side of the flags. This piece would eventually be hung at the entrance to the Lugu Lake guesthouse where Chicago stayed. A photograph of it on *The Long March* website archive was captioned, “The local Mosuo people pass through the entryway with Judy Chicago’s work,” introducing another irony.[^en-ch04-26] The women hired to perform a dance in the courtyard of Chicago’s guesthouse were dressed as Yi, another of the twelve ethnic minority groups who live in the region but whose system of kinship organization is patrilineal.

当朱迪·芝加哥在落水村展示一件反映其美国第二波女性主义对本质化的女性身份和普遍姐妹情谊的执念的作品时，她借助地方性来推广一种普遍性，而这种普遍性随后有效抹除了地方的历史与文化特殊性。在北京幻灯片讲座中，芝加哥介绍了她为《长征》创作的作品。《如果女人统治世界》由经幡组成（摩梭人信奉藏传佛教的一个变体），每一面都提出一个关于如果女人统治世界、世界会有何不同的修辞问题，并配以暗示正面回答的黑白绘画：神会是女性吗？男女会平等吗？性自由会盛行吗？会有嫉妒吗？会平等育儿吗？孩子会挨饿吗？老年女性会受尊敬吗？建筑会像子宫吗？会有私有财产吗？会有战争吗？这些问题的中文写在经幡背面。这件作品最终挂在芝加哥所住泸沽湖客栈的入口。一张照片在《长征》网站档案中的说明写道：“当地摩梭人穿过入口，经过朱迪·芝加哥的作品。”这引入了又一个讽刺。[^zh-ch04-26] 受雇在芝加哥客栈院子里表演舞蹈的女性被装扮成彝族——该地区十二个少数民族之一，但其亲属制度是父系的。


〔原书 147〕

This Western feminist use of women from elsewhere to argue that patriarchy is a monolithic, cross-cultural phenomenon produces “third world difference,” which in Chandra Mohanty’s critique effectively appropriates and colonizes “the constitutive complexities which characterize the lives of women in these countries.[^en-ch04-27] The twist of Judy Chicago at Lugu Lake is that she represents an interpretation of Western feminist art practice as more advanced, but through a search for primordial matriarchy presumed to still exist in China’s hinterlands. Once at Lugu Lake, Lu Jie would set her up as a pedagogue to Chinese feminist artists by assigning her the task of offering a personal critique of each of their works (figure 4.03). This framework positioned Chicago as spokeswoman for what Tani Barlow calls “international U.S. feminism,” the discursive formation in which U.S. women’s achievement of self-enlightenment becomes a sign of their advanced progress to then be shared with the rest of the world’s women.[^en-ch04-28] Chicago proposed to educate Chinese women on how to be feminist artists by instructing them in the utopian society of the Mosuo within their own nation’s borders.

这种西方女性主义利用他处女性来论证父权制是单一、跨文化现象的做法，生产出钱德拉·莫汉蒂（Chandra Mohanty）所批评的“第三世界差异”，实际上挪用并殖民了“构成这些国家女性生活特征的复杂性”。[^zh-ch04-27] 朱迪·芝加哥在泸沽湖的转折在于，她代表一种把西方女性主义艺术实践视为更先进的解释，却通过寻找假定仍存在于中国腹地的原始母权制来实现。一到泸沽湖，卢杰就把她安排为对中国女性主义艺术家的教导者，交给她逐一评论每位艺术家作品的任务（图4.03）。这一框架把芝加哥定位为白露（Tani Barlow）所谓“国际美国女性主义”的代言人——这一话语构型中，美国女性实现自我启蒙，成为其先进进步的标志，然后再与全世界女性分享。[^zh-ch04-28] 芝加哥提议向中国女性讲授她们本国境内的摩梭乌托邦社会，以教导她们如何成为女性主义艺术家。


〔原书 147, 148, 149〕

This instance is one in a history of encounters between Chinese and Western feminisms. While the original plan for site six participants to discuss excerpts of Julia Kristeva’s *About Chinese Women* was jettisoned, Kristeva serves as a cross-cultural precursor to Chicago.[^en-ch04-29] For Lu Jie, the invocation of Kristeva provided twofold symbolic capital: she is a canonical name in Western feminist theory, who was aligned during the global 1960s with French Maoists. In the early 1970s, she traveled to China with other *Tel Quel* deconstructionist writers, and her text based on this experience identifies a Chinese feminine difference that helps her imagine an alternative outside to the patriarchal symbolic order she had critiqued in France. In Kristeva’s psychoanalytic theorization, Western culture puts women in a double bind: if they enter the symbolic system of language, politics, time, and culture, they must identify as men, but if they inhabit the woman’s body, they remain silent, outside of the symbolic order. Her concept of *écriture féminine* proposes a way of writing that would disrupt phallic language and lead readers to experience *jouissance*, a blissful break from previously held subject positions. In *About Chinese Women*, Kristeva suggests that Chinese women retain a premodern symbolic power that places “mother at the centre” and provides an escape from the position in which Western women find themselves;[^en-ch04-30] furthermore, Chinese Communism liberated this archaic matriarchal order from a repressive Confucian tradition, enabling feminine *jouissance*.[^en-ch04-31] If Kristeva’s investment in a vision of matriarchy enabled her Maoist critique of the Western linguistic-symbolic system, Chicago’s was more universalizing: patriarchy everywhere has suppressed a primordial matriarchy everywhere. She understood Mosuo matriarchy as having survived in spite of Chinese Communism. Both of these preoccupations short-circuit attention to the rich history of feminist politics in modern China. The symbolic mobilization of these Western figures to generate international interest in *The Long March* silences the lives and voices of women who participated in the actual Long March—activists such as Cai Chang, Chen Congying, Deng Yingchao, Kang Keqing, and Wang Quanyuan, as well as writer and thinker Ding Ling, who joined them at Yan’an. Their experience as early members of the Chinese Communist Party ranged from work and study in France and the Soviet Union to leadership in women’s rights movements, from factory workers’ education and organization to combat and espionage.[^en-ch04-32]

这一实例属于中国与西方女性主义相遇史的一部分。虽然让第六站参与者讨论朱莉娅·克里斯蒂娃《中国妇女》摘录的原计划被放弃，克里斯蒂娃仍充当芝加哥的跨文化先驱。[^zh-ch04-29] 对卢杰而言，援引克里斯蒂娃提供双重象征资本：她是西方女性主义理论中的经典名字，在1960年代全球语境中与法国毛主义者结盟。1970年代初，她与其他《原样》解构主义作家一起访华，基于此行的文本指认了一种中国女性的差异，帮助她想象一个她曾在法国批判的父权象征秩序之外的替代选项。在克里斯蒂娃的精神分析理论中，西方文化使女性陷入双重束缚：如果进入语言、政治、时间和文化的象征系统，她们必须认同为男性；如果居留于女人身体，她们便保持沉默，处于象征秩序之外。她的“女性书写”（écriture féminine）概念提出一种写作方式，可以扰乱阳具语言，引导读者体验极乐（jouissance）——从先前主体位置中获得极乐式的断裂。在《中国妇女》中，克里斯蒂娃提出，中国女性保留一种前现代象征权力，把“母亲置于中心”，提供一条逃离西方女性所处位置的途径；[^zh-ch04-30] 此外，中国共产主义把这一古老母权秩序从压迫性的儒家传统中解放出来，使女性极乐成为可能。[^zh-ch04-31] 如果说克里斯蒂娃对母权制愿景的投入促成了她对西方语言—象征体系的毛主义批评，那么芝加哥的投入则更具普遍化色彩：各地父权制都压制了各地的原始母权制。她认为摩梭母权制尽管经历中国共产主义仍幸存下来。这两种执念都阻断了人们对现代中国丰富女性主义政治史的关注。为吸引国际社会关注《长征》而以象征性方式动员这些西方人物，使实际参加长征的女性——蔡畅、陈琮英、邓颖超、康克清、王泉媛等行动者，以及在延安加入她们的作家、思想家丁玲——的生活与声音沉默。她们作为中国共产党早期成员的经历，从在法国和苏联工作学习，到领导妇女权利运动，从工厂工人教育和组织，到战斗与谍报工作。[^zh-ch04-32]


〔原书 148〕

![*图4.03　艺术家Bai Chongmin（左）、Wu Weihe（中）在泸沽湖与朱迪·芝加哥（右）谈论他们的作品，《长征》摄制组在拍摄。James Tweedie 摄。*](web/assets/ch04-b027.jpg)

FIG 4.03 Artists Bai Chongmin (left) and Wu Weihe (center) in conversation with Judy Chicago (right) about their piece at Lugu Lake, being filmed by *The Long March* crew. Photograph by James Tweedie.

*图4.03　艺术家Bai Chongmin（左）、Wu Weihe（中）在泸沽湖与朱迪·芝加哥（右）谈论他们的作品，《长征》摄制组在拍摄。James Tweedie 摄。*


〔原书 149〕

While Judy Chicago’s positioning in *The Long March* centered her as an authoritative representative of Western feminist art, this framing obscures her history. In the United States she has long fought for recognition of her work. The Feminist Art Program that she and Miriam Shapiro founded at the California Institute of the Arts in 1971 constituted an institutional critique of women’s marginalization by the art system. Their first collaborative project, *Womanhouse* (1972), brought together twenty-eight women who transformed a deserted mansion into a site-specific art installation/happening that confronted restrictive social norms of female domesticity. Chicago’s *The Dinner Party*, which attracted popular attention when first exhibited in 1979, incited a wide range of critics to praise and disparage it. High art theorists dismissed its use of female craft traditions and vaginal imagery as a kitschy degradation of artistic standards. In the 1980s, poststructuralist feminists critiqued Chicago’s artistic manifesto for its essentialization of woman as a singular, universal category. Women of color feminists pointed out the exclusions enacted by her seating of primarily white women at the table.[^en-ch04-33] In 1990, when the trustees of the federally supported University of the District of Columbia voted to purchase the piece for their collection, conservative members of Congress attacked *The Dinner Party* as obscene and pornographic, and their public outcry brought an end to these acquisition plans.

朱迪·芝加哥在《长征》中的位置把她中心化为西方女性主义艺术的权威代表，而这一框架遮蔽了她的历史。在美国，她长期为获得对其作品的承认而斗争。她与米里亚姆·夏皮罗1971年在加州艺术学院创立的女性主义艺术项目，构成对艺术系统边缘化女性的机构批判。她们的第一个合作项目《女人屋》（1972）召集二十八位女性，把一座废弃豪宅改造成场域特定的艺术装置／事件，直面限制女性家庭角色的社会规范。芝加哥的《晚宴》1979年首次展出时引起大众关注，招致广泛批评者的赞美与贬低。高雅艺术理论家贬斥它使用女性手工艺传统和阴道意象，认为是以媚俗降低艺术标准。1980年代，后结构主义女性主义者批评芝加哥的艺术宣言把女人本质化为单一、普遍的范畴。有色人种女性主义者指出，她的餐桌主要让白人女性就座，实施了排斥。[^zh-ch04-33] 1990年，联邦资助的哥伦比亚特区大学董事会投票购买该作品入藏时，国会保守派议员攻击《晚宴》淫秽、色情，他们的公开抗议终止了收购计划。


〔原书 149, 150〕

A proliferation of ironies set the stage for the encounter at Lugu Lake. Judy Chicago in *The Long March* represented a Western center, although her position in the West vis-à-vis art world and feminist politics remained the subject of contention. Western feminists in the 1960s and 1970s, like Kristeva, looked to socialism in China as a response to patriarchy in their own societies, even as they emerged as more predominant world theoretical voices than their Chinese peers. Chinese feminists in the late twentieth and early twenty-first century attempted to decenter state-socialist feminism through a critique of how it failed them, while also rejecting the patronizing interventions of international U.S. feminism, such as those represented by Hillary Clinton in her 1995 speech on human rights at the UN Fourth World Conference on Women in Beijing.[^en-ch04-34] The Mosuo, imagined to exist at the margins of the Chinese state and modern world, serve as a cosmopolitan site for utopian reassessment of modern sexuality and gender relations, while contending with the imaginaries visited on their villages by outsiders from around the world. The historical Long March shifted its revolutionary center from east coast cities to the rural inland headquarters of Yan’an; and once the revolution was won, the peasantry remained a rhetorical center of the party, even as its leadership installed itself in the capital of Beijing. *The Long March: A Walking Visual Display* attempted to decenter the West as the primary location for contemporary art through a strategic return to the cultural praxis of a socialist past. The project, however, eventually fell apart before reaching Yan’an, and its main institutional outcome was a commercial gallery space in Beijing. Center-periphery relations are often theorized in colonial terms, in which power exercised in the imperial metropole pulls colonies into its orbit of control and influence, or in international economic and geopolitical terms, in which nations with the greatest wealth and power constitute a center that peripheral nations strive to displace or join. The cultural politics that emerged at Lugu Lake refute such a centripetal model. They reveal instead entangled histories, of gender produced through historical intersections with race, ethnicity, class, and nationality, in which interactions at the periphery might ignore, resist, undo, or reeducate the center.

不断增殖的反讽为泸沽湖的相遇搭建了舞台。《长征》中的朱迪·芝加哥代表西方中心，尽管她在西方相对于艺术界和女性主义政治的位置仍有争议。1960和1970年代的西方女性主义者——如克里斯蒂娃——把中国的社会主义视为对本国父权制的回应，即便她们后来成为比中国同行更主导的世界理论声音。二十世纪末、二十一世纪初的中国女性主义者试图通过批判国家社会主义女性主义如何辜负她们，来使其去中心化，同时拒绝国际美国女性主义的恩赐式干预——例如希拉里·克林顿1995年在北京联合国第四次世界妇女大会上关于人权的演讲所代表的那种干预。[^zh-ch04-34] 摩梭人被认为存在于中国国家和现代世界的边缘，却成为乌托邦式重新评估现代社会的性与性别关系的一个世界性场所，同时又要应对来自世界各地外来者施加于其村庄的想象。历史长征把革命中心从东海岸城市转移到内陆延安总部；革命胜利后，农民仍是党的修辞中心，即便领导层已把自己安置在首都北京。《长征：一个行走中的视觉展示》试图通过战略性地回归社会主义过去的文化实践，使西方去中心化，不再作为当代艺术的主要所在地。然而，项目最终在抵达延安前瓦解，其主要机构成果是北京的一个商业画廊空间。中心—边缘关系常以殖民主义术语理论化：帝国大都市行使权力，把殖民地拉入其控制与影响轨道；或以国际经济与地缘政治术语理论化：拥有最大财富和权力的国家构成中心，边缘国家努力取代或加入其中。泸沽湖产生的文化政治反驳了这种向心模式，反而揭示出纠缠的历史——性别通过与种族、族裔、阶级和国籍的历史交汇而生成，边缘的互动可能忽视、抵抗、瓦解或重新教育中心。


〔原书 150〕

Womanhouse Undone

拆解女人屋


〔原书 150, 151〕

Fourteen artists, largely from the southwestern provinces of Yunnan and Sichuan but also from as far away as Inner Mongolia, eventually chose to make the trip to Lugu Lake. While those affiliated with the Sichuan Fine Arts Institute in Chongqing or the Upriver Loft studio collective in Kunming, Yunnan, belonged to preexisting networks, the overall group represented a range of artistic commitments and generational perspectives. Their collectivity alone, assembled in a bus from Kunming to Lugu Lake, was rife with potential fault lines. They were joined by Shen Yu, the young and idealistic director of a self-initiated Chinese Women’s Art Research Center in Chongqing. I traveled with them, together with my partner who came along to help with filming. Judy Chicago and her husband, photographer Donald Woodman, traveled separately to Lugu Lake, together with Lu Jie, Qiu Zhijie, their curatorial assistant Lisa Horikawa, and Megan Connolly, another participant-observer from the United States. A professional film crew accompanied them. Even before these two groups converged on the village of Luoshui, questions and tensions mixed with excitement and anticipation.

最终有十四位艺术家选择前往泸沽湖，他们大多来自西南的云南、四川，也有远自内蒙古者。其中隶属重庆四川美术学院或云南昆明上游工作室群体的人属于既有网络，但整个群体代表了不同的艺术立场和代际视角。单是这个集合在昆明开往泸沽湖大巴上的集体，内部就潜藏着重重裂痕。与他们同行的还有沈宇（Shen Yu），一位年轻而理想主义的重庆自办中国女性艺术研究中心主任。我和他们一起旅行，我的伴侣同行帮助拍摄。朱迪·芝加哥和丈夫、摄影师唐纳德·伍德曼（Donald Woodman）另行前往泸沽湖，同行的有卢杰、邱志杰、策展助理 Lisa Horikawa，以及另一位来自美国的参与观察者梅根·康诺利（Megan Connolly）。一支专业摄制组跟着他们。甚至在两批人汇聚落水村之前，问题与紧张已夹杂着兴奋和期待。


〔原书 151〕

On the bus from Kunming to Lijiang, the first leg of the trip, artists Fu Liya and Wu Weihe discussed what they understood of Chicago’s proposed piece. When Fu said she’d heard it would be an installation of the one hundred art proposals Chicago had received from Chinese women, Wu responded that this sounded like a plan for an impressive conceptual artwork that unfairly relied on their efforts, while also detracting from their individual ideas. They guessed at the thinking behind Lu Jie’s decision to invite Judy Chicago. If he organized a Long March but didn’t include any women, it would be deemed backward instead of attracting international attention. Inviting someone famous like Judy Chicago would inspire a lot of female artists to participate. Wu couldn’t help but continue to ask, “But this exhibit is about China’s Long March, why did he invite a Western feminist?”

在从昆明到丽江的第一段大巴上，艺术家付丽雅和Wu Weihe讨论各自对芝加哥拟议作品的理解。付丽雅说，她听说那会是芝加哥从中国女性那里收到的一百份艺术方案的装置；Wu Weihe回应说，这听起来像一件令人印象深刻的概念艺术计划，却不公平地依赖她们的劳动，同时也削弱了她们的个人想法。她们猜测卢杰决定邀请朱迪·芝加哥背后的考虑。如果他组织长征却没有任何女性，就会被视为落后，而不是吸引国际关注。邀请朱迪·芝加哥这样著名的人，会激励许多女性艺术家参与。Wu Weihe忍不住继续问：“可这个展览是关于中国长征的，他为什么邀请一个西方女性主义者？”


〔原书 151〕

“Beautiful Lugu Lake—Mysterious Land of Daughters” read the tickets we purchased at the entrance to the Lugu Lake Nature Preserve after a second day of travel from Lijiang on narrow roads, switching back and forth through spectacular mountainous terrain. As the bus dodged rocks from recent landslides, heated discussion about the exhibition’s organization continued. Upon arriving in Luoshui, a line of hewn-log and tile-roof guesthouses and restaurants along the lakefront, the artists began scouting out locations for performance and installation pieces and making connections with locals whose cooperation they sought.

从丽江出发，在狭窄道路上又走了一天，在壮丽山区间盘旋之后，我们在泸沽湖自然保护区入口买到的门票上印着“美丽的泸沽湖——神秘的女儿国”。大巴躲避着近期山体滑坡留下的石块，关于展览组织的热烈讨论仍在继续。抵达落水村——湖畔一列木刻楞和瓦顶客栈、餐馆——后，艺术家们开始寻找行为和装置作品的地点，并与他们寻求合作的当地人建立联系。


〔原书 151, 152〕

That evening, the first group meeting between Judy Chicago and all of the participating artists took place in a Luoshui restaurant. The electricity had gone out, and as dusk dimmed the lakefront windows, white candle stubs lit the room. Color posters, their gloss weathered, of scenic landscapes, flower arrangements, European-style table settings, and pop stars, hung on the whitewashed walls. Through a translator, Chicago asked the artists to sit in a circle, which they did awkwardly around the perimeter of several round tables that had been pushed together. After they had introduced themselves, Chicago stood and presented her idea of how they might work together. Lisa Horikawa provided interpretation, with Lu Jie occasionally jumping in to clarify a point. Chicago began, “Thirty years ago, in the United States, I did a project with a number of women called Womanhouse. Some of you have heard of it. Have any of you heard of it? Yes. Ok! Some of you’ve heard of it, right? Well, it became very famous. Since I did that, other women have done Womanhouses all over the world.” She then described the inn where she was staying, separate from the artists’ lodging and some distance from the village, as so beautiful that she and Lu Jie had decided to spend their own money to rent out the entire place. She suggested that they all hang or stage their works there, following the model of the *Womanhouse* installation she, Miriam Schapiro, and their students had created in 1972. She implied that the location provided safety to exhibit without the interference of local officials, a concern passed on to her by Lu Jie, who had heard of official concern about his activity in Lijiang. When she asked those assembled for their opinion, the room fell silent. Eventually a few artists explained they had already chosen spots for their pieces and would have to assess the layout of her guesthouse before they could decide.

那天晚上，朱迪·芝加哥与所有参与艺术家的第一次小组会议在落水村一家餐馆举行。停电了，暮色使湖畔窗户暗淡下来，白色蜡烛头照亮房间。白墙上挂着风景、插花、欧式餐桌布置和流行歌星的彩色海报，光泽已被风化。通过翻译，芝加哥请艺术家们围坐成一圈；他们别扭地围坐在几张拼在一起的圆桌旁。自我介绍后，芝加哥站起来，讲述她关于大家如何合作的想法。Lisa Horikawa 担任口译，卢杰不时插话澄清。芝加哥开始说：“三十年前，在美国，我和一些女性做了一个叫《女人屋》的项目。你们有些人听说过。你们有人听说过吗？有。好！你们有些人听说过，对吧？嗯，它后来变得非常有名。自从我做了那个项目，世界各地的其他女性也做过《女人屋》。”随后她描述自己住的客栈——与艺术家住处分开，离村庄有些距离——美得让她和卢杰决定自掏腰包租下整座院落。她建议大家都在那里悬挂或展演作品，仿照她、米里亚姆·夏皮罗和学生们1972年创作的《女人屋》装置模式。她暗示，这个地点提供了安全，可以在没有地方官员干预的情况下展出——这是卢杰转达给她的担忧，他听说官方在丽江对他的活动有所关注。当她问在场者意见时，房间一片沉默。最后几位艺术家解释说，她们已为作品选好地点，需要先看过她客栈的布局才能决定。


〔原书 152〕

Chicago departed after they agreed to meet the next morning at the site of her proposed Womanhouse. The Chinese artists continued with their activities, with discussions going into the early morning. One group rushed to meet the new village chief, with whom they had arranged a tentative appointment. They needed local participants for their performances and spent hours around a fire explaining to him the relation of their pieces to local culture. The chief, in turn, explained for them in practiced detail the workings of Mosuo family structure. This earnest man in a cowboy hat was the one to describe for the outsiders their system of matrilineal descent; and it was he, not a woman, who could grant them the help they needed, but only after he returned from a trip to help dig a well and repair a road.

他们同意第二天早晨在芝加哥提议的“女人屋”地点见面，随后芝加哥离开。中国艺术家继续活动，讨论持续到凌晨。一群人赶去会见新村长，他们先前与他约了暂定会面。他们需要当地人参与行为作品，于是在火堆旁花了几个小时向他解释作品与当地文化的关系。村长则以熟练的细节向他们说明摩梭家庭结构的运作。这位戴着牛仔帽的诚恳男子向外来者描述他们的母系继嗣制度；也是他，而不是某位女性，能够给予他们需要的帮助——但前提是他先去帮忙挖井修路的行程结束。


〔原书 152, 153〕

Around midnight, most of the artists crowded into a room at their guesthouse and debated the pros and cons of accepting Chicago’s proposal. Objections were raised about a framework associated with a different feminist time and place—the 1970s in the United States, rather than one developed out of a Chinese historical context. Many expressed concern over whether the final project would be attributed to Chicago alone—the main problem many had with *The Dinner Party*—with the names of her Chinese collaborators erased.[^en-ch04-35] While some advocated for splitting from *The Long March* organization to proceed on their own, they reached a compromise the next morning in the form of their manifesto. As they worked on the wording, Fu Liya asserted, “Give us something unambiguous. If, in the end, it’s ‘Womanhouse,’ a piece by Judy Chicago and twenty Chinese female artists, we’re screwed, that’s absolutely not allowed! Authorship rights wanted!” The short text, which I translated into English, listed four demands:

午夜前后，大多数艺术家挤进客栈的一个房间，辩论接受芝加哥提议的利弊。有人反对这一框架，因为它关联着另一个女性主义时空——1970年代的美国，而不是从中国的历史语境中发展出来的。许多人担心最终项目是否会只归功于芝加哥一个人——这也是他们对《晚宴》的主要意见——而中国合作者的名字被抹去。[^zh-ch04-35] 一些人主张脱离《长征》组织自行行动，第二天早晨他们以宣言形式达成妥协。在推敲措辞时，付丽雅断言：“给我们一个明确的东西。如果最后是‘《女人屋》，朱迪·芝加哥与二十位中国女性艺术家合作作品’，我们就完了，绝对不允许！我们要求著作权！”这篇由我译成英文的短文列出四项要求：


〔原书 153〕
