[^en-ch05-4]: This inclusion of her self-portrait as artist within the larger painting is reminiscent of Velazquez’s appearance in *Las Meninas*. As Foucault has observed of this famous painting, the simultaneity of different subject positions, and the viewer’s shifting back and forth among them, incites a paradoxical relationship between reality and representation (Foucault, *The Order of Things*, 3–16).

[^zh-ch05-4]: 把自己的艺术家自画像纳入整幅画作，令人想起委拉斯开兹在《宫娥》中的出场。正如福柯在这幅名画中所观察到的，不同主体位置的同时并存，以及观者在其间的往返移动，激发出一种现实与再现之间的悖谬关系（Foucault, *The Order of Things*, 3–16）。

[^en-ch05-5]: Li, interview.

[^en-ch05-6]: The term she uses for realism is *xieshi* (realistic depiction). The opposite of *xieshi* or *xiesheng* (drawing or painting from life) is the traditional Chinese ink painting concept of *xieyi* (communication of ideas and feelings), characterized by loose, suggestive, sometimes almost abstract brushwork. During the early socialist period, *xieyi* painting was equated with elite literati painting and therefore deemphasized. As Julia Andrews notes in *Painters and Politics in the People’s Republic of China*, Chinese art education first adopted European styles of painting in the Republican era: “The presumption of many idealistic intellectuals was that Western media were better suited to modern, international art, or, in the language of the May Fourth Movement, to art that was more scientific” (48).

[^zh-ch05-6]: 她用来指称现实主义的词是"写实"（*xieshi*，写实的描绘）。写实或写生（*xiesheng*，据实物描绘或绘画）的对立面，是中国传统水墨画中"写意"（*xieyi*，传达意念与情感）的观念；写意以松散、暗示性、有时近乎抽象的笔法为特征。在社会主义早期，写意画被等同于精英文人画，因而受到淡化。正如安雅兰（Julia Andrews）在《中华人民共和国的画家与政治》中所指出的，中国艺术教育在民国时期首先采纳了欧洲绘画风格："许多理想主义知识分子的预设是，西方媒介更适合现代、国际性的艺术，或者用五四运动的话说，更适合更科学的艺术"（48）。

[^en-ch05-7]: For example, between 1953 and 1956, two dozen young artists affiliated with Chinese academic institutions were sent to Leningrad for a six-year course in oil painting at the Repin Art Academy.

[^zh-ch05-7]: 例如，1953年至1956年间，二十四名隶属于中国学术机构的年轻艺术家被派往列宁格勒，在列宾美术学院接受为期六年的油画课程。

[^en-ch05-8]: Xie, *Hongse niangzi jun*.

[^zh-ch05-8]: Xie, *Hongse niangzi jun*。

[^en-ch05-9]: Official Chinese critics praised the nineteenth-century French painter as early as 1954, and *Liberty Leading the People* became a history painting standard in Chinese art academy education. Commissioned for Beijing’s Military Museum, it still hangs there.

[^zh-ch05-9]: 中国的官方评论家早在1954年就开始赞扬这位19世纪法国画家，《自由引导人民》也成为中国美术学院教育中的历史画范本。艺术家陈逸飞和魏景山在1977年的《占领总统府》中借用了它的构图；这幅大型作品描绘中共击败国民党后升旗的场面。它受北京军事博物馆委托创作，至今仍悬挂在那里。

[^en-ch05-23]: This imperative to remember reverses the refrain of the first-person narrator in Lu Xun’s 1925 short story “Regret for the Past.” He is compelled to write, he records in his handwritten notes, to forget the death of his neglected and rejected lover and make a fresh start in life: “I want to forget. For my own sake I don’t want to remember the oblivion I gave Tsu-chun for her burial” (Lu, *Selected Stories*, 215). See also Lydia Liu’s reading of the story’s gender dynamics in *Translingual Practice*, 164–71.

[^zh-ch05-23]: 这种记忆的律令，逆转了鲁迅1925年短篇小说《伤逝》中第一人称叙述者的感叹。他在手记中写道，自己被迫写作，是为了忘记那个被他忽视又抛弃的爱人之死，从而重新开始生活："我想忘记。为了我自己，我不愿记住我为子君送葬所给予她的遗忘"（Lu, *Selected Stories*, 215）。关于这个故事性别动态的解读，另见刘禾（Lydia Liu）在 *Translingual Practice*, 164–71 中的分析。


## 第六章　打开长城


〔原书 206〕

Six: Opening the Great Wall

第六章　打开长城


〔原书 206〕

On May 17, 2001, several busloads of art enthusiasts and journalists arrived at Jinshanling, a site on the Great Wall 140 kilometers northeast of Beijing. They proceeded to climb the wall to view an installation created by a German artist named H. A. Schult. His piece consisted of one thousand life-size figures constructed from recycled consumer waste.

2001年5月17日，几辆大巴载着艺术爱好者和记者抵达金山岭——北京东北一百四十公里处的一段长城。他们沿城墙爬上，观看一位名叫 H. A. 舒尔特（H. A. Schult）的德国艺术家创作的装置。作品由一千个真人大小的人形组成，均用回收的消费垃圾制成。


〔原书 206〕

Before China, he had displayed these trash people—which he has described as “silent witnesses to a consumer age that has created an ecological imbalance worldwide”—at a re-created Roman village in Germany, the Arc de la Defence in Paris, and Moscow’s Red Square.[^en-ch06-1] As the assembled audience wandered through his installation, a woman suddenly emerged from their midst. Chinese artist He Chengyao had spontaneously stripped off her red shirt. Marching half-nude between the columns of Schult’s figures, she quickly diverted media attention and cameras toward her exposed torso. He Chengyao called her action performance art and retrospectively titled it *Opening the Great Wall (Kaifang changcheng*) (plate 15). Photographs taken that day by reporters appeared on numerous websites. Popular and art circle reactions ensued. Was what she had done art?

来中国之前，他已在德国一座复建的罗马村庄、巴黎拉德芳斯拱门和莫斯科红场展示过这些“垃圾人”——他称之为“消费时代的沉默见证者，这个时代造成了全球生态失衡”。[^zh-ch06-1] 当聚集的观众在他的装置间漫步时，一个女人突然从人群中走出。中国艺术家何成瑶自发脱掉了红色上衣。她半裸着在舒尔特的垃圾人队列间行走，迅速把媒体注意力和镜头引向自己裸露的躯干。何成瑶称自己的行动为行为艺术，事后命名为《开放长城》（Kaifang changcheng，图版15）。当天记者拍摄的照片出现在许多网站上。大众和艺术圈的反应随之而来。她所做的算艺术吗？


〔原书 206, 207〕

This moment proved to be a turning point in He Chengyao’s career. It also served as a turning point in how I understood my role as anthropologist in the field. Through my ongoing conversations with He Chengyao, which began before *Opening the Great Wall* and continued after, I came to appreciate how my participation in Chinese contemporary art worlds led to the production of ethnographic knowledge that, in Fred Myers’s words, “becomes inescapably part of what it represents.”[^en-ch06-2] In consideration of whether or not what He Chengyao did was art, I present several of the public responses to her performance on the Great Wall—as proliferating, conflicting interpretations of what it means for a woman to take off her clothes. The multiple discourses that it activated demonstrate the instability of a cultural object called art and what is at stake for those invested in how it represents China. I then turn to He Chengyao’s story, but at a moment before *Opening the Great Wall*. To understand the circumstances that made this performance possible, I give an account of her personal trajectory from a town in Sichuan to the cultural capital of Beijing. This narrative includes a family history I had recorded with her several months earlier, which unbeknownst to either of us at the time would shape her interpretation of her performance on the Great Wall and lead her to create two parallel series of photographed performances.

这个时刻成为何成瑶艺术生涯的转折点，也成为我理解自己作为人类学家在田野中角色的转折点。通过我与何成瑶持续的交谈——从《开放长城》之前开始，并在此后继续——我逐渐认识到，我对中国当代艺术世界的参与如何生产出弗雷德·迈尔斯（Fred Myers）所谓“不可避免成为其所再现之物一部分”的民族志知识。[^zh-ch06-2] 在思考何成瑶的行为是否算艺术时，我呈现公众对她长城行为的若干回应——关于一个女人脱掉衣服意味着什么，这些解读不断增殖、彼此冲突。它激活的多种话语，展示了一个名为艺术的文化对象的不稳定性，以及对那些关切艺术如何再现中国的人而言，其中的利害。然后我转向何成瑶的故事，不过在《开放长城》之前的那一刻。要理解使这场行为成为可能的境况，我叙述她从四川一个小镇到文化首都北京的个人轨迹。这段叙述包括我几个月前与她一起录下的家庭史；当时我们谁也不知道，它后来会塑造她对长城行为的解释，并促使她创作两个相互并行、以摄影记录的行为艺术系列。


〔原书 207〕

Interpreting He Chengyao’s Opening the Great Wall

解读何成瑶的《开放长城》


〔原书 207〕

I was not there when He Chengyao stripped off her shirt, diverting media attention and cameras away from Schult, but within days I began to hear stories of what had happened. Chinese friends of mine with no connection to the art world had seen photos of the event on the web and questioned whether any of it was art, Schult’s installation or He Chengyao’s public nudity. I also found myself puzzling over the news. I had known He Chengyao for several years and thought of her primarily as an oil painter, although she had recently moved to Beijing from Chongqing to take a one-year course on contemporary art at the Central Academy of Fine Arts.

何成瑶脱掉上衣、把媒体注意力和镜头从舒尔特那里引开时，我并不在场，但几天内就开始听到发生的事。与中国艺术界没有关联的朋友在网上看到事件照片，质疑其中是否有任何东西算艺术——舒尔特的装置还是何成瑶的公开裸露。我自己也反复琢磨这条新闻。我认识何成瑶好几年，主要把她当作油画家，尽管她最近刚从重庆搬到北京，在中央美术学院上为期一年的当代艺术课程。


〔原书 207〕

When He Chengyao called me a few weeks later, she was anxious and upset, on the verge of tears. She asked if I’d heard about her first attempt at performance art. She had come under attack by critics, including art commentators and fellow artists, who disparaged her action as immoral and profiteering. During a later conversation at her apartment, she asked me if I believed in spirit possession. What did I know, as an anthropologist, about this phenomenon? After being repeatedly questioned about her motivation that day, it seemed to her the most plausible explanation for what she had done.

几周后何成瑶打电话给我，她焦虑不安，几近流泪。她问我有没有听说她第一次尝试行为艺术。她受到批评者的攻击，包括艺术评论人和同行艺术家，他们贬斥她的行为不道德、为牟利。后来在她公寓的一次谈话中，她问我是否相信神灵附体。作为人类学家，我对这一现象了解什么？在反复被追问当天动机之后，这似乎成了她对自己行为最可信的解释。


〔原书 207, 208〕

Some of the critics who lambasted her performance expressed their opinions anonymously through website postings, but in her hometown of Chongqing, her husband’s art academy colleagues criticized him for letting her leave home to pursue an art career in Beijing. While certainly a response to her public exposure, their criticism was not necessarily directed at the question of female nude as art. Nude paintings were first publicly shown in the prc in 1979, and Yin Guangzhong’s *Great Wall* (figure 6.01) was shown that spring on Democracy Wall, where artists openly criticized the Cultural Revolution. Over two decades before He Chengyao, he conjoined the nude and this national symbol, in the depiction of a couple, the female nude facing forward, atop a pile of skulls. The Great Wall binds together the figures, who strain against its control.[^en-ch06-3] Nudity in oil painting (meaning by and large female nudity), although once considered a bourgeois form of expression, underwent a period of normalization in China during the 1980s and 1990s, and a growing market for this work provided an alternative to state patronage.[^en-ch06-4] The criticism of He Chengyao’s performance as immoral singled her out in a telling way. Several male performance artists in China have incorporated partial or full nudity in their work, but none had been attacked along these lines. Some of their performances also took place on the Great Wall. In 1998, for example, artist Ma Liuming enacted one of his performances of gender ambiguity—in which he makes up his face and long hair to accentuate a performative femininity but strips naked to reveal his male genitalia—by walking a ruined section of the Great Wall as another border transgressed. What seemed to be at issue was a woman exposing her own body for the public eye and calling it art.

一些猛烈抨击她行为的批评者通过网站发帖匿名发表意见，但在她家乡重庆，丈夫所在美术学院的同事批评他让妻子离家去北京追求艺术事业。这当然是对她公开暴露的回应，但他们的批评未必针对女性裸体作为艺术的问题。裸体画1979年首次在中华人民共和国公开展出，尹光中的《长城》（图6.01）那年春天在民主墙展出，艺术家们在那里公开批评文化大革命。比何成瑶早二十多年，他就把裸体与这一国家象征结合在一起，描绘一对男女，女性裸体面朝前方，两人位于一堆头骨之上。长城把人物捆绑在一起，而他们竭力反抗其控制。[^zh-ch06-3] 油画中的裸体（大体指女性裸体）虽曾被视为资产阶级表达形式，却在1980和1990年代的中国经历了一段正常化时期，这一作品市场不断扩大，为国家赞助提供了替代选择。[^zh-ch06-4] 把何成瑶的行为批评为不道德，以一种揭示问题的方式把她单独挑出。中国几位男性行为艺术家曾在作品中部分或完全裸体，却无人遭到这类攻击。他们的一些行为也发生在长城上。例如1998年，艺术家马六明在长城一段废墟上实施他关于性别含混的行为之一——他化妆、留长发以突出表演性女性气质，却脱光衣服露出男性生殖器——把长城当作另一条被逾越的边界。问题似乎在于，一个女人为了公众目光暴露自己的身体，并称之为艺术。


〔原书 208〕

![*图6.01　尹光中，《长城》，1979年。布面油画。Joan Lebold Cohen 摄。图片：密歇根大学董事会，艺术史系视觉资源收藏。*](web/assets/ch06-b008.jpg)

FIG 6.01 Yin Guangzhong, *Great Wall*, 1979. Oil on canvas. Photograph by Joan Lebold Cohen. Image: Regents of the University of Michigan, Department of the History of Art, Visual Resources Collections.

*图6.01　尹光中，《长城》，1979年。布面油画。Joan Lebold Cohen 摄。图片：密歇根大学董事会，艺术史系视觉资源收藏。*


〔原书 208, 209〕

Photographs of the performance and debate over its worthiness as art appeared in places beyond the usual art media sources. A website devoted to health issues, for example, published an article later picked up by several other websites; it compared He Chengyao’s performance to recent commercial spectacles in which scantily clad or naked women served as the main attraction. In an event described by the article’s author, four female models posed outside a telecommunications store, revealing their bare backs onto which the new design of a cell phone had been painted. The author states: “Currently, ‘disrobing’ slides toward a commercial objective. To disrobe in the name of art seems an easy way to attract the interest of the media, as easy as stir frying vegetables at high heat, but it only takes a little art experience and critical ability to realize that taking off one’s clothes in the name of art is really quite a clumsy and inferior effort.”[^en-ch06-5] He Chengyao’s performance was not art, in this editorialist’s assessment, because of its similarity to new gendered forms of commercialization in which the woman’s body literally becomes the medium for commodity image.

行为照片和关于它是否算艺术的辩论，出现在通常艺术媒体之外的场所。例如，一个关注健康问题的网站发表了一篇文章，后来被其他几个网站转载；文章把何成瑶的行为比作近期商业景观中半裸或裸体女性充当主要卖点的现象。在文章作者描述的一个活动中，四名女模特站在一家电信商店门外，露出赤裸的背部，上面画着新款手机的设计。作者写道：“如今，‘脱’滑向商业目的。以艺术之名脱衣，似乎是吸引媒体兴趣的捷径，像大火炒菜一样容易，但只要有一点艺术经验和批评能力就能意识到，以艺术之名脱衣服其实相当笨拙低劣。”[^zh-ch06-5] 在这位评论者看来，何成瑶的行为不是艺术，因为它类似于新出现的性别化商业化形式，其中女人的身体字面上成为商品形象的媒介。


〔原书 209〕

An altered photograph of the performance appeared in the August 2001 issue of *Vision 21*, a Chinese magazine, new that year, devoted to fashion, culture, and photography. The editors explained to He Chengyao that they had pixilated her chest so as not to violate a recent Ministry of Culture public memorandum prohibiting performances broadcasting pornography, superstition, or violence. Their choice to obscure her nudity strategically presented the photograph as news rather than art that might offend. A short text accompanied the image:

2001年8月，中国当年新创办的时尚、文化与摄影杂志《视觉21》刊登了一张经过修改的行为照片。编辑向何成瑶解释，他们给她的胸部打了马赛克，以免违反文化部最近禁止演出传播色情、迷信或暴力的公开通知。他们选择遮蔽她的裸体，策略性地把照片呈现为新闻，而非可能冒犯的艺术。配图短文写道：


〔原书 209〕

On May 17, 2001, at 3:00 PM, as German artist H. A. Schult displayed the one thousand trash people he had constructed from consumer waste and then transported to Jinshanling on the Great Wall, a brash woman flashed from the crowd of observers—Chinese artist He Chengyao. In a sudden movement, she pulled off her bright red shirt, grasped it in her hand, and like Delacroix’s Liberty Leading the People escorted the audience (including H. A. Schult) through the troops of trash people and leapt from the wall onto a beacon tower. In the words of discerning people, Goddess He had very intelligently raised an exposed yet restrained double-edged sword over the stage put up by Schult’s four million marks, and stole his thunder.[^en-ch06-6]

2001年5月17日下午三点，德国艺术家H. A. 舒尔特把他用消费垃圾制作并运到长城金山岭的一千个垃圾人展示出来时，一个鲁莽的女人从围观人群中闪出——中国艺术家何成瑶。她猛地扯下鲜红的上衣，抓在手里，像德拉克洛瓦《自由引导人民》中的自由女神一样，带着观众（包括H. A. 舒尔特）穿过垃圾人队伍，从城墙跃上一座烽火台。用明眼人的话说，何仙女非常聪明地在舒尔特花费四百万马克搭起的舞台上，举起一把裸露却有节制的双刃剑，抢走了他的风头。[^zh-ch06-6]


〔原书 209, 210〕

This critic likened her performance to *Liberty Leading the People*, in which a bare-chested woman with gun and French tricolor in hand leads armed citizens over piles of lifeless bodies, and thereby serves as an allegorical representation of revolution: a comparison that highlights the central role of woman in symbolically standing for the nation. Delacroix’s piece has often been noted as one of the first political works of modern painting. Sino-Soviet exchanges that led to the development of socialist realism as an international style adapted French academic painting to new political ends. *Liberty Leading the People* became a pedagogical standard, which academy-trained artists in China knew well. Chen Yifei and Wei Jingshan drew on its composition for their well-known national history painting, *The Taking of the Presidential Palace*, commissioned for the Military Museum in Beijing. The opening image of the 1961 Shanghai film production of *The Red Detachment of Women* also mirrors Delacroix’s composition and subject matter. In its woodcut print of female soldiers on the battlefield, a woman with her arm raised in the air emerges on the horizon, from behind the triangular shape of a red flag that cuts diagonally across her body. As explored in the previous chapter, the film’s heroine Wu Qionghua comes to represent the nation. Although He Chengyao did not include her likeness in her work, as Li Tianpain did, Wu Qionghua would become an important referent in her interpretation of her Great Wall performance.

这位批评者把她的行为比作《自由引导人民》：画中一个袒胸女人手持枪和法国三色旗，带领武装公民越过成堆尸体，从而成为革命的寓言式再现。这一比较凸显女人在象征民族时的中心角色。德拉克洛瓦的作品常被视为现代绘画最早的政治作品之一。促成社会主义现实主义发展为国际风格的中苏交流，把法国学院绘画改造成新的政治工具。《自由引导人民》成为教学范本，中国学院训练出来的艺术家都很熟悉。陈逸飞和魏景山为他们著名的国家历史画《占领总统府》借用了它的构图，该画受北京军事博物馆委托创作。1961年上海电影制片厂《红色娘子军》的开场画面也呼应德拉克洛瓦的构图和题材。在女兵战场的木刻版画中，一名女子高举手臂，从一面斜切过她身体的红旗三角形后面出现在天际。如上一章所论，电影女主角吴琼花成为民族的代表。尽管何成瑶没有像李天翩那样把吴琼花的形象纳入作品，吴琼花后来却成为她解释自己长城行为的重要参照。


〔原书 210〕

In response to the *Vision 21* article, one of He Chengyao’s friends, an artist and critic writing under a pseudonym, wrote a review in defense of her spontaneous performance:

针对《视觉21》的文章，何成瑶的一位朋友——一位用笔名写作的艺术家兼批评家——撰文为她的自发行为辩护：


〔原书 210〕

At first glance, He Chengyao, now called “Goddess,” can’t be doing anything else but plotting to borrow the ready-made stage erected by the German H. A. Schult’s huge monetary expenditure, all in order to find her own place in the limelight. Although the author does use the word “intelligent” to describe her, it seems a bit sour in tone since the whole article leads readers to believe that by stealing Schult’s thunder, He Chengyao opportunistically aimed to gain artistic fame. However, don’t forget that the exhibition of H. A. Schult’s artwork, for which he laid out the large sum of four million marks, employed the five-thousand-year-old Chinese symbol of the Great Wall. That if nothing else is profiteering. Not only is Schult the bigger opportunist, he was also first, but this is just a tangent to the topic at hand. Postmodern art is a competition of wits, and as such He Chengyao quite by chance aptly seized this opportunity.[^en-ch06-7]

乍一看，现在被称为“女神”的何成瑶，除了想借德国人H. A. 舒尔特花巨资搭好的现成舞台，为自己在聚光灯下找一席之地，还能做什么？虽然作者确实用了“聪明”一词来形容她，但语气似乎有点酸，因为整篇文章都在引导读者相信，何成瑶抢舒尔特风头，是机会主义地为了获取艺术名声。然而，别忘了，H. A. 舒尔特为展示作品花费四百万马克巨资，动用了有五千年历史的中国象征长城。这无论如何都是牟利。舒尔特不仅是更大的机会主义者，而且是先做的，但这只是题外话。后现代艺术是机智的竞赛，因此何成瑶纯属偶然地恰当抓住了这个机会。[^zh-ch06-7]


〔原书 210, 211〕

Four years later, in October 2005, He Chengyao and five other Chinese performance artists appeared in a program titled *China Live* at London’s Victoria and Albert Museum. The art reviewer who covered the performance series for *The Guardian* began her article with the following statement: “The great irony of these live performances by contemporary Chinese artists is that it gives British audiences the opportunity to see a wide range of work that has little or no legitimacy in its homeland.”[^en-ch06-8] The greater irony perhaps is the persistence of a narrow view of artistic expression as something only truly appreciated in the West. He Chengyao and other Chinese artists who succeed in attracting the attention of foreign art professionals make good on China’s national goal of “entering the world.” By performing in the Victoria and Albert Museum, He Chengyao’s work became validated as art, but in a way that covers up the domestic debate and contention, as well as the history of cultural encounter—from Delacroix to Schult in China—it lays bare.

四年后，2005年10月，何成瑶和另外五位中国行为艺术家参加了伦敦维多利亚与阿尔伯特博物馆题为“中国现场”的项目。为《卫报》报道这一系列行为的艺术评论者，以如下陈述开篇：“这些中国当代艺术家现场表演的巨大讽刺在于，它让英国观众有机会看到在其祖国几乎没有或完全没有合法性的广泛作品。”[^zh-ch06-8]更大的讽刺或许是，人们坚持一种狭隘的艺术表达观，认为它只有在西方才真正被欣赏。何成瑶和其他成功吸引外国艺术专业人士注意的中国艺术家，实现了中国“进入世界”的国家目标。通过在维多利亚与阿尔伯特博物馆表演，何成瑶的作品获得艺术认可，但这种认可掩盖了国内争论和冲突，也掩盖了它揭示的文化相遇史——从德拉克洛瓦到舒尔特在中国。


〔原书 211〕

Leaving Home

离家


〔原书 211〕

He Chengyao and I first met at the CourtYard Gallery in the summer of 1999, roughly three years before her *Opening the Great Wall* performance. This gallery represented a recent confluence of transnational money and culture in Beijing, where an artist from Sichuan and an anthropologist from the United States were both new arrivals. Neither of us knew that our chance encounter would eventually lead to an intermittent but prolonged conversation about gender and contemporary art, during which He Chengyao would move to Beijing and remake herself as a performance artist and I would adopt various roles in relation to her practice: interviewer, translator, videographer, and curator.[^en-ch06-9]

1999年夏天，我与何成瑶在四合苑画廊第一次见面，大约是她《开放长城》行为的三年前。这家画廊代表跨国资金与文化在北京的新汇流，一个来自四川的艺术家和一个来自美国的人类学家都是新来者。我们谁也不知道，这次偶遇最终会促成长达数年的断续交谈，关于性别与当代艺术；其间何成瑶会搬到北京，把自己重塑为行为艺术家，而我会在她的实践中承担多种角色：采访者、翻译、摄像师和策展人。[^zh-ch06-9]


〔原书 211〕

I was attending the opening party for the solo show of a female painter who had recently signed with the CourtYard Gallery. Handel Lee, a Chinese American lawyer based in Beijing founded the gallery in 1996 as a sideline interest to his legal work. In various interviews in the Western and Chinese press, Lee explained that he wanted to support Chinese contemporary art in Beijing, where opportunities to exhibit “avant-garde” work remained limited.[^en-ch06-10] He also wanted to cultivate a cosmopolitan appreciation of culture in the heart of China’s capital, a nexus of taste that could compete with the places he enjoyed frequenting in New York.

我当时参加一位刚与四合苑签约的女画家的个展开幕酒会。常驻北京的美籍华人律师李景汉（Handel Lee）1996年创办这家画廊，作为其法律工作之外的副业。在西方和中国媒体的各种采访中，李景汉解释说，他想在北京支持中国当代艺术，因为那里展出“先锋”作品的机会仍然有限。[^zh-ch06-10] 他也想在中国首都的心脏培育世界主义文化品味，建立一个足以与他喜欢光顾的纽约场所竞争的文化品味中心。


〔原书 211, 212〕

Handel Lee’s staff gutted and renovated the interior of an old stone courtyard building to accommodate the CourtYard restaurant and gallery, located on the moat surrounding the Forbidden City, directly across from the East Gate of the Imperial Palace. The house once belonged to a lieutenant of Yuan Shikai, commander of the North China Army who ruled from Beijing after the fall of the Qing Dynasty in 1911. During the Communist era, the building housed a factory before being partitioned into multiple family dwellings. With new property laws instituted during economic reform, the lieutenant’s descendants reclaimed the building. They sold it to Lee who himself, completing this story of restoration, claimed to be descended from Manchu members of the Qing court.

李景汉的团队拆除了紫禁城护城河畔一座旧石砌四合院的内部并重新装修，用来容纳四合苑餐厅和画廊；四合院正对故宫东门。这座房子曾属于袁世凯的一位副官；袁世凯是北洋军统帅，1911年清朝覆灭后在北京统治。共产党时代，这座建筑曾是一家工厂，后来被分隔成多户家庭住所。随着经济改革时期新财产法的实施，副官的后代收回了这座建筑。他们把它卖给李景汉，而李景汉本人也自称是清廷满族成员后裔，完成了这个修复故事。


〔原书 212〕

The ground floor of the CourtYard housed a restaurant serving Asian-European fusion cuisine, mainly patronized by an expatriate and tourist clientele. A curved staircase in the entryway led downstairs to a white-cube gallery. A small crowd had gathered for the event, and conversations took place in Chinese, English, and French. Someone offered me a ride to the postexhibit party, and as I joined the departing crowd, a former schoolmate of the exhibiting painter walked up beside me, took my arm, and introduced herself. He Chengyao bubbled with questions about my research. She herself had recently arrived in Beijing from Chongqing. She planned to stay for a few weeks to exhibit her paintings at the China Art Exposition, opening in the following week. She was an oil painter, a graduate from the Sichuan Academy of Fine Arts, but Beijing with its stylish new galleries beckoned.

四合苑一层是一家供应亚欧融合菜的餐厅，主要顾客是外籍人士和游客。入口处的弧形楼梯通向地下白色立方体画廊。一小群人聚集在活动中，谈话用中文、英文和法文进行。有人提出送我去展后派对；当我加入离开的人群时，参展画家的一位旧同学走到我身边，挽住我的手臂，自我介绍。何成瑶对我的研究连珠炮般提问。她本人最近刚从重庆到北京，计划待几周，在下周开幕的中国艺术博览会上展出画作。她是油画家，毕业于四川美术学院，但拥有时髦新画廊的北京在向她招手。


〔原书 212〕

I ran into He Chengyao several days later as I roamed through rows of numbered booths on the second floor of the massive International Exhibition Center, where the annual China Art Expo had been held since 1995. She and another former classmate split the reasonable expense of renting a small booth. Their works hung on opposite partition walls. Her classmate’s realist oil paintings depicted quaint views of Chongqing’s narrow, hilly alleys. He Chengyao’s paintings featured expressionist nude figures floating in a symbolic landscape of burnt ochre hills, solitary flowers, and land depressions shaped like watchful eyes. She later sent me a postcard of one of these paintings, *High Noon—Prayer* (figure 6.02), and then we lost touch.

几天后，我在巨大的国际展览中心二楼一排排编号展位间闲逛时又遇到何成瑶。中国艺术博览会自1995年起每年在那里举办。她和另一位旧同学分摊租用一个小展位的合理费用。他们的作品挂在相对的隔墙上。她同学的写实油画描绘重庆狭窄、多坡小巷的古朴景色。何成瑶的画作则描绘表现主义裸体人物，漂浮在烧赭色山丘、孤零零的花朵和形似窥视眼睛的洼地构成的象征风景中。她后来寄给我其中一幅《正午——祈祷》的明信片（图6.02），之后我们失去联系。


〔原书 212, 213〕

Over a year later, in the fall of 2000, I reconnected with her through a small Chinese-run gallery in Beijing exhibiting her work. The manager passed on a note from me. When He Chengyao called, we arranged to meet at an artists’ “salon” held in a new commercial development that combined business offices, stores, a hotel, and upscale apartments. The evening’s program included a screening of animated art films collected by two Chinese artists who had lived in New York for several years. Later we strolled toward the bright, steamy windows of a nearby hotpot restaurant. As we stirred vegetables and slices of mutton in the boiling pot of broth between us, she told me how she had come to Beijing this time. Through the connections of a friend, she managed to enter the *jinxiu ban* halfway through. This particular two-year “refresher” course served as an experimental introduction to contemporary art (*dangdai yishu*) theory and practice. This was the first time the Central Academy had offered such a course, and the instructor who initiated it remained under scrutiny as officials determined whether it would become a regular offering.

一年多后，2000年秋天，我通过北京一家由中国人经营、展出她作品的小画廊重新联系上她。经理转交了我的便条。何成瑶打来电话，我们约定在一个艺术家“沙龙”上见面；沙龙位于一个新商业开发区，集合了办公楼、商店、酒店和高档公寓。当晚活动包括放映两位在纽约生活数年的中国艺术家收集的动画艺术片。之后我们漫步走向附近一家火锅店明亮、蒸汽弥漫的橱窗。我们在中间沸腾的汤锅里搅动蔬菜和羊肉片时，她告诉我这次是怎么来北京的。通过朋友的关系，她在中途进入进修班。这个为期两年的“进修”课程，是对当代艺术（dangdai yishu）理论与实践的实验性介绍。这是中央美术学院第一次开设此类课程，发起课程的教师仍受审查，官员们在确定它是否会成为常规课程。


〔原书 213〕

![*图6.02　何成瑶，《正午——祈祷》，1999年。布面油画。艺术家惠允。*](web/assets/ch06-b023.jpg)

FIG 6.02 He Chengyao, *High Noon–Prayer*, 1999. Oil on canvas. Courtesy of the artist.

*图6.02　何成瑶，《正午——祈祷》，1999年。布面油画。艺术家惠允。*


〔原书 213〕

He Chengyao turned serious as she explained that this opportunity allowed her to escape from a life in Chongqing that felt increasingly oppressive. In later tellings of her departure narrative, she heightened the urgent drama of taking leave by describing how she’d gotten stuck in traffic on the way to the Chongqing station. She managed to jump on the Beijing-bound train only seconds before it pulled away. Her husband and nine-year-old son waved from the platform as the train gathered speed.

何成瑶严肃起来，解释说这个机会让她逃离了越来越压抑的重庆生活。在后来的离家叙述中，她强化了告别的紧迫戏剧性，描述自己去重庆火车站路上如何堵车，在火车开动前几秒跳上开往北京的列车。丈夫和九岁儿子在站台上挥手，火车加速。


〔原书 213, 214〕

In the mid-1980s, a decade and a half before this departure, she had married a painter she met at the Sichuan Academy of Fine Arts. In her early twenties, she gave birth to their son. Now that he was older and more independent, she felt she had to grasp the chance to emerge from the professional rut of the previous decade. In Beijing, she lived cheaply in an apartment near the Central Academy, housed temporarily in a defunct factory work unit in the northeast of Beijing while the new campus was being constructed. She felt judged by several of her classmates, many of whom were male or younger women, who viewed her move away from her family as a sign of unfaithfulness, even promiscuity. But her coursework introduced theories she felt injected new energy into her thinking about art. She now saw her previous paintings as trivial and unrelated to her life. She explained that she continued to paint only to make money. Selling works such as the one I’d recently seen in the gallery helped augment her meager finances. She told me that she had begun working on her first piece of dangdai yishu.

这次离开的十五年前，也就是1980年代中期，她嫁给了在四川美术学院认识的一位画家。二十出头时，她生下儿子。如今他长大、更独立了，她觉得自己必须抓住机会，摆脱过去十年的职业停滞。在北京，她廉价地住在中央美院附近的一间公寓；学院新校区建设期间，暂设在北京东北部一家停业工厂的单位里。她觉得自己受到一些同学的评判，其中许多是男性或更年轻的女性，他们把她离开家庭视为不忠、甚至放荡的迹象。但课程引入的理论让她觉得给艺术思考注入了新能量。她如今认为以前的画作琐碎，与自己的生活无关。她解释说继续画画只是为了赚钱。卖画——比如我最近在画廊看到的那幅——帮她补贴微薄收入。她告诉我，她已经开始创作第一件当代艺术作品。


〔原书 214〕

![*图6.03　何成瑶，《头发》，2001年。装置。艺术家惠允。*](web/assets/ch06-b026.jpg)

FIG 6.03 He Chengyao, *Hair*, 2001. Installation. Courtesy of the artist.

*图6.03　何成瑶，《头发》，2001年。装置。艺术家惠允。*


〔原书 214〕

I saw the piece several months later at an exhibit featuring works by members of her class. *Hair* (figure 6.03) consisted of three long plaits of human hair, each dyed a different primary color—glossy and almost iridescent yellow, red, and blue. A thin piece of glass sandwiched the thick black roots against a glass mount. Above this suspended synecdoche of changing style—a combination of old-fashioned braids and trendy new hair color—a silver plaque read:

几个月后，我在一个她班上成员作品展上看到这件作品。《头发》（图6.03）由三条长发辫组成，每条染成不同的原色——光亮、近乎虹彩的黄色、红色和蓝色。一块薄玻璃把浓密黑发根部夹在玻璃底座上。在这个悬置的变迁风格提喻——旧式辫子与时尚新发色的结合——上方，一块银色标牌写着：


〔原书 215〕

Hair

Time: End of the 20th Century—Era of Globalization

Place: Unearthed in China, Asia

Late 30th Century Superior Specimens Exhibit[^en-ch06-11]

头发

时间：二十世纪末——全球化时代

地点：亚洲中国出土

三十世纪末高等标本展[^zh-ch06-11]


〔原书 215〕

He Chengyao created this “found object” after observing the number of people in Beijing with hair dyed in shades of brown and blond, as well as brighter colors. She conducted research in salons around the city, taking photos and talking to customers. She noted that while many sought these hairstyles as a globalized fashion statement, they had to continually maintain this mark of distinction, since their black roots always reappeared. With this piece she began to explore the body as a conjunction of art and artifact—the body as a means of expression, a form of attire, which can symbolize different identifications, of urbanity, cosmopolitanism, or even ethnic Chineseness. He Chengyao purchased the braids for *Hair* from rural migrant women she approached on the street in Beijing and Chongqing. The resulting work of art embodies this transaction, in which hair exchanged for money ended up hanging on a museum wall, as well as a projective historicity that tries to assess the current era from the perspective of the distant future.[^en-ch06-12] He Chengyao’s shift from oil painting to dangdai yishu involved consciously playing with conventions of representation and museum display, blurring the representational real of ethnographic artifact with the presumed artfulness of the art object.

何成瑶在观察到北京许多人把头发染成棕色、金色以及更鲜艳的颜色之后，创作了这件“现成品”。她在全城美发沙龙调研，拍照并与顾客交谈。她注意到，许多人把这种发型当作全球时尚宣言，却必须不断维护这一区分标记，因为黑色发根总会重新长出。通过这件作品，她开始探索身体作为艺术与人工制品的结合——身体作为表达手段、一种装束，可以象征不同认同：城市性、世界主义，甚至民族意义上的中国性。何成瑶为《头发》购买的发辫，来自她在重庆和北京街头接触的农村外来女性。由此产生的作品体现了这一交易：头发换成钱，最终挂在博物馆墙上；同时体现一种投射性历史性，试图从遥远未来的视角评估当前时代。[^zh-ch06-12] 何成瑶从油画转向当代艺术，涉及有意识地玩弄再现和博物馆展示惯例，模糊民族志人工制品再现性的真实与艺术对象被假定的艺术性。


〔原书 215〕

After the exhibit, He Chengyao and I went to dinner with a Beijing curator we both knew. He pushed He Chengyao to explain the motivation behind *Hair*. She cryptically stated her disenchantment with the romanticism of her paintings, describing them as a commercial product that someone would hang in their living room for a few years before throwing them away. The curator’s line of questioning, which came close to accusing her of mimicking Western artists who have used hair as an artistic medium, eventually turned into a mini-tirade against Chinese teaching methods for contemporary art.[^en-ch06-13] He disparaged the practice of looking at slides of work by Western artists, arguing that it taught Chinese artists to copy, and claimed that the only Western artists worth teaching were Andy Warhol and Joseph Beuys. They had focused on the philosophical question of what it meant to be an artist engaged with society rather than on strict notions of content or form.

展览之后，何成瑶和我与一位我们都认识的北京策展人吃晚饭。他追问何成瑶解释《头发》的动机。她神秘地说自己已对绘画的浪漫主义不再着迷，把它们描述为商业产品，有人会在客厅挂几年，然后扔掉。策展人的追问近乎指责她模仿使用头发作为艺术媒介的西方艺术家，最终演变成一场对中国当代艺术教学方法的简短抨击。[^zh-ch06-13] 他贬斥看西方艺术家作品幻灯片的做法，认为这教中国艺术家抄袭，并声称唯一值得教的西方艺术家是安迪·沃霍尔和约瑟夫·博伊斯。他们关注的是艺术家参与社会意味着什么的哲学问题，而非严格的内容或形式观念。


〔原书 216〕

The Unspeakable

不可言说


〔原书 216〕

A week and a half later, in March 2001, He Chengyao arrived at my apartment. She had agreed to let me interview her about the experience of becoming an artist. I asked a standard opening question about childhood, and an unexpected monologue poured forth.[^en-ch06-14]

一周半后，2001年3月，何成瑶来到我的公寓。她同意接受我采访，谈成为艺术家的经历。我问了一个关于童年的常规开场问题，一段意想不到的独白倾泻而出。[^zh-ch06-14]


〔原书 216〕

Actually, outside of home, I don’t usually say too much about my family, because I didn’t grow up in a good environment. I think sometimes I’m not really willing to talk about my private life because it’s so different from that of other people. I don’t mean I just want to be like others, but the past gives me a lot of pain. Why? Well, now, I see this problem relatively clearly. I think every person has a different experience growing up, and that this experience can give a lot of impetus to one’s so-called future, and is very related to one’s worldview. So, I think, really, to understand an artist’s life experience provides a lot of inspiration for understanding the artwork. But now, I don’t look back... or speak about my experience of growing up.

其实在家外面，我一般不怎么说家里的事，因为我没有在好的环境中长大。我想有时我不太愿意谈私生活，因为它和别人太不同了。我不是说我只想和别人一样，但过去给我很多痛苦。为什么？嗯，现在我看这个问题比较清楚了。

我想每个人成长经历不同，这种经历会给人所谓未来很多动力，并且与世界观密切相关。所以我想，真的，了解一个艺术家的生活经历，对理解作品很有启发。但现在，我不回头看……也不谈我的成长经历。


〔原书 216〕

She laughed uncomfortably and confided that she’d only very recently tried to talk about certain episodes from her childhood but only with her husband.

她不自在地笑了笑，坦言她直到最近才尝试谈童年某些片段，而且只对丈夫说过。


〔原书 216〕

After referring to this past as a burden, she hesitated. I assured her that she should only talk about what she felt comfortable telling me. I explained that if I wrote or published anything, I would disguise her identity. She told me that, at this point, she would like me to use a pseudonym if I wrote about any of what she might say.[^en-ch06-15] Slowly, she continued.

在把过去称为负担之后，她犹豫了。我向她保证，只谈她觉得舒服的事。我解释说，如果我写作或发表，会隐去她的身份。她告诉我，此刻如果我写她可能说的任何内容，她希望我用化名。[^zh-ch06-15] 她慢慢地继续。


〔原书 216〕

After I came out of it, I saw that a lot of people hadn’t had an easy time. Why did I want to see my own past suffering as so painful? I think the reason lies in myself. This spring I’ve been thinking I should go see a psychologist. I feel like a caged wild animal. I just don’t feel comfortable. I really want to escape. There’s no concrete reason. After growing up, I thought there must be some underlying roots from my childhood that influenced me to feel this way. Why? When I was born, my mother and father... When my mother became pregnant, when she had me, she really didn’t know what... And she wasn’t married to my father. Because at that time in China, in the 1960s...

从那种处境走出来之后，我看到很多人过得也不容易。为什么我想把自己的过去看得那么痛苦？我想原因在我自己。这个春天我一直在想，我该去看心理医生。我觉得自己像一只被困在笼中的野兽。我就是觉得不舒服。我很想逃。没有具体原因。长大以后，我想童年一定有某些根源影响我产生这种感觉。为什么？我出生时，我母亲和父亲……我母亲怀孕、生我的时候，她真的不知道什么……而且她没有和我父亲结婚。因为当时中国，1960年代……


〔原书 216〕

She stopped. Confused, I asked, “Was it during the Cultural Revolution?”

她停住了。我不解地问：“是在文化大革命期间吗？”


〔原书 216, 217〕

“1964,” she replied. “The Cultural Revolution hadn’t started yet. At that time, people’s attitudes towards morality... in a socialist country, they saw this breach as very serious. My mother was only nineteen years old then.”[^en-ch06-16] Her voice rose in anger.

“1964年，”她回答，“文化大革命还没开始。那时人们对道德的态度……在社会主义国家，他们把这种越界看得很严重。我母亲当时只有十九岁。”[^zh-ch06-16] 她的声音因愤怒而升高。


〔原书 217〕

Really none of this is a problem. Unmarried, an unmarried mother, a single mother isn’t a problem, but back then, because of this, my mother and father had no work. They lost their jobs. Their experience was extremely bitter. I have to mention something even more removed. When my maternal grandmother (waipo) was thirty, her husband died. She had to take care of three children. My mother is the eldest. My uncle is number two. My mother and my uncle went to a ceramics factory. To me, what they did seems just like child labor. They were just teenagers when they went. Then the family conditions got a little better.

My father didn’t graduate from university. He was just one year away from graduating, but in his third year at university, there was a nationwide famine.[^en-ch06-17] He had a strong, solid physique, and he just couldn’t get enough to eat at school. He couldn’t stay any longer because all he felt from morning to night was hunger. He left school and went to a factory to work in art design. It was a ceramics factory. He painted flowers with glaze on ceramics.

其实这些都不是问题。未婚、未婚妈妈、单身母亲都不是问题，但在当时，因为这个，我母亲和父亲没有工作。他们丢了工作。他们的经历极其痛苦。我还得说一件更远的事。我外婆三十岁时，丈夫死了。她得照顾三个孩子。我母亲是老大，我舅舅是老二。母亲和舅舅进了一家陶瓷厂。在我看来，他们做的就像童工。他们去的时候才十几岁。后来家里条件好了一点。

我父亲大学没毕业。他还差一年毕业，但大学三年级时发生了全国性饥荒。[^zh-ch06-17] 他身体强壮结实，在学校就是吃不饱。他待不下去了，因为从早到晚只感到饥饿。他离开学校，去一家工厂做美术设计。那是一家陶瓷厂。他在陶瓷上用釉料画花。


〔原书 217〕

“Had he studied art before leaving university?”

“他离开大学前学过美术吗？”


〔原书 217〕

No, he just liked it. It was a hobby he did in his spare time. He studied a little of everything. Then, after the pregnancy with me, they both lost their jobs at the factory. At that time, the whole country was very poor. The material state of life was extremely low. My father did spare jobs. He went here and there to make a little money. I don’t remember things very clearly. But I know my mother was very pretty. By the time I could remember anything, my mother had gone crazy. My little brother and I were very scared.

没有，他只是喜欢。那是业余爱好。他什么都学一点。然后，我母亲怀了我之后，他们俩都丢了工厂的工作。当时全国都很穷。物质生活水平极低。父亲打零工，东奔西走挣点钱。我记得不太清楚。但我知道母亲很漂亮。到我开始记事时，母亲已经疯了。我和弟弟非常害怕。


〔原书 217〕

“What kind of mental illness did she have?”

“她得的是什么精神病？”


〔原书 217〕

He Chengyao simply stated, “Her mind became disorganized.” She slowly continued, “I think it had to do with the pressure on her. After giving birth to me, she wasn’t married and was still quite young. She was affected by all the judgmental comments made about her.”

何成瑶只简短地说：“她脑子乱了。”她慢慢继续，“我觉得和她承受的压力有关。生我之后，她没结婚，还很年轻。周围人对她的评判影响了她。”


〔原书 217〕

In a later version of this story that He Chengyao eventually wrote, she narrated with greater economy how her mother’s mental illness took the form of paranoid, antisocial behavior. She hit people and pulled their hair, stripped off her clothes and wandered the town’s streets.

在后来何成瑶写下的这个故事的版本中，她更简洁地叙述母亲的病如何表现为偏执、反社会的行为。她打人、扯人头发，脱光衣服在镇上街道游荡。


〔原书 217, 218〕

In my initial interview with her, she described the memories as they came to her, “In my recollections, I often see her as so frightening. She would hit my waipo and grab her hair. My waipo was a very traditional Chinese woman. After she became a married woman, she arranged her hair in a bun at the back of her head. My mom would grab her hair and pull it to the front. My memories are pretty scattered, but I remember being afraid. Every night my mom would run away. I don’t know where she went. She just wanted to run. She didn’t want to stay at home.

在最初的采访中，她随记忆所至描述道：“在我的记忆中，我常觉得她那么可怕。她会打外婆、抓她头发。外婆是非常传统的中国女性。她成为已婚妇人后，把头发盘在脑后。母亲会抓住她的头发往前拽。我的记忆很零散，但我记得害怕。每天晚上母亲都会跑出去。我不知道她去哪里。她只想跑，不想待在家里。


〔原书 218〕

At that time my family was pretty hard off. Only my dad went out to make money. My waipo really raised me. At that time my mother’s younger sister also had no work. Only my mother’s brother was still at the ceramics factory. We all lived together after my mother got sick. We all lived together like a traditional Chinese family. With my mom’s illness on top of everything else, we had to.[^en-ch06-18]

We rented someone else’s house. Behind the house was a river, and every summer after it rained, the water would rise and flood the bridge and our house. I remember when I was little, in the summer I would often be woken up in the middle of the night. They would call out—my childhood name was He Li—they would call, “He Li, hurry, wake up, get up, the water is rising.”

那时我家相当困难。只有爸爸出去挣钱。真正是外婆把我养大。那时母亲的妹妹也没有工作，只有母亲的弟弟还在陶瓷厂。母亲生病后我们都住在一起。我们像传统中国家庭一样住在一起。除了其他一切，再加上母亲的病，我们不得不这样。[^zh-ch06-18]

我们租别人的房子。房子后面有条河，每年夏天下雨后，水会涨起来，淹过桥和我们的房子。我记得小时候，夏天常在半夜被叫醒。他们会喊——我的乳名叫何丽——他们会喊：‘何丽，快醒醒，起来，水涨了。’”


〔原书 218〕

He Chengyao’s waipo, who held a combination of Buddhist and folk beliefs, would often invite fortunetellers to diagnose her mother’s illness. Her grandmother thought she had fallen ill through some offense to a dead person’s ghost. Even though they were really poor and seldom ate meat at the time, her grandmother would prepare a whole table full of food—fish, chicken, vegetables—to feed the visiting seer who would burn paper money to satisfy the ghosts or sprinkle water and rice in her mother’s room to ward off evil. When I asked if these methods had any effect, she laughed. “Of course they were useless! But they relieved my waipo’s heart a little. She thought that certainly my mother would get a little better. She really believed that she had gotten better. But in reality she hadn’t.”

何成瑶的外婆兼有佛教和民间信仰，常请算命先生诊断母亲的病。外婆认为她得罪了某个死人的鬼魂才生病。尽管当时家里很穷、很少吃肉，外婆仍会准备满满一桌食物——鱼、鸡、蔬菜——招待来访的灵媒；灵媒会烧纸钱满足鬼魂，或在她母亲房间里撒水撒米驱邪。我问这些方法有没有效果，她笑了：“当然没用！但让外婆心里安慰了一点。她以为母亲肯定会好一点。她真的相信她好了。但其实没有。”


〔原书 218〕

“There was one time,” she began, but then stopped to draw a diagram on a scrap of paper. She added to the sketch as she described the layout of their *tianjing* (sky well) house with rooms organized around a small open courtyard to one side. Several people slept in each room. A river and farm fields lay nearby. She went on to describe a night when she was really small. Her grandmother and a fortuneteller had left her alone when they went inside to burn money to the kitchen god. A table with a full meal laid out on it stood in the tianjing.

“有一次，”她开始说，随后停下来，在一张纸片上画示意图。她一边描述他们的天井房屋布局——房间围绕一侧的小露天庭院——一边在草图上添画。每个房间睡几个人。附近有河和农田。她接着描述自己很小的一晚。外婆和一位算命先生进厨房给灶神烧纸钱时，把她一个人留在外面。天井里摆着一桌丰盛的饭菜。


〔原书 219〕

It was dark, after eight o’clock. At that time there were no electrical lights. Oil lamps were lit. Aiyo, at night, everywhere was completely black. Wind blew through the tianjing. It blew the flames of the oil lamps back and forth. I was scared out of my wits. I always felt like there were ghosts, some thing following right behind me. It’s so frightening when you are little and listen to them say there are ghosts here and there.... I started to feel them everywhere, in front, in back, to the left and right, everywhere moving around me. The flames of the oil lamps flickered vaguely back and forth. I didn’t want to stay there. I thought of running to the kitchen where they had all gone. But I stood scared stiff by the tianjing. They told me to stand guard there while they were in the kitchen to make sure no cats ate the food on the table. Back then even cats were starving and couldn’t get their fill. [She laughs.] They were afraid cats would eat the food because after the food had been offered to the spirits, people could eat it.

天黑了，八点以后。那时没有电灯。点着油灯。哎呀，晚上到处一片漆黑。风吹过天井，把油灯火苗吹得摇来摇去。我吓得魂飞魄散。总觉得有鬼，有什么东西紧跟在我身后。小时候听他们说这里那里有鬼，太可怕了……我开始觉得它们无处不在，前面、后面、左边、右边，到处在我周围移动。油灯火苗隐约晃动。我不想待在那里。我想跑到他们都在的厨房。但我站在天井边吓得动弹不得。他们让我站在那里守着，他们去厨房，防止猫吃掉桌上的食物。那时连猫都饿得吃不饱。[她笑。]他们怕猫吃食物，因为食物祭过鬼魂之后，人还可以吃。


〔原书 219〕

“What did you think the ghosts were like?” I asked.

“你觉得鬼是什么样的？”我问。


〔原书 219〕

I thought they were green-faced and long-toothed with very long hair. I thought that when they walked, their footsteps made no sound and they could float through the air. Have you read Tales of Liaozhai?[^en-ch06-19] It was that kind of haunted feeling. At night I would sit together with the adults. If I sat behind them, I would fear there was something behind me. I would continually turn around to check, but there was never anything there. The oil lamps threw up huge shadows....

我想它们青面獠牙，头发很长。我想它们走路没有声音，能在空中飘。你看过《聊斋志异》吗？[^zh-ch06-19] 就是那种闹鬼的感觉。晚上我和大人坐在一起。如果我坐在他们后面，就怕身后有东西。我会不停回头查看，但那里从来没有东西。油灯投出巨大的影子……


〔原书 219〕

My waipo also liked to have fortunetellers read our fates—for my mother, me, my little brother, and my little sister. I remember one time we went next door to our neighbor’s house. They used charts to consult when you were born, things like that, and to make predictions. I didn’t understand what they were saying. I remember being woken up by my waipo from confused and hazy sleep. She’d call out, “He Li, we’re going home.” Then, after hearing them talk about this ghost and that ghost, I’d have to follow her down that dark passageway, with only the dim light of the oil lamp to light the way. The whole way I kept turning around to try to catch a glimpse of what was following behind me.

我外婆也喜欢请算命先生给我们看命——母亲、我、弟弟和妹妹。我记得有一次我们去隔壁邻居家。他们用图表推算你的出生时辰之类，做预测。我听不懂他们说什么。我记得被外婆从迷迷糊糊的睡眠中叫醒。她会喊：‘何丽，我们回家了。’然后，听他们谈了这个鬼那个鬼之后，我得跟着她走过那条黑暗的通道，只有油灯的微光照路。一路上我不停回头，想瞥见跟在身后的东西。


〔原书 219〕

With barely a pause, He Chengyao turned from talking about ghosts to soldiers.

几乎没有停顿，何成瑶从谈鬼转向谈士兵。


〔原书 219, 220〕

Back then there were some People’s Liberation Army [PLA] soldiers. This was at the time in foreign relations when China was relatively isolated. They had already broken relations with the Soviet Union. It was the 1960s. So the PLA comrades, [she smiled as she remembered the rhetoric] we should say they had “united with the residents.”[^en-ch06-20] There were a lot of PLA soldiers in our town. There was a military factory with a lot of soldiers. At that time the party was advocating for them to “learn from Lei Feng.”[^en-ch06-21] I think the “learn from Lei Feng” campaign began in 1964. Anyway, some PLA soldiers came to our house. There was one who could do acupuncture, using metal needles. I think my waipo was already worn out and at wit’s end. In this frame of mind, she let them give my mom acupuncture.

当时有一些人民解放军战士。那是中国外交上相对孤立的时期。他们已经和苏联断了关系。那是1960年代。所以解放军同志，[她笑着回忆那套修辞]我们应当说他们‘和居民打成一片’。[^zh-ch06-20] 我们镇上有很多解放军战士。有一家军工厂，很多士兵。当时党号召他们‘学雷锋’。[^zh-ch06-21] 我想‘学雷锋’运动始于1964年。总之，一些解放军战士来到我们家。有一个人会用金属针做针灸。我想外婆已经筋疲力尽、无计可施。在这种心情下，她让他们给我妈扎针。


〔原书 220〕

I asked if acupuncture can help cure mental disorders, and He Chengyao replied,

我问针灸能否治愈精神障碍，何成瑶回答：


〔原书 220〕

No, of course not. I don’t think so. They didn’t really understand this kind of illness. They wanted to try everything, every kind of folk prescription. Later they even made her eat earthworms. They prepared earthworms and white sugar together and gave it to her to eat. When I think of it now, it’s so disgusting. Really they didn’t have any scientific basis for what they did. They made a table, a long table, and put it here when they gave my mom acupuncture.

不能，当然不能。我不这么认为。他们并不真正了解这种病。他们什么都想试，各种偏方。后来他们甚至让她吃蚯蚓。他们把蚯蚓和白糖拌在一起给她吃。现在想起来很恶心。他们做的事真的没有科学依据。他们搬来一张桌子，一张长桌，放在那里给我妈扎针。


〔原书 220〕

She drew a rectangular table in the center of the house, just to the left of the tianjing. Then she drew a figure inside the rectangle and pierced it with short stabs of her pencil to indicate her mother’s body infiltrated with political and public meanings.

她在这座房子中央、天井左侧画了一张长方形桌子，然后在矩形里画了一个人形，用铅笔短短地刺戳，表示母亲的身体被政治和公共意义侵入。


〔原书 220〕

They came to our house every Sunday to “learn from Lei Feng.” They “learned from Lei Feng” by doing “good deeds.” When they came, my waipo prepared lots of things for them to eat. We were hungry, but she still gave them a lot to eat because they were helping us. Several PLA soldiers would press my mother onto a board, a long board. My mother wasn’t willing, so they had to restrain her. Several men would hold her down and stick needles in her. I don’t know if they put the needles into her correct acupuncture points. Why did my mother’s muscles shake so? Maybe they got the points wrong. They weren’t experts in this. That one PLA soldier, I can still remember him. He was from Nanjing and was called Jin Something. My waipo used to call him Little Jin.

他们每个星期天都来我们家‘学雷锋’。他们通过做好事来‘学雷锋’。他们来时，外婆准备很多东西给他们吃。我们饿着肚子，她还是给他们很多吃的，因为他们在帮我们。几个解放军战士会把我母亲按在一块板上，一块长板。母亲不愿意，所以他们得制住她。几个男人按住她，给她扎针。我不知道他们有没有扎对穴位。为什么母亲的肌肉抖得那么厉害？也许他们扎错了穴位。他们不是这方面的专家。那个解放军战士，我现在还记得。他来自南京，叫金什么。外婆以前叫他小金。


〔原书 220〕

After a long pause, I asked, “So you suspect that his skills weren’t very good?”

沉默了很久，我问：“所以你怀疑他的技术不太好？”


〔原书 220, 221〕

If they had been, then why did my mother shake so violently? Now that I think about it, I definitely think they didn’t do it correctly. Aiyo, I think my mother received so much bitter treatment. That’s why my heart aches so badly. And now I feel like there’s nothing I can do for my mom. She’s still the same. And right now, we don’t know where she’s gone. Last semester, after I came to Beijing, one time when I called home, I asked my dad about her. My dad said, “Your mom, we don’t know where she’s gone.”

如果好的话，我母亲为什么抖得那么厉害？现在想起来，我肯定他们做得不对。哎呀，我觉得我母亲受了那么多苦。所以我的心才这么疼。现在我觉得自己对我妈什么都做不了。她还是那样。而且现在，我们不知道她去了哪里。上个学期，我来北京之后，有一次打电话回家，问爸爸她的情况。爸爸说：‘你妈呀，我们不知道她去哪了。’


〔原书 221〕

“She ran away?” I asked.

“她跑了？”我问。


〔原书 221〕

Mmm.

嗯。


〔原书 221〕

“And hasn’t come home yet?”

“还没回家？”


〔原书 221〕

Yes.

是。


〔原书 221〕

“How long has it been?”

“多久了？”


〔原书 221〕

Right now, it’s already been several months.

现在，已经好几个月了。


〔原书 221〕

“And she still hasn’t come back?”

“还没回来？”


〔原书 221, 222〕

No.... Before I came to Beijing, before I came to study at the Central Academy of Fine Arts, I really wanted to move my mom to Chongqing so that I could take care of her. I wanted her to change environments. She was still in that county town, in Rongchang County. My mom is alone. Afterward my dad got married again. He divorced my mom and married someone else. My mom lives on her own. So because of this I feel full of regret. I feel like I haven’t done anything for my mother. Now that I’ve come to Beijing, I feel like I can do some things that I like, some creative activities. But if the price is to sacrifice my mother... I think my mother... because after she dies, after she’s gone... I think it’s really like my birth brought my mother her disaster. I feel like she gave her life for my everything.

One time I said to my younger sister, “Aiya, Mama was too fragile. If only she could have been just a little stronger when we were young, we wouldn’t have received so many shocks.” Even after I grew up, I always felt inferior. I’m still not very sociable.... My sister said to me, “Mama was so young. She just didn’t have the ability to accept that sort of cruel reality. She didn’t have that kind of psychological quality.”

I believe now that my mom’s body grew disorganized due to her experience. She used her own method to resist the pressure of the outside world. She escaped into her own world. This was her way. Now I can gradually reach this understanding.

She went once for medical treatment. She was treated several times. One time it seemed like she was better, but then after one or two months, she got sick again. After she’d been sick and then gotten better, she was still extremely sensitive. For example, if the two of us were talking in this room and she was in the next room, she’d think we were talking about her even if the content of our conversation had nothing to do with her. During the period when she was well, I thought our home was so happy. My mother was very skilled with her hands and could do traditional embroidery. She worked in a little shop, sewing and helping out. She earned some money. Then she fell ill again. She turned back again.

Then one time my mother died. It was still in this house.

没有……我来北京之前，来中央美术学院学习之前，真的很想把我妈接到重庆，好照顾她。我想让她换个环境。她还在那个县城，荣昌县。我妈一个人。后来我爸再婚了。他和我妈离婚，娶了别人。我妈独自生活。所以因为这个，我满心遗憾。我觉得自己没为母亲做什么。现在我来到北京，觉得自己可以做些喜欢的事，一些创作活动。但如果代价是牺牲我母亲……我想我母亲……因为她死后，她走了以后……我想，真的好像我的出生给母亲带来了灾难。我觉得她为我的一切付出了生命。

有一次我对妹妹说：‘唉，妈妈太脆弱了。如果在我们小时候，她能坚强一点，我们就不会受那么多惊吓。’即使长大以后，我也一直自卑。我还是不太善于交际……妹妹对我说：‘妈妈那么年轻。她就是没有能力接受那种残酷现实。她没有那种心理素质。’

我现在相信，我母亲的身体因为她的经历而混乱。她用自己的方法抵抗外部世界的压力。她逃进自己的世界。这是她的方式。现在我能逐渐理解这一点。

她曾去接受治疗，治了好几次。有一次似乎好了，但一两个月后，又病了。病好之后，她还是极其敏感。比如，我们两个在这个房间说话，她在隔壁，就会以为我们在说她，即使我们谈的内容与她无关。她好的那段时间，我觉得我们家好幸福。母亲手很巧，会传统刺绣。她在一家小店工作，缝缝补补帮忙，挣些钱。然后她又病了。她又变回去了。

后来有一次，我母亲死了。还是在这座房子里。


〔原书 222〕

He Chengyao gestured toward her drawing.

何成瑶朝她的画指了指。


〔原书 222〕

I don’t know what caused it, but they said she had died. I was still small. They placed her on a board, on a wooden door. They took the door down and laid her dead body out on it. I was very small, just a few years old, but I still remember. I saw my mom lying there with her face covered with coarse yellow paper, the sort of paper made by hand. My dad sat by her side. I saw a teardrop hanging on the tip of my father’s nose. He cried silently. My dad was still very young then, just in his twenties. I didn’t understand this death or its meaning for my life. I didn’t understand what was happening. I only thought it was strange to see my father crying.... My dad said he would go get a doctor to bring my mom back to life. My waipo told him not to go. She said my mom had tormented us. She asked him, “Haven’t we suffered enough?”

I thought my waipo was so cruel back then, but now I can see the tragedy of her life. How did she endure it all? Still she remained optimistic. I think she influenced some part of my personality. When facing something heavy, a serious situation, she could use a relatively light tone to talk about it. She was very strong.

My dad still wanted to fetch a doctor. He found a doctor, who gave my mom a shot. They called it something like a cardiac stimulant shot. I don’t know what medicine it was. And then she came back to life. If my dad hadn’t gone to find a doctor for my mom, then maybe that time they would have just buried her.

我不知道是什么原因，但他们说她死了。我还小。他们把她放上一块板，一扇木门。他们把门卸下来，把她的遗体摊在上面。我很小，才几岁，但我还记得。我看见妈妈躺在那里，脸上盖着粗糙的黄纸，手工做的那种纸。爸爸坐在她旁边。我看见一滴泪挂在他鼻尖。他无声地哭。爸爸那时还很年轻，才二十多岁。我不懂死亡，也不懂它对我人生的意义。我不明白发生了什么。我只觉得看到爸爸哭很奇怪……爸爸说他会去请医生，把妈妈救活。外婆不让他去。她说妈妈折磨了我们。她问他：‘我们受的苦还不够吗？’

当时我觉得外婆好残忍，但现在我能看到她人生的悲剧。她怎么忍受这一切？她仍然保持乐观。我想她影响了我性格的一部分。面对沉重的事情、严峻的局面，她能用比较轻的语气谈论。她非常坚强。

爸爸还是想去找医生。他找到一位医生，给妈妈打了一针。他们称为强心针之类。我不知道是什么药。然后她活过来了。如果爸爸没有去给妈妈找医生，也许那一次他们就把她埋了。


〔原书 222〕

After a long silence fell between us, He Chengyao continued her story but at a lower level of intensity. The haunting immediacy of childhood ghosts and her mother’s illness slid into the background as she moved more quickly through the years to arrive at her current situation.

我们之间沉默了许久，何成瑶继续讲，但强度降低了。童年鬼魂和母亲疾病那挥之不去的切身感退到背景中，她更快地略过随后几年，来到当前处境。


〔原书 222, 223〕

She told me that she once attended kindergarten for a few days. She laughed when she told me that she liked it because at the end of the day they gave every child a piece of candy, a treat she never had at home. Her family pulled her out after a few days because they needed her at home to look after her younger sister, their third child, who had recently been born.

她告诉我，她曾上过几天幼儿园。她笑着说，她喜欢那里，因为每天结束时他们给每个孩子一块糖，那是她在家从未吃到过的甜食。几天后家里把她接走，因为需要她在家照顾刚出生的妹妹，他们的第三个孩子。


〔原书 223〕

A couple of years later, her family sent her and her younger brother to live with her father’s parents in a town called Lianghe. Her paternal grandfather ( *yeye*) worked as a teacher in the middle school and thought it would be better for the children to move away from their mother and go to school. While she remembers nothing but affection and kindness from her *yeye*, her paternal grandmother (*nainai*) made it clear that she didn’t like them. Their father was her eldest son, and she felt their mother had unfairly burdened him and driven him to hard labor in order to take care of her and their three children. Her father moved from job to job in order to make enough money. After first losing his job at the ceramics factory, he had served as an elementary school teacher, but the pay was too low, so he went to work for a moving company. Then he shoveled coal at the train yard. He pulled carts like a coolie. He broke rocks.

几年后，家里把她和弟弟送到父亲父母所在的两河镇一起生活。祖父（爷爷）在中学当老师，认为孩子离开母亲去上学更好。她对爷爷的记忆只有慈爱，但祖母（奶奶）明确表示不喜欢他们。他们的父亲是她的长子，她觉得他们母亲不公平地拖累了他，逼他辛苦劳作来照顾她和三个孩子。父亲为挣够钱不断换工作。在陶瓷厂的职位最初丢失后，他当过小学教师，但工资太低，于是去搬家公司工作。后来在火车站铲煤。他像苦力一样拉车，砸石头。


〔原书 223〕

Then, for a while, her father managed to set himself up as a photographer. He Chengyao credits some of her early interest in drawing and painting to his vocation at this time as an itinerant image-maker. She described to me how he would take his camera to neighboring counties and towns and peddle his services as photographer. Eventually he rented a small shop in Rongchang and worked to develop contacts with local schools and work units. He took black and white group photos. She laughed, remembering that her dad took all of her class and graduation pictures. He took pride in this work, which finally enabled him to see himself as something of an intellectual and establish a connection back to his grandfather, who had once been a county secretary with beautiful calligraphy in the “old society.” Her father’s work became more regular, and he hung out a sign for his studio. In the late 1970s or early 1980s, a craze for the traditional folk craft of paper cutting swept across the country, and her father also began to create intricate paper cuts and sold them out of his photo studio.[^en-ch06-22]

后来有一段时间，父亲设法成为摄影师。何成瑶把自己早年对绘画的兴趣部分归功于他当时作为流动图像制作者的行当。她向我描述他如何带着相机到邻近县镇兜售摄影服务。最终他在荣昌租下一间小店，努力与当地学校和工作单位建立联系。他拍黑白集体照。她笑着回忆，爸爸拍了她所有班级照和毕业照。他为这份工作自豪，这终于让他把自己看作某种知识分子，并与曾祖父建立联系——曾祖父在“旧社会”当过县秘书，书法漂亮。父亲的工作更有规律后，他为自己的照相馆挂了招牌。1970年代末或1980年代初，传统民间剪纸风潮席卷全国，父亲也开始创作精细剪纸，在照相馆出售。[^zh-ch06-22]


〔原书 223〕

Once she began attending middle school, her father changed her name from He Li to He Chengyao (*chengyao* meaning “to become pure jade”), because he thought the character *li* (“beautiful”) was too common. She cried bitterly at the time of the change.

她上中学后，父亲把她从何丽改名为何成瑶（“成瑶”意为“成为纯洁的玉”），因为他觉得“丽”（“美丽”）这个字太常见。改名时她痛哭了一场。


〔原书 223, 224〕

After middle school, He Chengyao attended a vocational school for three years, and studied diligently to become a teacher. Teachers warned her that given her family’s situation, if she didn’t work hard, she wouldn’t be able to get a job. Upon graduation, she taught fifth and sixth grade math at the elementary school attached to the vocational school. She also began drawing more seriously and studied with one of her father’s friends who worked in the local Cultural Center. Several years later she tested into the art education department at the Sichuan Academy of Fine Arts in Chongqing.

中学毕业后，何成瑶读了三年职业学校，努力学习，想成为教师。老师警告她，以她家的状况，如果不努力，就找不到工作。毕业后，她在职业学校附属小学教五、六年级数学。她也开始更认真地画画，跟随父亲一位在当地文化馆工作的朋友学习。几年后，她考进重庆四川美术学院美术教育系。


〔原书 224〕

He Chengyao gradually connected her performance on the Great Wall with this story about her childhood and her mother’s experience. After the performance, she told me that she no longer wanted to be anonymous. She asked me to use her real name. When I was visiting her one fall afternoon in 2001, she showed me with a slight, shy smile her addition to a glossy volume on Western feminist art I’d given her as a gift some weeks earlier. In the back section of the book that listed biographies of individual artists, she had glued in her picture and handwritten under it her name and biographical details. She later interpreted *Opening the Great Wall* as the starting point of a career as a feminist artist, comparing her performance with another woman who publicly exposed her wounds, Wu Qionghua in *The Red Detachment of Women*. In 2003, He Chengyao sent me the following message:

何成瑶逐渐把她在长城上的行为与这段童年和母亲的经历联系起来。行为之后，她告诉我，她不再想匿名。她请我使用她的真名。2001年秋天一个下午我去看她时，她带着一丝羞涩的微笑，给我看她在我几周前送她的一本关于西方女性主义艺术、印制精美的书上的补充。在书后介绍艺术家生平的章节中，她贴上了自己的照片，手写姓名和生平信息。她后来把《开放长城》解释为女性主义艺术家生涯的起点，把自己的行为与另一个公开暴露伤口的女人——电影《红色娘子军》中的吴琼花——相提并论。2003年，何成瑶发给我以下信息：


〔原书 224〕

I am still in the early experimental stages of using feminism as a method for making my own art.... It’s like the scene in the film The Red Detachment of Women when Wu Qionghua, having suffered the extremes of oppression and shame, takes the stage and denounces the vicious landlord Nan Batian. All she can do is tear open her clothing and show everyone her wounds. Perhaps the hatred has been too strong, the “blood and tears” too many, leaving me instead with no way to speak. It’s also like a mute person who has suddenly been cured, yet she is still accustomed to using the gestures of sign language.[^en-ch06-23]

我仍然处在把女性主义作为个人艺术创作方法的早期实验阶段……就像电影《红色娘子军》中的场景：吴琼花遭受极度的压迫和羞辱后，走上台控诉恶霸地主南霸天。她所能做的就是撕开衣服，给所有人看她的伤口。也许仇恨太深，“血泪”太多，反而让我无法言说。也像一个突然被治好的哑巴，却仍然习惯用手语。[^zh-ch06-23]


〔原书 224, 225〕

He Chengyao revivifies, through her performance art, a revolutionary episode of female self-exposure, but freezes it and reperforms it at the moment before political training of how to properly speak her bitterness in service of socialist revolution.[^en-ch06-24] She does not speak. She performs an action. She does not sublimate the gesture of ripping open one’s clothes to a clear and victorious national cause. Nor does she shove it aside as part of a laughably naïve propagandistic vocabulary. Possessed by the spirit of her mother, denounced as immoral and driven mad, she strips off her clothes and wanders through the crowds gathered on the Great Wall. She channels the shock power of her mother’s disturbed, antisocial behavior into a personal politics of gender, trauma, and speechless history that attempts to articulate art together with everyday injustice.

何成瑶通过行为艺术复活了一个女性自我暴露的革命片段，却把它冻结，并在政治训练她如何正确诉说苦难、服务于社会主义革命之前的那一刻重新表演。[^zh-ch06-24] 她不说话。她完成一个动作。她没有把撕开衣服的姿态升华为明确而胜利的国家事业，也没有把它当作可笑幼稚的宣传语汇抛到一边。她被母亲的魂灵附体——那被斥为不道德、被逼疯的母亲——脱掉衣服，在长城上聚集的人群中游荡。她把母亲失常、反社会行为的震撼力量，转化为一种关于性别、创伤和无言历史的个人政治，试图把艺术与日常不公一起表达出来。


〔原书 225〕

Testimony

证词


〔原书 225〕

The two parallel sets of performances He Chengyao went on to create demonstrate a horizontal, formal dialogue with global contemporary art practice, at the same time that they dig into different layers of history. She embraced the transnational form of performance art, as it was introduced in her course at the Central Academy, and used it to excavate both personal experience and various sociopolitical uses of the exposed female body throughout twentieth-century China. During the summer after *Opening the Great Wall*, He Chengyao returned to Rongchang to visit her mother. Her husband and father, both bearing cameras, accompanied her. Her husband took the photographs for a series she titled *Mama and Me* (figure 6.04).

何成瑶随后创作的两个平行行为系列，既展示与全球当代艺术实践在形式上的横向对话，也深入不同历史层面。她拥抱中央美院课程介绍的跨国行为艺术形式，用它挖掘个人经历，以及二十世纪中国对暴露女性身体的各种社会政治利用。在《开放长城》之后的夏天，何成瑶回到荣昌看望母亲。丈夫和父亲都带着相机陪她。丈夫为她拍摄了题为《妈妈和我》的系列照片（图6.04）。


〔原书 225〕

In a later article about her evolving work as a performance artist, she writes: “This summer I returned home. In *Mama and Me*, my mother sits by herself on a stool at the side of a courtyard, playing with a rotten apple, when I quietly approach and stand behind her to document this moment through a series of photographs. This is the first time my mother and I had our picture taken together. With the aid of this medium, I have been able to reaffirm the family and blood connection that links me and my mother, and to partially satisfy a yearning of more than thirty years to support, touch, and embrace her.”[^en-ch06-25] Through photographic reproduction she gains distance on herself, standing together with her mother for an unconventional family portrait. Her mother wears only a pair of white pants. In the first image, she sits alone, looking down. In the third image, as He Chengyao takes off her shirt, her mother first seems aware of the audience of cameras. In the fifth image, He Chengyao’s mother looks up, her eyes meeting those of her daughter, whose head still remains beyond the viewer’s sight. In the final image, the daughter’s head enters the frame, and both women look down, returning doubled to the first.

在后来的文章中，她谈到自己不断演变的行为艺术创作：“这个夏天我回家了。在《妈妈和我》中，母亲独自坐在院子边的凳子上，摆弄一个烂苹果，我悄悄走近，站在她身后，用一系列照片记录这个时刻。这是我第一次和母亲一起拍照。借助这种媒介，我得以重新确认连接我和母亲的家族与血脉关系，并部分满足三十多年来想搀扶、触摸、拥抱她的渴望。”[^zh-ch06-25] 通过照片复制，她与自己拉开距离，和母亲站在一起，拍下一张非传统的家庭肖像。母亲只穿一条白裤子。第一张照片中，她独自坐着，低着头。第三张中，何成瑶脱下上衣时，母亲似乎第一次意识到镜头观众。第五张中，何成瑶的母亲抬起头，目光与女儿相遇，而女儿的头仍在观者视野之外。最后一张中，女儿的头进入画面，两个女人都低下头，双重地回到第一张。


〔原书 225, 226〕

For a related piece, He Chengyao selected the image from *Mama and Me* in which her mother looks up at her, in surprise or recognition. She combined it with photographs of herself and her son. *Testimony* (figure 6.05) provides a genealogical chart of matrilineal kinship, suggesting connection through bodily touch, but ending with her son alone, the space behind him empty. It stares back at the oppressions of patriarchal norms, suggesting alternative, affective webs of meaning and attachment, even as they are traumatically warped by societal pressures to comply with and replicate those norms. Does *Testimony* evoke a legacy of recognition and care outside the decorous bounds of convention; of mental disorder, escape, and abandonment; or of order resumed through the production a single male heir with his background erased? Familial relations and the gender politics of the nation and its art intertwine as the bodies of mother and daughter, the female figures who have served such symbolic purposes, are photographed by the unseen father and husband. In He Chengyao’s unfolding work, her own body became the primary medium through which she investigated this legacy of control and its embodied and psychological dimensions. Her work thus joins a constellation of experiments by feminist performance artists like Yoko Ono and Marina Abramović, who have offered their bodies to the spontaneous treatment, often shockingly violent, of their audiences.[^en-ch06-26] By staging the subjection of the female body, she unhinges it from the moral, emotional, symbolic work it has performed for the family and the nation. She thereby attempts to move beyond their modes of regulation.

在相关作品中，何成瑶从《妈妈和我》中选取母亲抬头看她、带着惊讶或辨认神情的那张照片，与自己和儿子的照片组合。《证词》（图6.05）提供了一条母系亲属谱系，暗示身体接触的连接，却以儿子独自一人结尾，他身后的空间空着。它回望父权规范的压迫，暗示另类的、情感性的意义与依恋网络，即使这些网络因要求人们服从并复制那些规范的社会压力而遭受创伤性的扭曲。《证词》唤起的是习俗体面边界之外的承认与关怀遗产，还是精神失常、逃离和遗弃的遗产，抑或是通过生产单一男性继承人并抹除其背景而恢复秩序的遗产？家庭关系与国家及其艺术的性别政治交织在一起，母亲和女儿——曾服务于此类象征目的的女性形象——的身体，被不可见的父亲和丈夫拍摄。在何成瑶不断展开的作品中，她自己的身体成为主要媒介，用来考察这种控制遗产及其具身与心理维度。她的作品由此加入小野洋子和玛丽娜·阿布拉莫维奇等女性主义行为艺术家的实验群，她们把自己的身体交给观众自发的、往往令人震惊的暴力处置。[^zh-ch06-26] 通过展演女性身体的臣服，她把它从为家庭和国家承担道德、情感、象征工作中松脱。她由此试图超越其规训模式。


〔原书 226〕

![*图6.04　何成瑶，《妈妈和我》，2001年。行为。摄影：Yan Yan。艺术家惠允。*](web/assets/ch06-b084.jpg)

FIG 6.04 He Chengyao, *Mama and Me*, 2001. Performance. Photography credit: Yan Yan. Courtesy of the artist.

*图6.04　何成瑶，《妈妈和我》，2001年。行为。摄影：Yan Yan。艺术家惠允。*


〔原书 226〕

Signing the Great Wall

签署长城


〔原书 226, 227〕

In the November 2001 graduation exhibition of work by students from her course in contemporary art at the Central Academy, He Chengyao included a recombination of images from her work of the previous spring and summer. The triptych, *Great Wall–Magnolia–Mama and Me* (figure 6.06), tied her spontaneous performance on the Great Wall to the previously invisible and unspoken history she documented in the series of photographs taken together with her mother. Bridging the gap is a photograph showing the top of a magnolia tree, whose delicate white buds open against a blue sky. This middle image has been rotated so that the tree branches reach across to link a narrative of personal recovery to an “excessive” public performance that elicited multiple interpretations in its aftermath. By drawing this connection, He Chengyao wrests the symbols of the Great Wall and the nude female figure away from their conventional signifying power. She also implicates herself in the recent history of the Great Wall as a transnational site for avant-garde art, ever since Andy Warhol first “opened” it in the early 1980s.

在2001年11月中央美院当代艺术课程毕业展上，何成瑶把此前春夏两季作品的图像重新组合。三联画《长城——玉兰——妈妈和我》（图6.06）把她自发的长城行为，与她跟母亲一起拍摄的系列照片中所记录的先前不可见、不可言说的历史联系起来。桥接两者的是一张玉兰树顶的照片，娇嫩的白花蕾在蓝天下绽放。中间这张图像被旋转，树枝伸向两侧，把个人康复叙事与一场引发多重解读的“过度”公开行为连接起来。通过画出这种联系，何成瑶把长城和裸体女性形象的符号从传统意指力量中夺走。她也把自己写入长城作为跨国先锋艺术场所的近期历史——自从安迪·沃霍尔在1980年代初首次“打开”它以来。


〔原书 227〕

Several Chinese artists told me that Andy Warhol had completed a characteristically playful and perceptive art performance on the Great Wall. After climbing the wall, he pulled out a piece of paper and drew a giant dollar sign: a sign for a sign. When I tried to confirm this account, I found it was almost true. In a documentary about his 1982 trip to China, Warhol draws the giant dollar sign and then signs it during a visit to a Chinese painter’s studio, exchanging it for the traditional ink painting presented to him.[^en-ch06-27] During shots of the Warhol entourage on their way to the Great Wall, the narrator’s voice announces, “Andy pointed out the Wall was the only man-made object visible from the moon with the naked eye, with the exception of the Los Angeles, California aqueduct.” On the Great Wall, Warhol answers a question about whether he thought people in China could relate to his art by mumbling, “Well, I gotta get into sign painting.” These comments, including the repetition of the apocryphal statement about what man-made structures can be seen from the moon, from the mouth of the pop master of replicable icons (capitalism’s Marilyn Monroe and communism’s Mao Zedong), point to the Great Wall as cultural sign par excellence.

几位中国艺术家告诉我，安迪·沃霍尔在长城上完成了一场典型顽皮而敏锐的艺术行为。爬上长城后，他拿出一张纸，画了一个巨大的美元符号：以一个符号交换另一个符号。当我试图核实这一说法时，发现它几乎是真的。在一部关于他1982年中国之行的纪录片中，沃霍尔造访一位中国画家的画室时画下巨大美元符号并签上名，用它交换对方赠送的传统水墨画。[^zh-ch06-27] 在沃霍尔随行人员前往长城的镜头中，旁白宣布：“安迪指出，长城是除加州洛杉矶输水渠之外，月球上肉眼唯一可见的人造物。”在长城上，有人问他是否认为中国人能理解他的艺术，他咕哝道：“嗯，我得去搞招牌画了。”这些评论——包括重复那个关于从月球可见什么人造结构的杜撰说法——出自这位可复制偶像（资本主义的玛丽莲·梦露和共产主义的毛泽东）的波普大师之口，指向作为典型文化符号的长城。


〔原书 227, 228, 229〕

Long after the Great Wall became militarily defunct, political leaders from Sun Yatsen to Deng Xiaoping revived it as a national symbol of China’s might and longevity as a civilization.[^en-ch06-28] In 1988, the 21st Century Group of experimental artists challenged this official symbolism with a performance on the wall that probed it as a site of wounded-ness. They wrapped their bodies and a section of the wall in white bandages.[^en-ch06-29] Two later large-scale art projects on the Great Wall explored a similar theme of memorializing wasted human life. In 1990, Xu Bing organized a crew of students and peasants to help him make ink rubbings from a thirty-meter-long section of the wall for *Ghosts Pounding the Wall*. Zheng Lianjie’s performance *Binding the Lost Souls* in 1993 involved gathering ten thousand broken stone bricks from fields at the foot of the wall. Participants carried them to the top, where they wrapped each one with a strip of red cloth. By the 1990s, the Great Wall became an ideal site for experimental art, especially performance art, because of its relative remove from the city. The unpredictability of performance art made it highly suspect in the eyes of state censors who often shut down exhibits that included performance of any type. When in 2000 three Chinese organizers initiated the First Open Art Platform Performance Art Festival, performances by Chinese, Japanese, and Finnish artists took place at the Juyong Gate of the Great Wall. The wall had become a veritable institution of Chinese avant-garde art.[^en-ch06-30]

长城在军事上失效很久后，从孙中山到邓小平的政治领袖把它复兴为中国文明力量与长寿的民族象征。[^zh-ch06-28] 1988年，21世纪实验艺术家小组在长城上实施行为，挑战这一官方象征，把它探询为一个创伤场所。他们用白绷带包裹身体和一段城墙。[^zh-ch06-29] 后来两个长城大型艺术项目探索了类似的纪念被浪费人类生命的主题。1990年，徐冰组织一群学生和农民，协助他从一段三十米长的城墙拓印，创作《鬼打墙》。1993年，郑连杰的行为《绑缚失落的灵魂》收集了城墙脚下田地里的一万块碎石砖。参与者把它们搬到墙顶，用红布条逐一包裹。到1990年代，长城成为实验艺术、尤其是行为艺术的理想场所，因为它相对远离城市。行为艺术的不可预测性使国家审查者高度怀疑它，他们常关闭任何包含行为艺术的展览。2000年，三位中国组织者发起第一届开放艺术平台行为艺术节，中国、日本和芬兰艺术家的行为在长城居庸关举行。长城已经成为名副其实的中国先锋艺术机构。[^zh-ch06-30]


〔原书 228〕

![*图6.05　何成瑶，《证词》，2001年。行为。摄影：Yan Yan。艺术家惠允。*](web/assets/ch06-b089.png)

FIG 6.05 He Chengyao, *Testimony*, 2001. Performance. Photography credit: Yan Yan. Courtesy of the artist.

*图6.05　何成瑶，《证词》，2001年。行为。摄影：Yan Yan。艺术家惠允。*


〔原书 228〕

![*图6.06　何成瑶，《长城——玉兰——妈妈和我》，2001年。行为三联画。摄影：田义斌、何成瑶、Yan Yan。艺术家惠允。*](web/assets/ch06-b090.jpg)

FIG 6.06 He Chengyao, *Great Wall–Magnolia–Mama and Me*, 2001. Performance triptych. Photography credit: Tian Yibin, He Chengyao, Yan Yan. Courtesy of the artist.

*图6.06　何成瑶，《长城——玉兰——妈妈和我》，2001年。行为三联画。摄影：田义斌、何成瑶、Yan Yan。艺术家惠允。*


〔原书 229〕

![*图6.07　何成瑶，《向马塞尔·杜尚致敬》，2001年。行为。摄影：洪磊。艺术家惠允。*](web/assets/ch06-b091.jpg)

FIG 6.07 He Chengyao, *With Respect to Marcel Duchamp*, 2001. Performance. Photography credit: Hong Lei. Courtesy of the artist.

*图6.07　何成瑶，《向马塞尔·杜尚致敬》，2001年。行为。摄影：洪磊。艺术家惠允。*


〔原书 229〕

With her half-nude body, He Chengyao took over the Great Wall as sign and made it her personal stage, stealing it and the media apparatus away from H. A. Schult, as well as Chinese male performance artists who throughout the 1980s and 1990s used the wall for works of political dissent and macho *liumang* testing of human limits.[^en-ch06-31] *Opening the Great Wall* represents an intersection of multiple image worlds: those of woman as national allegory, from Delacroix’s *Liberty Leading the People* to Mukhina’s *Woman and Collective Farm Worker* to the 1989 Goddess of Democracy amalgam; of Chinese artists and the Great Wall; of foreign artists and the Great Wall; and of feminist performance art. He Chengyao’s mimesis of a Chinese avant-garde already integrated into the political economy of the commodity-sign flaunts a nude torso as superfluous spectacle that garners media attention and angry commentary on how she has cheapened herself and art: “that’s not art.” Yet the mimetic performance of her mother’s transgressive behavior refers to the experience of suffering, the traumatic realism of being made into an expressionless sign, silenced of subjectivity.

何成瑶以半裸身体接管长城符号，把它变成个人舞台，从H. A. 舒尔特以及整个1980和1990年代利用长城进行政治异见作品和男子气概流氓式人体极限测试的中国男性行为艺术家那里，偷走了长城和媒体机器。[^zh-ch06-31] 《开放长城》代表多个图像世界的交汇：女人作为民族寓言的图像，从德拉克洛瓦《自由引导人民》到穆希娜《工人与集体农庄女庄员》，再到1989年民主女神混合体；中国艺术家与长城；外国艺术家与长城；以及女性主义行为艺术。何成瑶模仿已经整合进商品符号政治经济的中国先锋艺术，炫耀裸露的躯干作为多余奇观，引来媒体关注和愤怒评论，说她贬低了自己和艺术：“那不是艺术。”然而，她对母亲越轨行为的模仿行为指向受苦经验，指向被变成无表情符号、被剥夺主体性的创伤性现实主义。


〔原书 230〕

This real cannot be represented. It can only be repeated, reembodied only to be denied again. She reopens the wound of the sign.

这个真实无法被再现。它只能被重复，只能被重新赋形，然后再次被否认。她重新打开符号的伤口。


〔原书 230〕

Playing Chess with the Historical Avant-Garde

与历史先锋派下棋


〔原书 230〕

During 2001, as He Chengyao began exploring this personal history, she also embarked on a parallel set of photographed performance pieces. These experiments in embodied performance and photographic documentation enacted a chess game of sorts with two father figures of the Western historical avant-garde, Marcel Duchamp and Joseph Beuys. Through these exercises, she performs a mimesis of pivotal moments in their development of forms that sought to overthrow institutionalized notions of autonomous art. By literally inserting her body into the now canonical art history of the avant-garde, she acts on it in a mode of investigating the limitations of their critique, drawing particular attention to the Other occluded by universalized narratives of radical rupture.

2001年，何成瑶在开始探索这段个人历史的同时，也启动了一组平行的摄影行为作品。这些具身行为与摄影记录的实验，与西方历史先锋派的两位父亲人物——马塞尔·杜尚和约瑟夫·博伊斯——进行某种棋局。通过这些练习，她模仿他们发展那些试图推翻制度化自主艺术观念的形式的关键时刻。通过把自己的身体字面插入如今已成经典的先锋艺术史，她以一种考察其批判局限性的方式作用于它，特别关注被普遍化的激进断裂叙事遮蔽的他者。


〔原书 230, 231〕

Just after she had made a break from painting, He Chengyao turned to the work of Marcel Duchamp, specifically the transitional moment in 1912 when he began to depart from painting. With its single-frame reference to serial photography, *Nude Descending a Staircase, No. 2* blurs the difference between painting and mechanical reproduction. It outraged early audiences denied the enjoyment of consuming what Duchamp referred to as “retinal art” created to please the eye.[^en-ch06-32] In *With Respect to Marcel Duchamp* (figure 6.07), He Chengyao returns to this seminal moment in modern art and through continued serialization takes the game one step further. She performs the nude, becoming the body stripped for spectacular viewing, and with the aid of a long photographic exposure disappears into a blur. She staged this exercise in one of Beijing’s new private galleries, the China Art Archives and Warehouse, a joint project of European and Chinese artistic directors, the most famous being Ai Weiwei. This site, like others partially managed by foreign intermediaries, played an important role in integrating Chinese contemporary art with the international art market and in cultivating the idea of art as a liberating reversal of socialist art in service to the state. As these institutions took hold in China, He Chengyao returned to Duchamp’s deconstruction of gendered spectacularity. She engaged with the historical avant-garde not in a cynical or derivative way but in a way similar to a chess move that restructures the game’s meaning, its history, and anticipated future. She cites across time and space, not as attribution or homage, but to shift understandings of the world-making power of images.

刚脱离绘画时，何成瑶转向马塞尔·杜尚的作品，特别是1912年他开始离开绘画的过渡时刻。《下楼梯的裸体，第2号》以单帧参照连续摄影，模糊了绘画与机械复制之间的差异。它激怒了早期观众，使他们无法享受消费杜尚所谓为取悦眼睛而创作的“视网膜艺术”。[^zh-ch06-32] 在《向马塞尔·杜尚致敬》（图6.07）中，何成瑶回到现代艺术的这一开创时刻，通过继续系列化把游戏推进一步。她表演裸体，成为为奇观观看而剥光的身体，并借助长曝光消失在模糊中。她在北京一家新私人画廊——中国艺术文件仓库——实施这一练习；该机构由欧洲和中国艺术总监共同主持，最著名的是艾未未。这个场所以及其他部分由外国中介管理的场所，在把中国当代艺术整合进国际艺术市场、培育艺术作为对服务于国家的社会主义艺术的解放性颠倒这一观念方面，发挥了重要作用。随着这些机构在中国立足，何成瑶回到杜尚对性别化奇观的解构。她与历史先锋派的接触不是犬儒或派生的，而类似一步重新构造游戏意义、历史和预期未来的棋。她跨时空引用，不是为了注明出处或致敬，而是为了转移对图像创造世界力量的理解。


〔原书 231〕

![*图6.08　何成瑶，《以马塞尔·杜尚为对手》，2001年。行为。摄影：Han Lei。艺术家惠允。*](web/assets/ch06-b097.jpg)

FIG 6.08 He Chengyao, *With Marcel Duchamp as My Opponent*, 2001. Performance. Photography credit: Han Lei. Courtesy of the artist.

*图6.08　何成瑶，《以马塞尔·杜尚为对手》，2001年。行为。摄影：Han Lei。艺术家惠允。*


〔原书 231〕

In 1963, five years before Marcel Duchamp’s death, the Pasadena Art Museum held a retrospective of his work. Los Angeles photographer Julian Wasser arranged for a photo shoot of the artist at the museum and came up with the idea of photographing Duchamp playing chess with a nude woman, an art student who agreed to participate.[^en-ch06-33] Duchamp cooperated and played several games with the student at a table set up in front of his work titled *The Bride Stripped Bare by Her Bachelors, Even*. While critics have argued for a nuanced deconstruction of gender relationality in Duchamp’s work, these notorious photographs by Wasser demonstrate the function of the authorial Duchamp as “Dada’s Daddy,” trumping at chess his bride stripped bare.[^en-ch06-34] He Chengyao’s *With Marcel Duchamp as My Opponent* (figure 6.08) returns not just to the art of Duchamp, but to the media spectacle of Duchamp. She sits half-nude at a table in her apartment playing against an absent opponent. By reference to a historical photograph, she invokes a clothed, male, Western presence who does not yet recognize her, and she challenges him not only to his beloved game of chess but also to the Chinese game of go.

1963年，马塞尔·杜尚去世五年前，帕萨迪纳艺术博物馆举办了他的回顾展。洛杉矶摄影师朱利安·瓦塞尔安排艺术家在博物馆拍照，想出让杜尚与一名裸体女人下棋的主意；那是一位同意参与的艺术学生。[^zh-ch06-33] 杜尚配合，在作品《被单身汉剥光的新娘，甚至》前摆设的桌旁与学生下了几盘棋。尽管批评者论证杜尚作品对性别关系有细致解构，瓦塞尔这些臭名昭著的照片显示，作为作者的杜尚功能如同“达达之父”，在棋局中击败被剥光的新娘。[^zh-ch06-34] 何成瑶的《以马塞尔·杜尚为对手》（图6.08）不仅回到杜尚的艺术，也回到杜尚的媒体奇观。她半裸坐在公寓桌旁，与一个缺席的对手下棋。通过参照一张历史照片，她召唤一个尚不承认她的、着衣的男性西方在场者，并向他发起挑战，不仅要下他钟爱的国际象棋，也要下中国围棋。


〔原书 231, 232〕

He Chengyao then moved on to Joseph Beuys, declaring adherence to his belief that “art heals wounds,” and performed a personal reworking of one of his spontaneous “actions.” In a 1964 festival of Fluxus artists held at the Technical College Aachen in Germany, Beuys performed a piece that angered several audience members to the point that they stormed the stage.
